In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized cancer tissue samples. Our specific application involved classifying images of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, and we simulated a FL environment using a dataset of histopathological images. Compared to a centralised learning approach, we found that federated learning yielded similar accuracy results, but with the added benefit of security and data protection. However, the FL approach did come at a cost of increased computational complexity and communication costs, particularly when using a large number of clients. Despite these challenges, we believe that federated learning holds promise for collaborative medical image analysis, particularly in applications where data privacy and confidentiality are a top priority. Our code is openly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/alexandre1989/fl_til.

Recently, a more efficient approach to controlling quadrupedal robots has been developed through reinforcement learning (RL). This method can automatically generate skill-specific controllers without manual input, which is particularly beneficial given the complexity of nonlinear dynamics involved. However, RL struggles with reward sparsity and quadrupedal robots' challenging dynamics, such as maintaining balance on a balance beam. Our novel RL-based approach incorporates an adaptive generator to create diverse and efficient motion patterns for the given tasks. This generator, based on an evolutionary algorithm, is trained independently from RL and can produce an endless stream of motion. This way, RL can focus on optimizing the generated motion rather than being constrained by a pre-defined discrete motion search space. We have successfully applied this method to control a quadrupedal robot to navigate a balance beam and showcase its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, our method demonstrates greater policy stability and faster training convergence. With this adaptive generator, RL can develop a seamless and efficient control system for a wide range of tasks in complex and diverse environments. The developed policy can also transfer well to similar tasks and demonstrate consistent performance in different conditions. This groundbreaking approach has opened up the possibility for RL to adapt and optimize generative models, thereby significantly expanding its applicability to tasks in dynamic environments. The source code for this research has been made available at https://github.com/Arjun-Ren/RL-TrajGen. The video of our quadrupedal robot navigating a balance beam can be found at https://youtu.be/z4H3U3UH5_g. The video of our robot performing a range of tasks including crawling, jumping, and carrying a box can be found at https://youtu.be/1k7p7tTj3M. Closed-loop system performance can decline over time due to plant characteristic changes, necessitating controller redesign without complex modeling processes often associated with such systems. Fortunately, reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to optimizing model-free nonlinear controller designs without extensive system modeling. Despite the efficiency of this method, its reliance on numerous trial-and-error experiments can degrade plant quality and necessitate frequent maintenance. In order to mitigate this limitation, a proposed model-free, two-step design approach aims to improve the efficiency and adaptability of reinforcement learning designs. The initial step involves an offline estimation of plant parameters using a dynamic system model and the second step involves the implementation of a reinforcement learning control (RLC) technique. The proposed two-step approach was successfully tested on a nonlinear flight control system and compared to other control methods, demonstrating improved performance and a more suitable balance between these competing objectives. The proposed method was able to reduce the number of experimental trials by as much as 65% with only a minor loss in performance. The results further showed that the estimated plant parameters were accurate enough to facilitate successful model-based RLC designs, confirming the efficacy of this approach. A step-by-step construction method is developed to formulate a simplified dynamical equation for a two-dimensional active nematic's direction, describing its behavior outside of equilibrium with a particular linear progression. This equation incorporates fluctuations that arise from molecular movement in the direction of the nematic, as well as directional and planar stress in the system. Using a dynamic renormalization technique, it is demonstrated that the nematic's direction exhibits tumbling motion that is damped and diffuses at a rate proportional to wave vectors' squared magnitude. This research also explores the impact of three key factors - nematic's directional flexibility, binary interactions' strength, and layer confinement effects - on this dynamics. Ultimately, it is found through renormalization that the nematic's direction exhibits a specific type of instability known as the Euler collinear instability in two-dimensional active nematics. Furthermore, it is found that this instability may potentially be suppressed by coupling within flexural modes in nematics confined to extremely thin layers. Developing models from source code necessitates access to an abundance of labeled information. However, trained models are frequently specialized in a task-specific manner, which undermines their transferability to other tasks. This study presents novel pre-training strategies, complemented by a graph-based code representation, enabling a versatile model to be developed using vast amounts of unlabeled code. Our proposed technique necessitates neither extensive program segmentation nor semantic parsing. Instead, it relies on a code representation capable of capturing vital program attributes and a novel pre-training objective, enabling a proficient code analyzer to be trained. Our results demonstrate that this model, pre-trained on unannotated open-source code, matches the performance of similarly trained models pre-trained on manually written unit tests, a significantly more resource-intensive endeavor. Additionally, this model surpasses previously groundbreaking code completion methods in a transformer architecture. Our source code is accessible at https://github.com/grasp-aidl/kcma. Experimental evidence suggests that the proposed representation and pre-training objectives facilitate a deep comprehension of program semantics. To validate this, we conducted simple program verification experiments, yielding success rates of 76.8% for detecting off-target modifications and 27.4% for detecting non-functional changes. These outcomes position our model as an emergent code understanding model, surpassing existing program analysis models in a transformer architecture for forecasting code. Our model also excels in generating code based on natural language instructions, a code modification task. Specifically, our model outperforms Min-Char, the top-performing model in a transformer architecture for code generation, by 7.2 and 18.2 percentage points in exact match and edit distance, respectively. By incorporating the forward-backward algorithm and the extrapolation technique from Anderson acceleration, we develop a globally convergent solution that outperforms existing methods. The advantages and limitations of multicast beamforming for millimeter-wave systems have received little attention in the design of hybrid precoders. To fill this gap, we develop the first integrated design of analog transmit precoders and digital receive combiners for multicasting in mmWave systems with multiple antennas at both the transmitter and receiver. By combining semidefinite relaxation and Cholesky decomposition, we sequentially optimize and maximize the effective throughput of the system. Analytical calculations of the complex analog precoder phases are also provided to facilitate a faster, iterative solution. Our numerical results demonstrate the substantial increase in throughput that can be achieved using our hybrid precoder design, which significantly outperforms conventional systems and approaches optimal performance at relatively low signal strengths. Additionally, our findings show that analog precoder phases converge rapidly, with the rates of convergence dependent on the strength of the signals. These properties enable the use of simpler, analog-only precoder designs at lower signal strengths. Our results are confirmed by further simulations that show our design yields considerable performance improvements, particularly at lower signal strengths. These simulations also reveal the influence of transmitter and receiver antennas on system performance. Notably, the use of fewer analog transmit precoders yields greater performance improvements when there are fewer antennas at the transmitter. This phenomenon highlights the potential of mmWave technology to be a valuable component in the development of future wireless systems. Crucially, however, further research is needed to fully understand the interactions between system scales and designs. This challenge could be approached by drawing on knowledge from device development. Specifically, the properties of mmWave radios, such as their limited bandwidth and directional transmission, could be leveraged to identify key design principles and encourage the use of multicasting in scalable, efficient mmWave systems. The potential benefits of such designs include reduced latency and increased throughput per unit area, which could be crucial for the next generation of wireless systems. These improvements could be particularly important in areas like emergency response and self-driving cars, where mmWave technology may play a vital role in ensuring public safety. The development of scalable, efficient mmWave systems also has the potential to revolutionize industries like cloud computing and remote surgery, which may require rapid and reliable multicasting of data in the future. The technical approach used here, which combined tools from information and communication technology with advanced mathematical techniques, may also contribute to the development of innovative radio frequency components and circuit designs. Federated Learning adoption has been hindered by communication challenges. A new Federated Learning paradigm, Federated Distillation, has been developed with distinct communication properties. In contrast to conventional Federated Adaptive Distillation, which enhances model adaptation with distillation, our focus lies on the data aggregation method in Federated Distillation. This study investigates the separation of model and distillation learning processes, leading to a more efficient communication protocol that is less sensitive to latency and data transmission issues. Specifically, it explores a novel aggregation technique within Federated Distillation and proposes a communication procedure called Label Embedding, which significantly reduces data transfer volume by multiple orders of magnitude. By combining these efficiencies, a significant reduction in communication rounds is achieved, with comparable accuracy performance. Our approach demonstrates superior communication efficiency while maintaining high accuracy performance, paving the way for practical applications in complex models and high-resource data sets. Experimental results show that Federated Distillation can achieve the same level of accuracy as standalone training, but with much faster convergence and much reduced communication data volume, representing a 97% reduction in transmission volume while only slightly increasing test accuracy. Additionally, a significant reduction (up to 8x) in communication latency can be observed with little to no performance loss. These efficiencies indicate that precision can remain unchanged even with very limited communication. Such efficiencies could prove beneficial in various other ML applications. The proposed Pseudo Distillation label embedding technique employed in this study is found to produce results comparable to previously established techniques, also yielding reduced data transfer volume and transmission volume observations. The findings reveal that pseudolabels can effectively replace true labels in certain scenarios, thereby facilitating model convergence without requiring actual label transmission from the clients to the server. The presented techniques demonstrate superior performance over existing FL models, also showing that the FL model parameters can remain unchanged for extended periods, thereby necessitating manual code modifications to implement the proposed techniques. The code for FD and PDE can be jointly accessed at the provided address. The current approach does, however, experience performance degradation when dealing with nonconvex problems, particularly when dealing with models possessing many parameters. Future research directions are also presented, including the extension of FD to encompass a variety of other FL paradigms, such as FL with generated data, Federated Learning with generated models, and FL with generated data and models. The work may also be extended to encompass a joint hardware and software design approach for FL. The possible mechanisms for achieving this are also presented. The study also reveals that the FL community lacks existing literature on practical Federated Learning implementations

A key feature of Named Data Networking (NDN) is its ability to support future-proof services on large networks of interconnected computers. Our study examines how to effectively manage the flow of service requests across an NDN-based network, considering the varying capabilities of each node to process and generate data. Focusing on service workflows with connected components, we develop an algorithm for online, distributed control of each node's decision-making processes. Our proposed Service Discovery Assisted Dynamic Orchestration (SDADO) method aims to achieve lower overall delays and optimal data transmission rates. It combines queuing strategies and routing discipline based on topology, using network information acquired through a new discovery approach, allowing for efficient performance under uncertain conditions. We validate SDADO with analytical models and numerical simulations demonstrating reduced end-to-end delays and optimal data transmission rates. Furthermore, our findings confirm the significant impact of varying node capabilities on system performance. Our work through simulation reveals a performance improvement in delay and data transmission rate for a range of workflow sizes, particularly in networks with dispersed capabilities and large workflow scales. However, data transmission rates show minimal dependence on node capabilities and workflow size, and remain optimal under any capability distribution. Conversely, end-to-end delays are shortest and data transmission rates are optimal in highly centralized networks. Our research contributes to the understanding of managing cloud services and computing systems over NDN networks through distributive, dynamic control mechanisms. These mechanisms use previously established models for future studies and optimizations. In particular, our findings suggest the importance of considering the capabilities and data transmission limits of each node in distributed decision-making processes. Future works can build upon our research by exploring the economic implications of supporting service workflows in NDN networks. Additionally, we propose future studies on evaluating the resilience of NDN-based service networks using quantitative performance metrics. Such studies can lead to the development of robust and efficient models for online control and distributed decision-making processes. Furthermore, we can investigate whether capabilities can be inferred or learned from network behavior, and how to effectively implement and verify the efficiency of service orchestration systems. These research directions can further contribute to the fundamental knowledge on supporting service workflows in NDN networks. Meanwhile, our proved SDADO method remains an efficient and dynamic model for online control and distributed decision-making processes. Moreover, we confirmed through simulation the potential performance improvement in delay and data transmission rate for a range of workflow sizes in NDN networks. These findings can provide practical values to system designers and administrators in the NDN domain. Finally, our work remains relevant to the research community due to the growing adoption of NDN

The conventional approach in multi-objective optimization assumes a pre-defined utility function, or it's learned through interactive feedback or a complete Pareto front determination. However, defining a utility function can be challenging in real-world problems due to the implicit, explicit, or unexpressed nature of user preferences. Interactive learning methods demand extensive user input over time. Comprehensive multi-objective optimization results including all Pareto optimal solutions aren't feasible due to the exponential explosion of such a dataset and the difficulty of their interpretation. This work develops an efficient utility function learning method that incorporates prior knowledge to minimize the need for user input while training. This method is particularly effective when explicit or implicit user preferences are represented as mathematical expressions. Using prior knowledge such as upper and lower bounds for each objective function helps reduce the search space and quickly recovers optimal performance once user input is received. Our proposed approach is evaluated through experiments involving sample problems including a bi-objective optimization problem formulated as a pareto-front discovery task and two real-world problems involving the field of materials science. The advent of online collaboration tools like GitHub has made it easy for software developers to share and reuse code across various repositories, often employing clone-and-own or forking techniques. These practices not only facilitate the reuse of existing code but also enable the creation of multiple, variant versions of the same software, which can provide multiple benefits. However, maintaining such diversity of software variants is a labor-intensive task, especially when the number of repositories grows large. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach called meta-maintenance, which involves identifying multiple connected repositories related to a single shared code base and developing effective strategies to maintain and evolve all of these repositories simultaneously. To test the feasibility of this approach, we conducted a study of Open Source software repositories on GitHub, which showed that a significant portion of GitHub developers are engaged in maintaining software variants of this type and that meta-maintenance could save a developer up to 40% of their maintenance workloads. Furthermore, exploring the conceptual connections between software maintenance tasks might hold the key to further increasing the efficiency of meta-maintenance. Based on these findings, we discuss the implications of meta-maintenance for the fields of software maintenance, interaction design, and online collaboration. Ultimately, we envision meta-maintenance as a powerful tool for empowering a new class of GitHub developers - the'meta-maintenance developers' - who could use their expertise to increase the efficiency of maintenance tasks across a wide range of repositories. To support this vision, we provide a detailed description of the meta-maintenance developer's role and present a practical action plan for realizing this role in practice. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we also include a comprehensive prototype implementation of our meta-maintenance method, along with a set of accompanying technical tools and resources. This prototype shows how meta-maintenance could be successfully applied in a real-world setting of software maintenance tasks. These technical details are available in a companion document. To conclude, our study offers a new perspective on software maintenance that could contribute to the development of more efficient interaction designs for GitHub and other online collaboration platforms, as well as new approaches to empirical software research that focus on the analytical examination of shared code bases and their maintenance tasks. We believe that presenting this new perspective - which comes from an in-depth empirical study of GitHub developers and their maintenance tasks - could facilitate future research in this area. To support this, we present a research agenda that includes key questions and topics for further investigation. This research agenda is documented in a companion paper. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we also include a prototype implementation

This paper primarily addresses the Yamabe flow's behavior on a compact manifold with a specific type of Riemannian metric and nonzero scalar curvature. We demonstrate that when the scalar curvature's sign and a certain geometric characteristic do not align, the Yamabe flow's solution will either lack or have weak solutions. Furthermore, drawing inspiration from Struwe's work on the mean curvature flow, we establish that under these conditions, the flow will either not have or have weak solutions with one endpoint in $L^{\frac{2}{1-p}}$. We show that when the initial data are members of a specific class, the solution will converge to a Ricci flat metric, which is consistent with Kahler convergence theory's predictions. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-source single-target and multi-source single-target approaches have been the main strategies used in cross-domain recommendation, with most of them focusing on addressing data sparsity within a single target dataset. However, these methods overlook the potential of discovering multi-conditional relationships across multiple target datasets. To address this gap, we introduce a new paradigm called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR), which enables multi-source and multi-target recommendation in tandem. In this paradigm, we leverage the shared information between multiple donor datasets to enhance the recommendation quality in multiple receiver datasets. To achieve this, we propose a novel Enhanced Comprehensive Aspect Preference Learning (ECAP) technique that models the latent factor as a multi-aspect representation and learns their inter-relationships across multiple donor datasets. Furthermore, our ECAP has an adaptive enhancement module that allows for a dynamic adjustment of the comprehensive aspect preference in an online manner. Through theoretical analysis and proof, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our ECAP. Experimental evaluations conducted on real-world datasets validate the efficacy of our ECAP-based MSDCR paradigm, which outperforms separate and combined implementations of single-target and multi-target approaches through a comprehensive aspect preference. The source code is available at: https://github.com/jaemnong/ECAP. MSDCR could be valuable for handling data sparsity in the context of cross-domain recommendation. In a donor-acceptor setting, our ECAP-based MSDCR paradigm offers a novel approach for tackling data sparsity across multiple target datasets. It has the potential to be applied in various industries including e-commerce, where recommendation systems are widely employed. From a theoretical perspective, our ECAP provides insights into learning the latent structure of preference data through joint aspect embedding and comprehensive aspect preference. These aspects can contribute to the body of existing recommender systems research and influence future development in cross-domain recommendation and data sparsity mitigation. In particular, our ECAP can be utilized to enhance the understanding and analysis of user behavior in online shopping, which is particularly crucial for converting users into loyal customers. The effectiveness of our ECAP is attributed to the comprehensive aspect preference learned through the donor datasets, which facilitates improved generalization and targeting in the receiver datasets. To investigate the transportation and yield production of the $J/\psi$, $\psi(2S)$, $\eta_c$, and $\chi_c$ charmonium states as well as the $B_c$ state in a hot and evolving quark-gluon plasma at the LHC, we utilize the Boltzmann-Venuel equation approach and leverage the color-pure transport model for the simulation. The results obtained suggest that the behavior of bound states follows a characteristic trend observed in previous studies, whereas the $B_c$ meson exhibits unique transport dynamics influenced by a longer dissociation rate and a slower recombination rate compared to charmonium states. Consequently, the $B_c$ distribution is predominantly suppressed, leading to a significantly reduced yield of $B_c$ mesons, with the $B_c$ branching ratio for $B_c \to J/\psi p$ being much lower than that of $X(3872) \to J/\psi \pi^+$ under similar conditions. The $X(3872)$ also displays unique characteristics stemming from its putative $\psi(2S)$ and $J/\psi$ molecular components, resulting in distinct behavior across various temperatures. The simulation further indicates that $X(3872)$ survival rates decrease significantly at higher temperatures, especially when the medium-induced dissociation rate exceeds 5/8 GeV$^2$ at a 10 times stronger magnitude than that of $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$. The resulting $X(3872)$ yield production is predominantly attributed to its $\psi(2S)$ component, with contributions from the $J/\psi$ molecular component diminishing rapidly as temperature increases. Notably, we also investigated the transport dynamics of the $X(3872)$ in a medium at a temperature of 100 MeV, focusing on its unique characteristics and the effects of the vector and radial decay modes on its behavior. We discovered that the $X(3872)$ distribution is mainly influenced by the radial decay mode in this condition, with mixing leading to distinct behavior among the different $X(3872)$ components. Moreover, we obtained $X(3872)$ yield production results that are in line with LHC observations. The occurrence of local moments is a common feature in many disordered materials and unsaturated transition metals. This phenomenon can be understood through different models, which however show a significant difference in the nature of the disorder-induced correlation. Specifically, the Anderson insulator model leads to a weak and power-law decaying correlation, whereas the Hubbard model in the presence of disorder and double occupancy repulsion results in a strong and power-law decaying correlation. Studying the interplay between these two effects in a one-dimensional Hubbard chain with quasicontinuous site disorder, using a numerical cluster density matrix renormalization group approach, we found that the strength of the repulsive double occupancy potential significantly influences the nature of the disorder-induced correlation. In the absence of double occupancy repulsion, the correlation is weak and power-law decaying, whereas an adequate double occupancy repulsion leads to a strong and power-law decaying correlation, akin to the random singlet state observed in non-interacting systems. Moreover, the location of the system within the phase diagram, distinguishing between an insulating phase at half filling and a metallic phase at half filling, coincides with the boundary separating the weak and strong correlation regimes. Our findings have important implications in understanding the properties of certain materials, particularly when considering the effects of chemical disorder in systems with interactions. Additionally, these results may contribute to the development of a theoretical model describing the properties of the Kondo insulator samarium hexafluorosulfate. A comparison with the results obtained from different numerical approaches, as well as an analytical approximation based on a small cluster model, is provided, and the relevant results are discussed. Furthermore, we explore the effect of long-range bond disorder on the phase diagram and the nature of the correlation, and our results are also connected to the properties of the system when subjected to a magnetic field. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the properties of a one-dimensional Hubbard chain under disorder and the influence of the double occupancy potential, and the resulting phase diagram is presented in a comprehensive manner. Additionally, we obtained the critical exponent of the correlation length using different numerical methods and found that the results agree within the numerical precision. Our study offers a thorough explanation of the role of interaction in the system when subjected to disorder, and the corresponding phase diagram is presented in a clear and concise manner. Robots that learn from observations in real-world environments using inverse reinforcement learning can face obstacles when experts' demonstrations are marred by extraneous data from their surroundings. This unwanted information is usually eliminated in controlled settings, but when impossible, it needs to be filtered out. However, tracking down the source of this extraneous data is a challenging task, especially with large amounts of data involved. A new approach utilizes a hierarchical Bayesian model to analyze both expert and extraneous data, effectively acknowledging the diverse range of observations a robot may encounter. Building upon an existing algorithm, it extends to handle a variety of observations, including partial occlusion and extraneous data, distinct from its original context of controlled settings. Our model outperforms current methods in a simulated environment inspired by industrial sorting tasks. This method promotes the discovery of key actions directly from observations, reducing reliance on ground-truth rewards and action labels. As a result, it opens the door for a broad range of learning tasks beyond its initial application in inverse reinforcement learning. Although developed for a specific case, its concepts can be adapted to various contexts, such as learning policies, abstracting action spaces, or uncovering hidden factors in data. Additionally, integrating this method with maximum entropy techniques, as well as utilizing state and action features, further enhances its capabilities and flexibility. A crucial aspect of our model involves utilizing expert data to localize relevant information in a distribution over possible states and actions, effectively identifying key data while filtering out noise. This is accomplished through a novel prior distribution designed to filter out extraneous data, followed by using the resulting optimized distribution to generate a reward function. Our model consists of two interconnected layers: the first analyzes observations while incorporating a prior distribution adapted for inverse reinforcement learning, and the second generates a distribution over possible states and actions. As an alternative to deep neural networks, our model leverages two Bayesian networks to mimic this behavior. We introduce a multi-phased deep reinforcement learning strategy to overcome control issues in complex scenarios. The standard application of deep reinforcement learning, though efficient in handling high-dimensional control problems, faces limitations in dealing with problems possessing specific properties such as irregular rewards or dynamic sensitivities. To address this limitation, our approach divides the problem into two distinct phases - planning and imitation - to effectively tackle these control issues. The planning stage involves determining an achievable and safe action plan using predicted measurements, followed by an imitation stage where an optimized policy is generated by learning from the previous planning stage's experiences. The implementation of a deep actor-critic algorithm during the imitation stage proves particularly beneficial in learning diverse and dynamic action policies. The proposed method is successfully tested on two representative control problems in aerospace and automation, demonstrating its capability in solving control issues effectively. The results show that our approach outperforms established planning and control techniques, achieving notable improvements in convergence speed (up to 1000x), computation time (up to 100x longer), and overall performance (up to 30% better). The induced diversity in our approach's actions is also found to be advantageous. The developed method is designated as Diversity First Deep Reinforcement Learning (DfDRL), with its Python code available on GitHub for easy integration into existing Deep RL projects. The DfDRL approach is believed to offer numerous benefits across a wide range of complex control systems. To enhance scalability, our approach can easily integrate existing model predictive control methods for problems with known dynamics, leveraging system parameters and characteristics to inform planning and imitation decisions. The performance of DfDRL can further be refined by incorporating other safe reinforcement learning techniques that leverage regularized policies and risk-averse Q-learning. The applicability of DfDRL is extensive, spanning use cases such as quadcopters, aerial vehicles, and other domains that present complex control challenges. The approach demonstrates a promising future potential in safely navigating a wide range of difficult control environments. The associated assets are available on a GitHub repository under the following link: https://github.com/achilamb/DiversityFirstDRL. To accomplish this, it incorporates two main processes for growing central black holes within high-redshift galaxy precursors that produce abundant star formation. These mechanisms involve the movement of smaller stellar-mass black holes towards a central area through gaseous friction, resulting in a substantial black hole seed with a mass of $10^{3-5}$ solar masses in a relatively short timeframe. This paper introduces a unified solution designed specifically for data-driven investigators working individually or in small groups. Our electronic lab journal is generated automatically from experimental notes and files, subsequently displayed on a website powered by Django. By seamlessly gathering metadata, this system minimizes manual documentation for laboratory staff and prevents errors commonly associated with entering repetitive metadata manually. Moreover, due to its reliance on extensively documented open-source libraries, users can efficiently tailor the electronic lab journal software to their requirements. Our electronic lab journal incorporates a range of innovative features, including advanced search capabilities, a dynamic search engine interface, and a user-friendly interface for effortlessly navigating historical data. We outline the technical groundwork for our electronic lab journal, highlighting both the benefits and challenges associated with utilizing this platform. Ultimately, we present our lab journal as a versatile solution capable of meeting the distinct data management needs of users within small research teams. Due to its adaptable nature, this lab journal can be tailored to accommodate various laboratory requirements. High-entropy alloys, prized for their remarkable strength and flexibility in their composition, are gaining significant attention due to the unexplored possibilities they present. Lastly, this review will discuss ongoing difficulties and suggest future research directions, including quantifying uncertainties and using AI to guide inverse materials design. The measure of a vector-valued function's nonlinearity is essentially its deviation from affine functions. Researchers have proposed and refined hypotheses about a specific bound for this nonlinearity; Liu, Mesnager, and Chen initially proposed a general upper limit in 2017, which Carlet later supplemented with a lower bound using differential uniformity as a reference point. Our research refines this existing lower bound using straightforward methodology based on properties of APN functions. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of Sidon sets within elementary abelian 2-groups, and also examines larger sets derived from the Fisher's and Golomb's sequences, all while contributing to the ongoing partial results table and updating known nonlinearity records for several vector-based Boolean functions. 

Additionally, our research establishes that certain elementary Sidon sets are comprised entirely of regular $n$-gons, and also identifies a family of vector-based Boolean functions with the differential uniformity of $d=2$ and nonlinearity exceeding $2^{n-1} - 2$. Our study also yields further insights into the nature of Sidon sets and their relation to the Burrowes-Cohen conjecture. We verify the conjecture for $n \leq 12$ and present partial results for higher values of $n$. 

Lastly, our research discloses a family of vector-based Boolean functions with nonlinearity exceeding $2^{n-1} - 2$ and degree $3$. This finding marks the first instance of such a function existing within a finite field. Our research also illustrates how degree-$3$ APN structures can be utilized to create highly non-linear vector-based Boolean functions. 

Our thesis also offers strategic suggestions to further explore and refine the nonlinearity's upper and lower bounds. Specifically, we provide guidance on identifying degree-$3$ Elementary Sidon sets and examining the properties of the Fisher-Golomb sequences. These suggestions have the potential to further advance the nonlinearity's lower bound in the future.

This approach allows us to provide a clear and direct proof for the nonlinearity's lower bound without utilizing more complex tools often used in similar research papers.

We build on existing research by Sun and Kechris-Quorning to demonstrate that for any acylindrically hyperbolic group G, it is possible to create a probability-measure-preserving action, G acting on (X, mu), which has faithfulness but is neither essentially free. This implies G can be associated with a weakly mixing non-trivial, faithful invariant random subgroup. Additionally, it is proven that non-elementary hyperbolic groups possess a characteristic random subgroup sharing the same properties. It is also established that certain groups, such as free groups and surface groups, have a characteristic random subgroup that is virtually nilpotent, thereby providing a interpretation of a prior result by Hinton. We further show that it is possible under certain assumptions for a group to possess a characteristic random subgroup that is abelian, and provide an example of a group, along with its characteristic random subgroup, that is non-abelian. Finally, it is demonstrated that the existence of a characteristic random subgroup for a group with a certain probabilistic characteristic is dependent on a certain group theory parameter, and that this characteristic is present in non-virtual torsion groups. The work relies on established research as well as basic probability theory, and provides a new perspective on research by Sun and research by Kechris-Quorning. The writeup includes additional examples and analysis not present in the original paper. It also addresses questions posed by Hinton and provides further speculation. The faithfulness but non-essentially free actions described can have implications in various fields including topology, dynamics, and probability theory. The action of G on X can potentially be used to study the properties of G using methods from these fields. There's an underlying assumption that quantization also improves model generalizability, however this theory hasn't been formally explored. This study treats binary weights as stochastic random variables under rounding, and analyzes distribution propagation through the neural network's layers. The observed structure within the eigenvalues of the QNTK significantly resembles that of the traditional neural tangent kernel (NTK), particularly in the convergence of the eigenvalue distributions as the network size increases. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane, bounded by stochastic loops, which can be coupled with Gaussian free fields under specific boundary conditions. Specifically, they demonstrated that the field is related to the derivative of a logarithmic potential on the imaginary surface given by the collective pairwise interactions of points in the subdomains. Subsequent work by Rhodin established the link between Gaussian free fields and the Kostlan partition function in random matrix theory, resulting in multiple realizations of imaginary surfaces that could be paired with these fields. Given that SLE is known to be a probabilistic model that generates self-avoiding paths in the complex plane, Rhodin also showed that the local times of the fields can be transformed into multiple competing Stochastic Log-Gases driven by multiple realizations of the fields. More recently, Gipps developed a direct proof that the Dolganov-Margulis framework, which uses the statistical mechanics of the Stochastic Log-Gases, can be applied to imaginary surfaces coupled with Gaussian free fields. This current work relies on the connection between the local times of the fields, the discrete Gaussian free field, and the Schramm-Loewner evolution, establishing a direct relationship between the logarithmic potentials on the imaginary surfaces and the BKP hierarchy. Specifically, it demonstrates that the discrete Gaussian free field is linked to the negative potential of a unique solution to the BKP hierarchy, while the negative potential of a unique solution to the BKP hierarchy is related to the discrete Gaussian free field. Furthermore, it shows that the imaginary surfaces can be indexed by points in the upper half-plane, resulting in a domain that is coupled with a Gaussian free field under specific boundary conditions, a relationship that is driven by the statistical mechanics of the Stochastic Log-Gases. Finally, it is worth noting that the imaginary surfaces, which are coupled with Gaussian free fields under specific boundary conditions, have been proven to converge to the Fermionic Lagrangian in the random matrix theory as the number of points in the subdomains increases. A more detailed description of the results and their underlying assumptions can be found in the main text of this current work. A brief overview of the necessary background information in random matrix theory and the Dolganov-Margulis framework can also be found in the appendices of this current work. Additionally, a brief summary of the results can be found in arXiv:2110.07857. Several related works are ongoing and will be presented at upcoming mathematical conferences.

Researchers in neuroscience hypothesize the brain utilizes diverse coordinate systems, such as body-centric, world-based, and others, to represent 3D environments. Conversely, advancements in reinforcement learning present a novel approach that might serve as a more plausible model for spatial perception and navigation in biology. Focusing on reinforcement learning methods that encourage agents to achieve target images, we examine representations learned within this framework and compare them to those discovered through neuroscientific research. Our analysis suggests the representations learned within this framework are not fixed and can dramatically change when the learning objective is modified. This finding's association with neuroplasticity supports the idea that the brain's spatial representation mechanisms could be similarly dynamic. Furthermore, the representations learned within this framework exhibit a singular, consistent feature - the incorporation of predictive cues. We propose this aspect of these representations may mirror a universal characteristic of spatial representations across various tasks and domains, including those investigated through neuroscientific research. Our work offers initial evidence that reinforcement learning can provide a novel and innovative perspective on spatial representation mechanisms, which could lead to new insights in neurobiology. These insights might lead to the development of more effective, human-like AI methods. Furthermore, examining these representations provides a novel, reverse perspective on data that might facilitate new understandings of biological representation systems. We suggest a two-way approach, incorporating knowledge from neuroscience to improve AI models, while also utilizing AI models to shed new light on biological mechanisms and our understanding of them. By exchanging concepts and ideas between these two domains, we can foster cross-pollination and advance our knowledge of both spatial representation and reinforcement learning. In systems with electronic flat bands, quantum properties such as superconductivity, magnetism, and topological orders are frequently encountered.  Although the existence of flat bands is established in certain structures with geometric frustration like the kagome lattice, flat-band induced correlation effects are rarely observed in such systems, especially when they contain multiple atomic orbits.  Recently, research has found that a non-magnetic Kagome metal compound, consisting of Vanadium, Tin, and Iron, exhibits an unusual, flat-band-driven magnetism that can be controlled.  By applying external magnetic fields, it is possible to transition between two distinct ferromagnetic states corresponding to different fillings of the atomic shells.  Notably, the change between these states is characterized by a significant decrease in electrical resistance.  To explain this phenomenon, it must be noted that the response to external magnetic fields is highly sensitive to the changes in the magnetic configurations at the atomic level.  By utilizing an electronic structure model, it is possible to reproduce the experimentally observed magnetic phase diagram and the associated resistance changes with exceptional accuracy.  Furthermore, it is observed that the most significant decrease in electrical resistance occurs when the spins are freely aligned in an und directions, and that this effect is highly non-linear when magnetized in multiple directions.  These properties originate from a highly flat and multi-orbitally interconnected band structure, along with geometric frustration that leads to highly connected nodes with exceptional density.  Ultimately, this breakthrough finding opens a new door in materials science, revealing previously unexplored connection between complex electronic structure and magnetism that can be controlled. This study examines electronic correlation within confined hydrogen, helium and lithium ions in their base states using entropy measures. Different wavefunctions are used to better account for inter-electronic interactions. The resulting entropy values show sensitivity to these interactions. In situations of extremely tight confinement, Coulomb effects are minimized and models treating particles as independent or non-interacting pairs in an impenetrable sphere are increasingly applicable. Energy estimates derived from these models align well with existing literature values. In the case of hydrogen, deviations from the simple independent particle model become noticeable in energy estimates at energies below 1 Rydberg. In the case of helium, this threshold is at energies of around 2 Rydberg, and in the case of lithium, it is at approximately 5 Rydberg. Information entropies were found to be a effective way to monitor the onset of electronic interactions. They also showed promise in identifying the nature of electronic exchange interactions. In the case of hydrogen, entropy measures correctly identified the ground state even when wavefunctions used were not specifically modified to account for this interaction. For helium, entropy measures correctly identified the ground state for this interaction in certain confined scenarios. In the case of lithium, entropy measures correctly identified the ground state for this interaction in all confined scenarios where it applied. It also introduces an annotation framework that facilitates the management of attribute data within process models. Our model refinement approach, though generally applicable, has significant practical implications in the healthcare and financial domains due to their extensive use of data-driven processes. This technical report is an extension of our previous paper published at the BPM 2020 conference. Our work has novel connections to two distinct research fields, specifically data mining and process mining, as we have examined how our approach can contribute to the detection and analysis of irregular process patterns. Wildfires disrupting solar energy significantly through atmospheric aerosols,
resulting from diminished solar radiation reaching Earth, can be monitored by
Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) data streams retrieved from geostationary satellites.
However, multi-source satellite data streams often have varying missing data
rates and errors, making precise AOD estimation and prediction challenging.
Therefore, a practical need exists to develop a physics-based statistical method
for wildfire AOD forecasting by integrating heterogeneous satellite data streams.
By incorporating spectral analysis, the proposed method merges multiple satellite
datasets with an underlying advection-diffusion equation driving AOD propagation,
including bias correction to compensate for model biases and Fourier series errors.
This approach was tested using California wildfire AOD data provided by the NOAA,
along with numerical examples demonstrating its accuracy and predictive capability
for accurately forecasting AOD even in the presence of significant noise. Moreover,
the methodology has been made accessible through an open-source implementation.

Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this research, we studied how site-to-site effects impact our ability to detect individual and group differences, and our analysis suggests that multisite studies are feasible when utilizing large sample sizes and strong research questions. Our data collection was based on actual, rather than simulated, fMRI datasets from N=345 young, healthy subjects, acquired across eight scanning sites, all of which utilized 3T scanners and varied scanning protocols. Our findings demonstrate that commonly used statistical methods can successfully identify individual and group differences at the site-level, but not across all sites. However, machine learning techniques can help detect differences on a site-to-site level. Our data also show that, in a practical application, multisite studies yield similar sensitivity and specificity rates in sex classification. Our study concludes that while modern multisite resting-state functional MRI research is practical and feasible, it is essential to have large sample sizes and strong research questions to achieve reliable results. Additionally, our data and analysis provide a practical guide for researchers in this field. Our future work will focus on investigating whether these findings can be extended to more complex research questions in various fields, such as clinical and cognitive sciences. Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
mainly driven by the widespread use of language blending in social media across 
multi-lingual countries such as India, Mexico, Europe, and parts of the USA. 
Given their importance, developing word embeddings for code-mixed languages has 
become a pressing concern. A major obstacle in achieving this goal is 
overcoming the limitations imposed by language switch points. Statistical models 
are unable to efficiently capture the characteristics of these transition points 
owing to the high variability in observed data examples. This research paper 
investigates the effectiveness of applying switching point-based positional 
encoding methods to process code-mixed languages like Hinglish, resulting in only 
marginally improved outcomes relative to state-of-the-art models, although 
initial findings suggest that positional encoding could be a valuable technique 
for training sensitive language models that account for position-based language 
usage patterns in mixed texts. Code and data are accessible at this GitHub 
repository: https://github.com/AYESWEAT/PESTO. Hinglish-specific datasets can be 
downloaded here: https://github.com/AYESWEAT/PESTO/tree/master/Data. Models can 
be hosted on HuggingFace model hub at this link: https://huggingface.co/AYESWEAT.

Fisher developed the Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection using the concepts of average excess and average effect, where he initially defined these ideas somewhat abstractly. However, some experts believe that reframing his theories using statistical methods such as covariance and regression would clarify these concepts, both are part of classical statistical analysis. We propose an interpretation where Fisher's average excess and average effect are intended to represent a fundamental distinction between statistical correlation and causality, and according to this understanding, the average effect particularly signifies the average difference in genetic change resulting from an allele, and this interpretation aligns with the views of some earlier commentators. We demonstrate that when effect is defined as an outcome of an allele's influence on a trait, and when an appropriate statistical model is utilized, the average effect indeed embodies a causal interpretation, and this interpretation is consistent with the principles of linear regression. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the average excess, as perceived by Fisher, bears a resemblance to a measure of partial correlation within a linear model. The understanding of Fisher's average effect as a causal measure is useful for numerous contemporary purposes, particularly in the application of causal inference theories to the study of evolutionary genetics. Additionally, this interpretation allows for an original proof of Slatkin's "uniqueness" theorem, which illustrates the unique contributions Fisher made to the field of evolutionary genetics. This unique theorem presents a model where an allele's initial genetic difference and selected allele share a direct correlation, and under these conditions, any connections between selected and non-selected traits are ultimately eradicated. Furthermore, our analysis shows that when the criteria of Slatkin's theorem are met within a linear model, the mathematical structure of Fisher's average effect bears a resemblance to the fundamental non-zero eigenvalue that results from double latent vector decomposition, and this has significant implications for the study of evolutionary dynamics. In conclusion, our understanding of Fisher's average effect as a measure of causality offers a unified and clarified interpretation of his theoretical contributions and provides a foundation for future advancements in the application of modern statistical techniques to the study of evolutionary genetics. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates the ongoing relevance and innovation of Fisher's original ideas. Simulations of second-long black hole-neutron star mergers in numerical relativity are conducted to obtain a comprehensive picture of the inspiral, merger, and post-merger stages.  The analysis across various initial and computational configurations reveals universally similar evolution processes, regardless of setup variations.  The disruption of the neutron star leads to mass ejection accompanied by a massive accretion disk formation; the magnetic field within this disk then undergoes amplification due to various instabilities and turbulent forces, inducing the dynamo and angular momentum transfer.  The subsequent mass ejection by viscous magnetohydrodynamic turbulence begins roughly 300-500 milliseconds post-merger, persists for several hundred milliseconds; meanwhile, a magnetosphere is formed around the black hole, producing a focused strong electromagnetic outflow lasting about 0.5-2 seconds.  The model without a strong initial magnetic field in equatorial planes, however, necessitates a different efficiency in mass ejection and energetic processes by comparison to models with stronger initial magnetic fields, especially in those with non-zero magnetic fields in the polar regions.  The various models also exhibit comparable properties in gravitational wave amplitude and strain, although some variations exist among different neutron star models.  Notably, neutron star models affecting mass ejection and energetic processes but not magnetogenesis or electromagnetic emission remain unclear.  Moreover, second-long simulations are deemed insufficient to capture the late-stage post-merger mass ejection of neutron star matter; therefore, further high-resolution HD simulations using approximate GR schemes are recommended to investigate this phenomenon. By applying a precise electromagnetic model, we computed the optical force acting on each particle and derived equations to assess the influence of graphene's surface plasmons. To better assess the Emergency Department's admission process, we analyzed average response curves for treatment duration. Extending the time for treatment is considered an effective strategy for improving admissions; nonetheless, empirical evidence supporting this claim is difficult to gather. The treatment duration is impacted by various unmeasurable patient factors and coincides with the admission decision, which are challenging variables to manipulate. We depicted the admission process as a complex network, which revealed that the average response curves cannot be determined without nonparametric modeling due to confounding factors influencing patient health. We therefore adopted a parametric model, incorporating an unobserved patient health variable, to analyze data from a large hospital treating abdominal pain patients (28,862 patients). Our study found that shortening the Emergency Department treatment time to two hours decreases admissions by nearly nine percentage points and expanding the time by half an hour minimizes admissions without noticeably altering readmission and revisit rates. The proposed model is versatile, allowing for various cost functions to be examined under distinct patient health scenarios. Based on our research, improving admissions through longer treatment times may not always be the best approach due to nonrandom patient health distributions in the Emergency Department context. Our study highlights the significance of accounting for different patient health patterns when evaluating treatment policies. We also demonstrate how our average response curve framework can be applied to Emergency Department research and treatment policy analysis. Furthermore, our approach is adaptable to analyzing various Emergency Department treatment policies. Specifically, we investigated the effectiveness of treating patients sooner in the Emergency Department, which is another critical policy to evaluate. Our analysis shows that policy-specific average response curves are essential for making informed policy decisions based on empirical evidence. Lastly, our model is relevant to numerous treatment settings, such as DCEM and GERD therapy, as evidenced by our data, which also underscores the importance of considering nonrandom patient health patterns when evaluating treatment efficacy. We therefore believe that our findings are clinically significant and support the use of empirical evidence in treatment policy decisions. We also showcase the versatility of our approach by applying it to distinct medical contexts, specifically DCEM and GERD therapy, which demonstrates the vast potential of our method for treating patients in various medical settings. Unlike traditional pixel-based approaches, PatchNet leverages patch-wise correlation features. This results in a compact network that runs at a remarkably low computational cost of 58MFLOPs, approximately $5\times$ simpler than MobileNetV2. Our research showcases the effectiveness of PatchNet on object detection in videos and visual tracking, yielding substantial performance gains and comparable or even better results. This study investigates how basic autonomous entities akin to Braitenberg vehicles can manifest complex, unpredictable movements. Employing a robot design proposed by Steve Mesburger and Alfred Hubler in "Chaos in Wall Following Robots", the autonomous entities use a straightforward distance sensor to navigate, with the added limitation of a narrow "phi" field of view. As these agents maintain a consistent forward velocity, they rely on the sensor to adjust their path accordingly: rightward when close to obstacles and leftward when distant from them. In a linear environment, the autonomous entities maintain a consistent distance from their surroundings and proceed along a fixed path. However, when faced with periodic patterns in the environment, such as in the form of wide, waveform-shaped ground features, the autonomous entities begin to follow these patterns. A simple mathematical representation of these ground features allows for the creation of a dynamical system, which can be studied for its various states. In this case, the autonomous entities exhibit wall-following behaviors that transition suddenly and unpredictably between different patterns, known as bifurcation. As the field of view (phi) narrows, the autonomous entities become increasingly locked to certain patterns, known as attractors, and remain in these patterns indefinitely. Conversely, widening the field of view causes the autonomous entities to become locked to different patterns, known as Hopf bifurcations. Ultimately, the effect of this dynamic behavior is seen in the autonomous entities' ability to mimic the behavior of Hubert Ferlini's robot, which uses a more complex distance sensor to navigate. A theoretical model is developed to study this dynamic behavior, with simulations showing that it too can manifest complex, unpredictable movements. Experimentation with actual robots, using different ground features and field of view settings, reveals the diversity of patterns that these basic autonomous entities can exhibit. In particular, when faced with a pattern of wide, horizontal blocks and narrow, horizontal gaps, the autonomous entities become locked to different patterns, known as attractors, and remain in these patterns indefinitely. Changing the field of view causes these entities to switch between various patterns, with narrower views causing them to become locked to certain patterns and wider views causing them to become locked to different patterns. Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view. Smoke produced by laser ablation in such operations obstructs the surgeon's visibility, highlighting the need for smoke removal to ensure a clear view. To apply smoke removal techniques effectively, it's essential to accurately distinguish between smoke and non-smoke images, which poses a challenge as current methods are incomplete. To overcome this issue, we have developed an image enhancement technique that extracts crucial information from RGB images to differentiate between smoke and non-smoke content. Leveraging a weighted least squares optimization framework, we employ statistical features derived from bivariate histograms and specific image characteristics, which are then used to train a classifier for binary classification of smoke or non-smoke content. We have tested our approach on the Cholec80 dataset and achieved notable results, with a 4% improvement in accuracy and F1-score over standard RGB image performance, as well as increased AUC score. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions and shows an average reduction of under one tenth in gate fidelity for every frequency error of 100 Hz when using abelian symmetry, primarily due to a high level of frequency robustness rather than decoherence rates. Furthermore, this concept is theoretically extended to non-abelian symmetry with the potential for applying the same techniques to qudits. We believe this method could significantly improve the operation of complex quantum systems, particularly those involving longer chains of ions. If a 100 kHz error tolerance is maintained, the gates can be repeated around ten times a second, although this rate significantly drops when frequency errors exceed 10 Hz per minute. This research is crucial for the development of more robust quantum computing systems. We have investigated other methods for enhancing the resilience of Molmer-Sorensen gates, such as incorporating additional optical pulses, and found that these alternatives protect against different types of errors but come with the cost of increased decoherence. Ultimately, we have discovered a trade-off between resilience and work rate, and this understanding is critical for designing the optimal Molmer-Sorensen gates. Given the widespread adoption of Gaussian amplitude modulation in quantum computing systems, we have described a range of methods for implementing resilient quantum operations, and these techniques are relevant to a broader range of applications, including cold atoms and superconducting qubits, through the incorporation of alternative schemes for generating entanglement. This research has explored different design choices and their consequences. We have proposed an alternative method, the MS Gate II, using a single frequency for both the carrier and sidebands, and found it offers superior frequency robustness with minimal additional complexity. MS Gate II has distinct advantages, particularly a more consistent pattern of excitation and less prominent sidebands, and we have demonstrated its implementation using either abelian or non-abelian symmetry, and even without using a logical qubit, thereby preserving the benefits. We have discovered the MS Gate II can provide robust quantum operations with minimal added complexity and rapid repetition, and this concept is applicable across different types of qubits. We have studied the performance under the influence of frequency errors and found that in the vast majority of situations, the gates remain nearly fault-free

This reduction involves eliminating unnecessary operations, factors, and copies. Current approaches rely on heuristic algorithms that are inefficient due to their random nature. This study introduces the first deterministic algorithms for eliminating factors and redundant rotations in quantum circuits with recurring patterns. These algorithms guarantee optimal results within a certain time frame. Specifically, they guarantee a deterministic QAOA algorithm for simulating Hamiltonian evolution with $O(\kappa^2 n^3)$ steps and optimal circuit size. Additionally, they develop a deterministic algorithm for compiling circuits with $O(\kappa^5 n^2)$ complexity. This finding implies that certain quantum algorithms can be made scalable without the need for classical post-processing. This reduces the program size by eliminating unnecessary quantum operations, factors, and copies. This study also introduces the first known deterministic algorithm for compiling quantum circuits with recurring patterns in linear time and the circuit size. This breakthrough is made possible by introducing a new concept, circuit section overlap, which enables efficient recombination of circuit segments. These algorithms guarantee optimal results within a certain time frame and factor the quantum circuit into its underlying factors and quantum subspaces. This study presents experimental results for reducing circuit size in real-world circuits, particularly CNOT-Roy, IsingXY and Shor's algorithm, which show substantial size reductions. For instance, a 5-qubit CNOT-Roy circuit with 16 repeated CNOTs can be compiled in 15 steps, whereas the best previous approach required around 200 steps. Moreover, a 16-qubit Shor's algorithm circuit with 128 repeated CNOTs can be compiled in 1,290 steps, whereas the best previous approach required around 20,000 steps. These results demonstrate that deterministic compilation can significantly decrease program size while achieving comparable results. A recent approach to optimizing techniques employs average-case analysis, enabling more nuanced convergence assessments than conventional worst-case results, yet this analysis demands more information about the data - specifically, assuming the existence of third-order statistical moments. This higher requirement complicates evaluating the efficacy of such methods. We investigate this issue by confirming the universality and robustness of the quasi-Newton L-BFGS optimization algorithm when tested under various distributions of data, demonstrating its ability to achieve comparable performance regardless of the distribution, even when only second-order moments are available. Our analysis contrasts with earlier studies on optimization which often required third-order moments for accuracy. From a practical perspective, this finding indicates that relying on low-order statistical moments suffices for optimizing techniques to work consistently across diverse data sets. To validate our theoretical estimates and demonstrate the reliability of our conclusions, extensive numerical experiments were conducted, utilizing a novel hybrid bound that bridges classical worst-case analysis with modern average-case approaches. This hybrid method enables bridges between these two approaches, providing more precise insights than conventional worst-case results while remaining more accessible than average-case analyses. We believe that our hybrid approach will become a valuable tool in the optimization community for achieving a finer grain size of understanding when evaluating the performance of optimization algorithms. Our confirmation of L-BFGS's average-case robustness challenges the conventional wisdom that optimization algorithms with robust worst-case performance perform poorly in real-world applications. On the other hand, our investigation reveals that not only can such algorithms perform well on average, but they can also achieve comparable results when compared with techniques specifically designed for optimizing tasks under diverse data conditions. Furthermore, our findings stress the importance of considering statistical moments in optimization analysis, urging the development of more sophisticated tools to describe the behavior of optimization algorithms, especially when dealing with complicated data sets. To facilitate this, we propose a statistical evaluation framework that can compare optimization methods with varying amounts of statistical information. We believe that this framework will contribute to future research in this area by opening up new avenues for exploring the average-case performance of optimization algorithms. Code for replicating the numerical experiments in this study is made accessible through a public GitHub repository. Additionally, we provide a detailed guide that walks through the implementation of our proposed hybrid analysis approach. This implementation draws from established libraries and tools, while also introducing novel extensions to existing frameworks, as described in the supplementary material accompanying this study. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/puclaus/only-tails-matter. This study is partially funded by the ANR (Agence Nationale de la Recherche

We have developed a message-passing algorithm designed to accurately determine the location and track of mobile objects within areas with multiple signal paths that may experience blocked or obstructed visibility. The proposed adaptive probabilistic algorithm estimates a mobile device's position by leveraging data from multiple anchors, taking into account the timing and amplitude variations in signal components and associated uncertainties. Utilizing an adaptable noise model, the algorithm enables accurate estimation of the agent's position, even without precise knowledge of the surrounding environment. The algorithm dynamically adjusts its operation in real-time according to changes in signal strength and the likelihood of direct line-of-sight visibility with each anchor. Numerical testing demonstrates that the algorithm remains effective in areas with intense signal interference and temporary obstructions. The algorithm's performance is showcased in a variety of scenarios, including a indoor environment with a line-of-sight obstruction and a area with varying levels of signal interference. The results reveal that the algorithm consistently provides accurate estimation of location and tracks mobile objects with sufficient data from multiple anchors. The number of used data packets directly influences the algorithm's accuracy, with increased packet loss resulting in diminished performance. However, the algorithm remains accurate down to half the total available data packets, even in the absence of direct line-of-sight visibility with any anchor. The algorithm's adaptive nature enables reliable operation over a wide range of signal conditions, with noticeable performance degradation only in extremely extreme cases. Measurements of joint polarization states for $W$ and $Z$ bosons in $W^{\pm}Z$ production processes have been reported. These measurements were derived from $139$ fb$^{-1}$ worth of data from proton-proton collisions at a $13$ TeV center-of-mass energy, obtained with the ATLAS detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider.  $W^{\pm}Z$ candidate events, resulting from the decay of these bosons into electrons and muons, have been used to quantify longitudinally polarized vector boson pair production, an event that is here reported for the first time, occurring at a statistical significance of $6.6$ standard deviations.  Fiducially-integrated joint helicity fractions for these $W$ and $Z$ polarizations show alignment with the next-to-leading order predictions from the Standard Model of physics.  Additionally, joint helicity fractions for individual $W$ and $Z$ polarizations have been separately measured, resulting in parameters $F_0 = 0.067 $ for $W^+Z$ and $F_0 = 0.071 $ for $W^-Z$, both of which matching the Standard Model predictions within a $2$ standard deviation margin.  This study marks the first observation of joint polarization states for $W$ and $Z$ bosons. It further verifies the SM predictions for joint polarization phenomena while also setting a limit on an anomalous dimension affecting these production processes, ultimately yielding a limit of $-20$ TeV at a $95$% confidence level.  This study further demonstrates the capability of the ATLAS detector to analyze polarization effects in highly energetic proton-proton collision data. This capability may enable detection of deviations from Standard Model predictions for rare processes involving polarized particles. Research indicates that the Cotton tensor offers a way to extend our understanding of gravity beyond what general relativity provides. Additionally, the Cotton tensor's field equations include any solution derived from Einstein's equations, both with and without a cosmological constant, as well as indicate that this constant can be seen as an integral component rather than an external factor. A theory's vacuum state is better characterized by a zero value for the Cotton tensor, as opposed to the vanishing of the Ricci tensor, revealing new insights. A static and spherically symmetric solution that is comparable to Schwarzschild was found. Although the Cotton tensor's equations include derivatives of a third order, they simplify to equations of a second order due to their intrinsic variational properties. This is similar to $F(F_{\mu\nu,\tau}x^\tau) = 0$ for a vector field's equations, where the covariant derivative is denoted by $\tau$. As a result, the Cotton tensor's equations exhibit an inherent simplicity and suggest a fundamental, universal principle. This could lead to future discoveries in fundamental physics. Furthermore, the Cotton tensor's equations may have hidden insights into symmetries and conserved quantities. A method for formulating dynamical action and developing symmetries in the theory was explored, which could facilitate future developments.
