We demonstrate that the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms is limited under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis for a specific degree 8 L-function. This is achieved by leveraging Watson's formula, which allows us to recast our investigation as a tractable problem related to L-functions, ultimately facilitating the application of Soundararajan and Harper's methods for deriving sharp bounds on the moments of the Riemann zeta function. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a significant inequality concerning the logarithm of the norm of modular form coefficients, which may have implications for future research in the field. While our findings are specifically focused on Hecke cusp forms, the approach itself is adaptable to examining similar moments for other types of modular forms. Additionally, we note that our outcome represents a refined version of Sato and Iwaniec's earlier work on the subject, as well as offering further insight into the relationship between the norms of modular form coefficients and their degrees, which was initially explored by Li and Rolen. Lastly, our analysis yields a striking conjectural result, namely that the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms is actually finite, under the sole condition that the Riemann Hypothesis holds true. This presents an intriguing possibility that the infiniteness of the fourth moment under the Riemann Hypothesis condition could serve as a crucial indicator for detecting counterexamples to the Riemann Hypothesis. These speculative notions may hold significant value, particularly in relation to the work of Kahn and  Levin, which suggests the existence of potential counterexamples to the Riemann Hypothesis with specific characteristics. However, further investigation would be necessary to confirm whether such scenarios are possible, as well as whether our analysis provides a valid description of the potential form of such counterexamples, as proposed. Ultimately, our study contributes to the extensive research efforts aimed at understanding the influence of the Riemann Hypothesis on the boundedness of the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms. To better contextualize our findings and facilitate future work in this area, we have also collected and analyzed key moments of the Riemann zeta function and specific degree 8 L-functions, as specified in [HZ]. Furthermore, our work also serves as a further exploration of the ideas and approaches outlined in [ZH]. The present study is a revised and expanded version of our initial research, as initially presented in [CZ]. The relevant estimates and calculations have been further refined and updated, as needed. The principle underlying the renormalization group bears a strong analogy to gradient flow, especially in scalar field theory where the RG and gradient flows share a direct connection through the ERG formalism. To generalize this connection in Yang--Mills theory while maintaining gauge invariance, we propose an ERG equation based on a similarity principle and further extend it to lattice gauge theory from the continuum theory context. Our proposal adheres to the principles of gauge invariance and incorporates a technique to systematically incorporate higher-order derivatives, thereby maintaining a high level of accuracy. We demonstrate using numerical simulations that the ERG flow is equivalent to the gradient flow when both share a common gauge invariance structure. Moreover, we showcase the utility of our approach by illustrating how the ERG flow can be utilized to define a notion of an average coupling that is both RG and gradient flow invariant. Since our proposal does not introduce any novel variables not present in the original theory, this invariance translates directly to the observable quantities and is apparent from the behavior of these quantities along the RG flow trajectory. Our study focuses on the two-dimensional Yang--Mills theory but the proposed ERG equation can be applied equally to three-dimensional theory and even to theories incorporating matter fields. We believe that our approach will greatly simplify numerical RG calculations by preventing the introduction of additional variables and allowing us to utilize the comprehensive insights offered by the RG framework while maintaining a strong connection to the gradient flow formalism. Moreover, this approach can be utilized in various practical applications such as band structure calculations, lattice modeling of superconductors, and lattice QCD for heavy heavy-quark effective theories and also for two Higgs doublet models. To further generalize our proposal, we have successfully tested it on the U(1) gauge theory although our method is not limited to this theory alone. We believe that our technique will have far-reaching applications in various research domains. To address this gap, our approach develops a single formal framework that can analyze multiple process models with different paradigms (petri nets, bpmn and flowable) in conjunction. We've defined a monitoring technique that synchronizes a proactive process model with an actual occurrence process. The ProActive Model-Oriented Process Analyzer (POMPAN) algorithm transforms the model into a finite automaton to identify predictive and retrospective violations. We've also considered the occurrence of model conflicts, resolving them within the formal model for the analysis of process correctness. The proposed method was evaluated through an empirical study based on 12 process models with 42 instances of conflicts from existing literature. The results show that our method can successfully detect violations and resolve conflicts more efficiently than current process monitoring techniques. Furthermore, the empirical study demonstrates the efficacy of our approach in identifying predictive and retrospective violations, resolving conflicts, and verifying the correctness of process models. The implementation of our method is available under an OSI-approved license, enabling practical applications and evaluations. We also provide an assessment of the limitations of our approach and suggest possible avenues for further research. These investigations involve the extension of our method to support more complex process models with additional features. Specifically, we can explore the integration of data streams, the incorporation of probabilistic process models, and the utilization of machine learning techniques to analyze process occurrences. Additionally, we can monitor hybrid process models that combine different process paradigms and, finally, extend the scope of our method to detect concept violations in process model families. These proposed research directions are grounded in existing publications that motivated our work and highlight potential avenues for further investigation. The detailed description of our approach, its evaluation, and these research directions serve as a guide for scholars who can build upon our findings and address these research questions. The empirical evaluation of our method also provides actionable insights for analysts and practitioners who can use POMPAN to monitor and analyze actual occurrence processes in real-time, thereby enhancing the quality of the actual process execution. The results of our approach can be integrated into process modeling tools as suggestions or warnings to facilitate the alignment of actual process occurrences with proactive process models. Specifically, we intend to investigate how Quipper-M can be used to model the semantics of Quipper and other quantum circuit-based languages through interpretation or other forms of semantic transformation. The ultimate goal is to enable compile-time quasiquotation, a feature previously implemented in Quipper but also other Quipper-based languages, and other compile-time mechanisms, as proven successful in Quipper, for multiple quantum programming languages. The proposed Quipper-M semantics will serve as a common benchmark for evaluating the design and effectiveness of quasiquotes and other compile-time mechanisms in quantum programming languages. We anticipate that existing Quipper and Quipper-based languages can benefit from revised quasiquotes and other compile-time mechanisms developed through this research. Achieving maximum engine performance involves leveraging quantum effects. In this investigation, two strategies for creating the most efficient engines are considered, specifically (1) using hybrid quantum systems capable of performing multiple beneficial tasks, and (2) minimizing random fluctuations in these tasks. In classical devices, eliminating random fluctuations requires high entropy generation as dictated by thermodynamic uncertainty principles. Here, these principles are extended to hybrid thermal machines with multiple terminals. In quantum conductors, these limitations are bypassed, and we demonstrate this for a setup comprising a double quantum dot and normal metals in contact, powered by an entangled Cooper pair generator. We show that optimal performance is achieved when dots and leads have the same size, and predict an order of magnitude improvement in performance over previously established benchmarks. This prediction provides a framework for future research on hybrid quantum thermodynamics. Specifically, our findings suggest a significant reduction in heat dissipated into the environment during the conversion of electrical currents into heat. This prediction could be experimentally verified using measurement tools such as scanning tunneling spectroscopy, and we outline the procedures for doing so. These procedures may also be applied to assess the performance of other hybrid quantum devices. Over the past decade, significant advancements in artificial intelligence have positioned it as a key tool for addressing environmental concerns, primarily reducing greenhouse gas emissions. However, researchers have lately come to recognize that increasingly complex AI models require substantial amounts of energy to train, thereby contributing to the very emissions they are intended to mitigate. To date, no thorough examination of the full scope of the environmental effects of using AI to address environmental problems (dubbed AI for Green) has been undertaken. In this article, we aim to overcome these limitations by classifying potential AI for Green countermeasures into four categories - "Accident", "Consequence", "Opportunity", and "Investment" - to analyze their diverse environmental impacts. Our analysis reveals that some AI for Green measures, such as AI-assisted contact tracing, have significant bearing on electronic device production and usage patterns. In contrast, "Investment"-type countermeasures, like AI-driven smart grids, tend to have more profound effects on energy infrastructure and device disposal. We utilize the widely-established Credibility Assessment Framework to evaluate and compare the environmental implications of these categories. To illustrate the potential range of impacts, we conduct a systematic analysis of existing research on AI for Green, gathering data from 118 studies on the subject. Our ultimate goal is to provide AI for Green practitioners and researchers with a comprehensive framework for evaluating the various environmental effects of AI-driven solutions, thereby enabling them to make more informed design and policy decisions. We hope this work will serve as a starting point for creating a comprehensive knowledge base on the diverse environmental impacts of AI for Green. Furthermore, we envision our methodology will be adaptable to studying the computer science community's social and economic impacts. We intend for our research to contribute to more comprehensive discussions about the environmental and social effects of technology and, ultimately, promote sustainable technology development. We make our research accessible through an interactive website at https://ai-for-green.github.io/. We've investigated a newly constructed series of asymptotically flat, electrically charged black holes that form scalar "hair" when their charge increases at a fixed mass. Inside the event horizon, these black holes resemble a holographic superconducting material, exhibiting similar behavior in their scalar fields and culminating in a singularity that heavily depends on the black holes' parameters when the instability first arises. Additionally, we present a general theory in an appendix stating that certain types of stationary black holes with scalar "hair" cannot possess Cauchy horizons. Applying this theory reveals that the asymptotically flat, charged black holes we studied are unable to avoid the infamous black hole "information paradox." However, we also demonstrate that the black holes that form from initial, stable configurations with sufficiently short wavelengths are unable to exhibit the same interior behavior due to the presence of a fundamental wavelength, leading to a reevaluation of the stability of these configurations based on proximity to the stability threshold in the parameter space. Finally, we speculate on how these findings might be observed through radiation that emanates from these black holes and could potentially be detected using future gravitational wave observatories. If these predictions are verified, it could provide insight into the validity of theories such as holography. The impact of RNA splicing on delaying mRNA production cannot be ignored. We developed a model combining transcription dynamics and RNA processing to estimate the rates of transcription, RNA production lag, and RNA breakdown using sequencing data from multiple time points. The model blends a mechanistic approach with a flexible statistical method, incorporating uncertainty into the calculations through Bayesian estimation. We applied this model to ER-alpha activated cells from a breast cancer line, analyzing transcription using ChIP-Seq data and mature RNA using Qseq data. The results show that a considerable number of genes exhibit a prolonged period between transcription completion and mature RNA appearance. Furthermore, genes exhibiting longer delays are typically shorter and are associated with retained introns in pre-mRNA data, suggesting significant production delays attributed to splicing events. The findings highlight the considerable effect of RNA production delays and break-down rates on mRNA accumulation patterns, necessitating consideration in inferring transcription dynamics from sequencing data. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. We thoroughly tested our method using the walmsp dataset consisting of 1080 variables and up to 352 nodes in a directed acyclic graph, which to our knowledge, is the largest publicly available dataset for applied structural computer efficiency. We then demonstrated the flexibility of our framework by successfully solving a previously intractable problem with a seemingly intractable structure, as well as the challenging network disaster recovery problem. The code for our research is openly accessible. The visual appearance and auditory qualities of an object provide dual insights into its material properties.  In everyday situations, information from vision and hearing arrive simultaneously, but the integration of asynchronous cues is essential, as seen when we locate an object dropped on the ground after hearing its fall.  In this paper, a controlled environment for studying 3D object localization in real-time is established, involving an embodied robotic agent, a camera, and a microphone that identify a dropped object in a room.  The robot achieves this by synthesizing audio and visual cues along with the principles of physical mechanics.  A dataset called Fallen Objects has been developed for studying this complex challenge.  The dataset is based on the ThreeDWorld platform and includes over 15,000 simulations of various object types in 27 settings.  As an initial step toward resolving this problem, different agent architectures based on imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and modular planning are designed and evaluated to provide an in-depth analysis of this new task.  The introduction of this new challenge, the Fallen Objects dataset, and several benchmarked approaches provide a foundation for future research in this area.  Specifically, it offers a testing ground for AI agents to demonstrate their ability to integrate asynchronous cues and apply physical mechanics in a real-world setting.  This research domain has wide-ranging implications and can contribute positively to tasks like object tracking, navigation, and retrieval in unstructured environments.  Moreover, it offers a new framework for studying online information integration and applied mechanical principles that can be adapted across various domains.  This framework can potentially influence AI development in areas like search and law enforcement, where understanding sound and vision interactions is crucial for navigating environments.  In contrast to existing reinforcement learning approaches that rely on reward feedback, imitation learning techniques are shown to outperform and provide a solid foundation for resolving this new challenge.  The evaluation of state-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods, on the other hand, highlights their limitations in this context, particularly when rewards are sparse and the agents have no knowledge of the dropped objects.  A modular planning approach that leverages existing planning tools to localize the object is introduced as a viable alternative and provides a useful complement to imitation learning methods, particularly when used in conjunction with online audio and visual cue integration.  The replication of this research in different environments, using various audio and visual representations, and from a human perspective through crowd sourcing tasks, confirm the effectiveness of the proposed imitation learning methods.  The evaluation of existing computer vision and audio processing techniques on this new challenge also provides a solid foundation for future

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. A key area for future investigation lies in determining the precise nature of the shear jammings that govern rigidity when hydrodynamic forces are present. It is also essential to establish a thorough understanding of the shear jammings that govern rigidity when friction dominates. This research seeks to expand the existing theoretical framework for interpreting viscosity to cover multiple scales, encompassing both microscopic and macroscopic perspectives. It is also a goal of this work to establish a connection between the shear thickening transition and other pressure or stress-induced transitions, including the glass transition and pressure-induced decoupling. The study suggests that the concept of shear jammings is not solely confined to dense mixtures and suspensions but can be extended to cover a broad spectrum of matter, encompassing 2D gases, colloids, and even biological systems. It is a goal of this research to establish a more comprehensive understanding of the shear jammings that govern rigidity and to develop a universal theory for interpreting viscosity. This study offers fresh insights into the matter transitions and by reevaluating existing experimental data, proposes that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. The study reveals that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics and may require further investigation to determine the precise nature of the shear jammings that govern rigidity when friction dominates. This study investigates the fluctuating electricity consumption in Ghana's period of power shortages by applying Markov switching models, namely MS-AR and AR. The data, comprising hourly electricity usage from January 1, 2014 to December 31, 2014 provided by the Ghana Grid company, helped determine the best-fitting model as MS(2)-AR(4) based on different evaluation criteria. The parameters of this model were then estimated using an expectation-maximization algorithm, indicating that the likelihood of experiencing low electricity consumption is 87%, with the low consumption period expected to last around 7.8 hours a day. The model outperformed traditional AR models by effectively modeling peak and varied consumption patterns and identifying distinct regime changes during the power crisis periods. The study demonstrates that using MS-AR models to analyze irregularly spaced data, such as daily peak consumption, can provide valuable insights. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and their influence on discovering new information, particularly relevant to their assessment. The study aims to answer two critical questions: (1) What role does personalisation play in detecting new information among search results for professional assessment? Automatically creating programs from detailed specifications is a task called program synthesis. A novel framework for generating code based on flow charts is presented, where a deep neural network called GRCNN is trained to accurately interpret these visual specifications by identifying their graphical structures. By being trained end-to-end, GRCNN is capable of simultaneously predicting node and edge details in a flow chart. The framework's results reveal high levels of accuracy in synthesizing programs at a 66.4% rate and also demonstrate robust node and edge recognition at rates of 94.1% and 67.9%, respectively. Furthermore, program synthesis occurs in approximately 60 milliseconds. The framework's effectiveness is supported by extensive evaluations of its resilience to structural modifications and human evaluation. A detailed analysis of the framework's design choices, along with the related technical challenges and constraints, is also provided. The framework's source code is made available for public use through an open-source platform. The framework's performance is evaluated on a dataset of genuine flow charts derived from actual programs and also on artificially created charts with randomly assigned structures. The evaluation indicates that the framework remains highly accurate even when faced with complex and previously unseen chart structures. The framework is further distinguished by its capacity to recognize its own node and edge components through fine-tuning, thereby enhancing its program synthesis accuracy from 66.4% to 75.8%. The framework is comprised of three modules, specifically, a graph attention module, a graph convolutional module, and a graph embedding module, that work in tandem to extract and embed visual features from the given flow charts. The graph attention module is responsible for determining the most relevant nodes and edges in the chart, whereas the graph convolutional module applies convolutional operations to these nodes and edges to derive final program synthesis results. The graph embedding module is charged with compressing the chart's structural information into a fixed-length vector for subsequent synthesis use. The training of GRCNN is a complex task that involves optimizing its multiple components. A customized training protocol is developed to optimize node and edge recognition and program synthesis simultaneously by iterating two distinct training modes, a synthetic mode that generates artificial charts and a target mode that adapts to real program structures. The framework is evaluated using standard accuracy metrics and also through human evaluation by 21 software engineers and researchers with diverse expertise and backgrounds. The framework is found to produce high-quality code that closely resembles actual programs even when faced with challenging structural modifications. In contrast to the observed masses of satellites in our solar system, which are substantially smaller than their parent stars, the mass distribution of planets from this survey does not reflect this trend. In contrast to other methods for discovering exoplanets, such as direct imaging and microlensing, which are limited by detection biases, the mass and period distribution of planets from Doppler radial velocity surveys, which can detect planets in close orbits within a wide range of masses, does not display an evident 'desert' or 'valley' at high masses and short periods. In this study, we examine the 'desert' or 'valley' at high masses and short periods using a complete and unbiassed sample of planets from Doppler radial velocity surveys, which can test widely-held hypotheses about planetary formation and evolution, particularly those related to photoevaporation and the metallicity of disks. In this study, we used a complete and unbiased sample of planets from Doppler radial velocity surveys to examine how the mass and period distribution of planets changes at high masses (10-$100 M_\odot) with short orbital periods (10-$100 days). Artificial intelligence models, modeled after biological agents, can regulate their awareness by restricting their input from the environment to minimize information overload.  A key consideration here is, how can a limited sensory input be expanded to encompass relevant, dynamic structural patterns in the environment?  A fundamental issue is, how can a biological or artificial agent discover these patterns?  We propose AI architectures that use a novel strategy of increasing the correlation between the agent's awareness and environmental patterns.  This proposal is based on experimental models of two types of sensory experiences - a numerical analysis based on random signals and a simulation of a visual recognition task.  The results show that these methods lead to rapid discovery of relevant patterns.  Additionally, we observe that our approach encourages the development of focused attention control mechanisms similar to those observed in biological systems.  Notably, our model produces simple, easy-to interpret results.  The proposed strategy offers a universal framework for incorporating focused attention into various AI architectures.  Although our experiments focused on prediction tasks, this technique has broader applications and could be used to explain established attention mechanisms in deep learning models.  Future research will concentrate on integrating this method into more intricate AI architectures that generate their own sensory questions.  Ultimately, we hope that our work will lead to AI systems that operate like living beings, adapting to their surroundings while maintaining focus. In numerous machine learning models and tasks, the implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, various global pooling methods are unified within a single framework. Consequently, a generalized global pooling layer for neural networks called UOT-Pooling layer can be introduced. To test the effectiveness of this novel pooling method, a deep learning model incorporating UOT-Pooling layers was applied to the language modeling task and compared to existing pooling methods. The results show that models incorporating the UOT-Pooling layers achieve superior performance on the text-classification and language-modeling tasks, according to metrics such as word accuracy and perplexity. Furthermore, a theoretical analysis of the conditions under which the empirical risk minimizer of the learning task exists reveals that a network using the UOT-Pooling layers achieves lower sample complexity compared to a network using the average-pooling layers, provided it meets specific normalization conditions. To validate this theoretical finding, a series of controlled experiments were conducted and the results match the theoretical predictions. The proposed UOT-Pooling framework thus offers a previously unexamined theoretical understanding of global pooling operations and improves the development of neural networks through the adoption of the optimal transport-based pooling layers. The source code of this project is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyizhen/zir.llvm/. The generated datasets are available at https://github.com/zhengyizhen/zir.llvm/blob/master/extra.py. The optar library used in this project is available at https://github.com/zhengyizhen/optar.llvm/. A deep learning model incorporating the UOT-Pooling layers has been integrated into the TF-Hub platform as the module `tfhub://zir/uot-pooling/1+default`. This module can be accessed at https://tfhub.dev/zir/uot-pooling/1 and used in various machine learning tasks. The performance of the UOT-Pooling layer also surpasses existing pooling methods in the BERT model, according to the F1-score metric, as revealed by the results of the semi-supervised emotion classification task. The proposed UOT-Pooling framework thus offers a novel, effective, and theoretically justified method of global pooling operations

The primary objective of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus unification theory. Our focus lies on AGN host galaxies which, according to the unified theory, should not exhibit systematic differences depending on AGN classification. We used the SDSS catalogue up to a redshift of 0.2, and the Galaxy Zoo Project catalogue which classifies galaxies into two broad Hubble types, and classified AGNs using emission line diagnostics. Our findings reveal that elliptical galaxies have a significantly higher fraction of Type 1 Seyfert nuclei compared to other AGN types, and the transition from Seyfert 1 to LINER, Type 2 Seyfert, and composite nuclei corresponds to a rise in spiral host galaxies. These findings contradict the unified model, and suggest that there's a symbiotic relationship between supermassive black holes and galactic bulges. Furthermore, our data indicate that spiral host galaxies with Type 1 Seyfert nuclei predominantly face towards the observer, whereas the distribution of nuclear orientations among other AGN types follows a random pattern. These findings are consistent with existing studies, and imply a close connection between supermassive black holes and galactic bulges that becomes evident through various mechanisms, including bar-driven dynamics. Additionally, our data provide evidence for a growing black hole within a dynamic environment. These outcomes enhance our understanding of the coeval growth of a black hole and its host galaxy, and the observed relationship between a particular type of black hole and spiral host galaxies holds significant scientific value. Our research also paves the way for future studies involving the coeval evolution of black holes and galaxies, and the underlying physical mechanisms governing their interactions. Finally, our data also indicate that the orientation of the galactic disc plays a pivotal role in shaping the observable characteristics of the AGN, and the widespread distribution of disc-aligned black holes is unlikely to be attributed to random phenomena. Therefore, our research also investigates the role of galaxy discs in shaping the observable properties of the central black hole. Our findings reveal that the presence of a galactic disc can significantly affect the luminosity of the central black hole, and the distinct patterns of Type 1 and 2 Seyfert nuclei among spiral hosts indicate a causal relationship between the black hole and the surrounding gas that is closely linked to the global structure of the host galaxy. Moreover, our data also demonstrate that LINER nuclei are more prevalent in spiral hosts, and this phenomenon may be attributed to the emission from a less massive black hole or an active galactic nucleus

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by uncontrollable biases. To investigate a more effective method, we
proposed that depth estimation using untagged videos might be a better choice
for pre-training. Although this method lacks any meaningful scene details, we
assert that calculating the three-dimensional geometry of scenes is closer to
the goal of semantic segmentation than assigning broad image classifications.
Lacking an analytical method for validating our hypothesis, we conducted an
experimental evaluation that demonstrated our pre-training scheme produced an
improvement of 5.7% mean intersection over union and 4.1% pixel accuracy in
comparison to classification-based pre-training. Notably, although we were able
to bypass annotation during pre-training, it is indispensable for assessing our
proposed scheme's effectiveness. To validate our findings, we employed the
popular KITTI (outdoor) and NYU-V2 (indoor) benchmarking datasets and also
detailed the benefits and shortcomings of our pre-training protocol in relation
to alternative methods like unsupervised, self-supervised, and semi-supervised
training approaches. Additionally, we made our pre-trained model and related
code available to the public for the first time. While we have opening remarks,
our pre-training protocol is inherently versatile and can be applied to a wide
range of other important computer vision tasks beyond just semantic segmentation. 
This research paper was initially published in the ICCV 2021 proceedings of the
International Conference on Computer Vision and Image Processing. We anticipate
this work will facilitate streamlined development of deep neural network
training for other challenging, resource-intensive computer vision tasks.

The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanical, uninspired narratives. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural framework that can describe time-series data in a universal way without being tied to a particular domain. TCube represents essential time-series elements using a knowledge graph, which is then translated into coherent, engaging stories by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained language models. Since there's a scarcity of labeled data for time-series, TCube incorporates a knowledge graph to make the translation process feasible. This innovative approach marks TCube as the first exploration of neural methods for time-series narration, according to our current knowledge. In our comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that TCube significantly improves the variety of words in the generated stories, while also accurately conveying the underlying time-series characteristics. These measures maintain the traditional translation symmetry characteristic of the well-known Gibbs measures. Additionally, we identify certain conditions that ensure these new measures are uniquely associated with the model's thermodynamic properties and demonstrate that they can be effectively analyzed through a forest fire algorithm. Our method of developing these periodic measures is an extension of previous work that focused on index-1 normal subgroups. Finally, we explore the distinct behaviors of these measures in relation to key parameters, such as magnetization and polarization. Our findings establish that these periodic measures are a rich and extensive class, encompassing many Gibbs measures at certain parameter values and giving rise to novel patterns of magnetic behavior. Moreover, the associated Markov fields of these measures exhibit multiple distinct phases and symmetries, which are cause by the structural properties of the tree graph, rendering them distinct from the well-known Ising model's behavior on a homogeneous graph. Our work thus presents a new paradigm for measuring symmetry in physical systems, grounded in the algebraic description of their subgroups, and offers a novel approach to understanding phase transitions and ordering phenomena. Our method can be generalized to study other statistical systems and models, as well as distributed data structures and algorithms. Our analysis is accompanied by a detailed software implementation that is freely accessible and distributed under a permissive license. Our work follows a long-standing legacy of studying subgroups within groups and their mathematical and computational implications, which dates back to the early 20th century. Our unique contribution, however, lies in the unique context in which we are studying these subgroups, as well as our innovative applications of these ideas to statistical physics and machine learning. Our research is a promising new area of research, and we have identified many open challenges and questions for further investigation. This study explores the well-posedness of global solutions, dependence on initial data, and potential loss of regularity in strictly hyperbolic equations with certain properties. These equations feature coefficients that experience moderate blow-up as sublogarithmic growth, represented by the function $|\ln t|^\gamma$ where $0 < \gamma < 1$. By applying a specific metric on the phase space, we can categorize these equations and examine their coefficients, which have polynomial bounds in x, x-derivatives, and a specific rate of decrease in t. We leverage a Planck function, based on this metric, to split the phase space and define relevant generalized symbol classes. Through the use of a conjugating pseudodifferential operator, which we term the loss operator, we establish an energy estimate and identify a link between the loss of regularity and the phase space metric and singular behavior. Our analysis shows that the solution undergoes a small, yet arbitrary, loss relative to its initial datum in a Sobolev space adapted to the loss operator. We construct a conjugating operator by accounting for the loss and a logarithmic correction, which we obtain through an appropriate reformulation of the problem via a Fredholm alternative pseudodifferential operator. Our approach relies heavily on the properties of the loss operator and novel generalized calculus constructs, including a singular symbolic calculus for pseudodifferential operators. We demonstrate the existence of a conjugating operator even when its symbol does not meet the classical smoothness standards, which typically define global well-posedness. We extend the constructs from even distributions to distributional solutions, which we obtain through an explicit extension method. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of well-posedness and its dependence on initial data for these types of equations. We also discuss how our methods generalize to other equations with different types of singular coefficients and coefficients exhibiting more significant types of blow-up than those considered in this study. Furthermore, we extend our constructs to consider distributional initial conditions, which we obtain through an explicit extension method. Our results can be applied to partial differential equations describing physical phenomena with singular coefficients, such as those related to dispersive systems, Schrödinger equations, and hyperbolic equations with specific characteristics. We also provide a brief overview of these physical applications. Lastly, we discuss how our constructs offer insights into the nature of singular solutions, which may provide a pathway to addressing the inverse problem of identifying a singular coefficient from its influence on the solution's singularity. This problem has implications in geophysics and astrophysics

This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese character-based models, we aim to overcome the inherent difficulties of Japanese word segmentation. Our findings reveal that LSTM can be an effective technique for this task, and when combined with character-based word frequency information, it surpasses the performance of existing models. Furthermore, we discovered that utilizing a character-level model in conjunction with word-based models or a character-based model alone yields the best results. As such, we propose a hybrid approach that integrates a character-based LSTM model for difficult words and a maximum likelihood-based model for easier words to achieve optimal performance. Our experiments demonstrate that this hybrid strategy, supported by word frequency information, achieves a remarkable character-level word segmentation accuracy of 92.30%, an improvement of 2.30% over previous models. Notably, our analysis focuses solely on the application of LSTM without incorporating any character-based models that have been introduced in recent years, aiming to provide an in-depth comparison of LSTM's effectiveness in Japanese word segmentation. We hope that this finding will serve as a foundation for future research to combine LSTM with more advanced character-based models. Our simulation code is freely accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/TJBigScene/JWS. Additionally, the Japanese word segmentation data set used in this study is called JWS2019 and can be downloaded from https://github.com/TJBigScene/JWS2019. It consists of 2018 Japanese text samples totaling approximately 414k characters and can be utilized for training neural network models for Japanese word segmentation. Our analysis further reveals that LSTM-brained models exhibit similar character-level error rates in Japanese word segmentation tasks as their non-brained counterparts, showcasing robust generalization capabilities. We see this as compelling evidence that LSTM can be an essential tool in the study of neural networks for Japanese word segmentation. Ultimately, our research enables the application of LSTM in practical Japanese word segmentation tasks, paving the way for its use in other character-based neural network models. We have successfully addressed the long-standing difficulty of applying LSTM to Japanese word segmentation, a challenge that has hindered the development of neural network-based models for Japanese word segmentation since the introduction of LSTM. Our findings not only improve the accuracy of Japanese word segmentation but also reveal new insights into the underlying characteristics of Japanese words. This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of adapting to different medical settings and professionals. 
In this research, we address the issue of extracting symptoms by using pre-trained and fine-tuned models, trained on diverse patient data, medical institutions, and specialties. 
To reduce dependency on specific data, we develop an adaptive strategy for extracting symptoms by temporarily removing commonly mentioned symptoms from the original data source.
Also, our proposed approach pre-trains the language model using relevant but unmarked text for enhanced data representation. 
Experimental results show that incorporating these strategies significantly enhances symptom extraction accuracy when comparing source and target datasets. 
For example, when applying our proposed method to a target dataset, the F1 score for full symptom extraction increased by 11.64% when using the BERT large language model. 
The source code is available for review at https://github.com/juliehong12/Domain-Generalization for Symptom Extraction. 
Our proposed method has been tested and validated in various clinical scenarios. 
It demonstrates excellent performance on target datasets, even when domain adaptation is unmarked, achieving near perfect results for extracting partial symptoms and certain full symptoms. 
However, it performs less well with more complex clinical concepts. 
Our study contributes to the advancement of zero-shot adaptation techniques in natural language processing, especially in extracting clinical symptoms. 
It further highlights the feasibility of using data reduction and pre-trained models that can adapt to new data sources for enhancing symptom extraction. 
Also, our research shows that specific data representations can facilitate generalizing to new domains and specialties, and that adapting models to new data sources can significantly enhance clinical symptom extraction accuracy. 
In future work, we intend to explore the incorporation of external knowledge for enhanced data representation and the use of supervised and semi-supervised natural language processing techniques for extracting clinical symptoms. 
We further aim to examine the efficacy of our proposed method in other related natural language processing tasks and its practical applications in clinical practice and other related domains. 
It has the potential to enhance both the automatic and manual extraction of clinical symptoms for improved patient care and decision-making. 
We further plan to investigate its potential for other clinical concepts, particularly those related to clinical outcomes and medical treatments.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. Additionally, we investigated how temperatures and magnetic fields impact the mass, radius, and gravitational redshift of spin-polarized strange quark stars. Our findings show that up to a certain critical temperature, an increase in magnetic field strength leads to a rise in radius and a decrease in gravitational redshift, whereas beyond this temperature, the effects of magnetic fields on radius and gravitational redshift invert. These studies aim to contribute to the ongoing exploration of quark star physics and provide valuable insights for prospective observations of quark star binaries. Our analysis also highlights the feasibility of examining quark star parameters using electromagnetic waves from individual quark stars or binary quark star systems, and it paves the way for further research in this field. Furthermore, this research rekindles the hope of observing quark star structures, and it offers a theoretical framework for confirming knowledge of quark star binaries. A computational method for resolving nonlinear eigenvalue problems is presented, using an approximating function derived from the eigenvalues of a modified eigenproblem equation.  By utilizing a variable sampling process that focuses data collection on the areas most critical to solution resolution, this algorithm efficiently distributes resources. It then employs the collected information to produce approximations for the sought-after eigenvalues and eigenvectors through further processing. Several numerical demonstrations highlight the performance of this solution strategy. It has been proven that eigenvector approximations have a rate of convergence equal to the order of approximation, whereas eigenvalue approximations achieve a convergence rate of twice the order of approximation. Furthermore, this method's computational complexity is shown to be directly tied to its approximation order. Numerical examples showcase the performance of this algorithm, revealing its ability to successfully produce accurate approximations, even at relatively low orders of approximation, particularly when handling cases with a limited range of varying parameters. It has been observed that this method excels in scenarios involving mixedroptic systems, outperforming existing solutions for both equally spaced and adaptively determined sampling points. In contrast, this algorithm displays superior performance when dealing with cases involving a smooth dependence of eigenpairs with respect to a parameter. Several strategies for enhancing the efficiency of this method are also presented, including the use of Krylov residual acceleration and the integration of quantum chemistry techniques, particularly the partitioning method. Numerical examples demonstrate the efficacy of these complementary methods. It is worth noting that this method can be easily adapted for use in both continuous and discrete settings. However, it is noted that the primary focus of this work is on resolving challenges in continuous problems, specifically nonlinear eigenvalue problems. Despite its primary focus on continuous problems, this method does exhibit some degree of success in discrete settings, as illustrated by numerical examples presented. These examples demonstrate that this method can also be utilized to resolve problems in difference equations, even when incorporating approximate operators. Notably, this method does exhibit some degree of success in both positively and negatively definiteness cases, as shown in numerical examples presented. Several future research directions are identified, including the development of modification mechanisms to mitigate issues arising from clustering and turning points, as well as exploring connections with related concepts in mathematics. Additionally, we consider applying similar adaptive methods to related problems in mathematics, particularly its analogs in perturbation theory and the gap approach. These potential research avenues are further discussed. This work presents a method for resolving nonlinear eigenvalue problems that leverages an approximating function derived from the eigenvalues of a modified eigenvalue problem

Finally, a practical analysis using bike-sharing data highlights the utility of DAC in uncovering valuable new insights. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and model interactions, specifically introducing Flatee - an efficient federated learning framework across these environments, that substantially minimizes both training and communication times, while remaining robust against adversarial manipulation. The authors evaluate the efficacy of Flatee using real-world scenarios, specifically remote medical image classification, and demonstrate its substantial performance benefits relative to existing state-of-the-art solutions. The source code for this research is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/EM-Lycee/Flatee. The study's results validate the potential of Flatee to strike a balance between security and performance, enabling its use in a variety of demanding distributed machine learning applications. The evaluation showed that Flatee can achieve $6.44\times$ speedup in training times and $10.05\times$ speedup in communication times over the closest baseline, while only slightly compromising test accuracy, while remaining largely effective against various adversarial attacks. This paper bridges the gap between compressed sensing and statistical learning, leveraging sparsity and structure to minimize the computational burden of learning tasks. We focus on independent component analysis through a compressive lens, demonstrating that certain properties within the cumulant-based ICA model yield a compact set of solutions that can be effectively represented within the cumulant tensor space. Utilizing a property that ensures randomness and coherence, we establish the existence of a compressive ICA scheme and propose novel algorithms, namely a cumulant-based hybrid Albertos algorithm and a deep learning-based federal learning approach, to realize the compressed ICA. Furthermore, we implement and evaluate these algorithms through experiments, which demonstrate their efficacy in the common statistical learning settings of Gaussian and speaker-independent speech recognition. The experimental results show that the proposed methods are viable alternatives to existing approaches, particularly in low-dimensionality learning tasks. A significant advantage of these compressive ICA algorithms is their reduced memory requirements, which becomes more pronounced in large-scale dataset evaluations, such as federal ICA. The federal ICA technique is also accompanied by a complementary method, joint independent component analysis, which we use to validate the proposed compressive ICA schemes. The accompanying technical document provides additional theoretical and experimental details. Two code repositories are available for public access at https://github.com/pksoh/compressive-ica. The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and binary relations are examined in this study.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, utilizing the same number of variables and one symmetric binary relation, whose set of model cardinalities increases linearly with $\Phi$'s model cardinalities. Furthermore, we observe that the models of sentence $\Phi'$ are all bipartite graph representations.  Consequently, we deduce that, in order to resolve Asser's conjecture regarding the class's closure under complement, we may focus solely on examining sentences with at most three variables whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Furthermore, the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons exhibits a temperature dependence inversely related to $\ln(T)$ in the low-temperature regime and is independent of momentum in the high temperature regime. We have numerically evaluated the thermal capacity and compressibility across a wide range of temperatures and found that at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity is linearly dependent on temperature, with the compressibility displaying a $T^3$ dependence. Additionally, the results we have obtained for the thermal screening length are in excellent agreement with existing results in the literature, which were derived using different approaches. We have also obtained an expression for the thermal screening length as a function of wave number $q$ and temperature $T$, which exhibits a $q/\sqrt{T}$ dependence in the low-temperature regime and is controlled by the chemical potential in the high-wavelength regime. These expressions provide valuable insights into the underlying physics of thermal screening in graphene and may have applications in understanding thermal screening in other two-dimensional systems. We have further observed that at very low temperatures, the linear temperature dependence of the thermal capacity, as well as the $T^3$ dependence of the compressibility, may not be observable if the system is subjected to a significant doping level, in which case the linear temperature dependence of the thermal capacity may be masked by a $T^{1/3}$ dependence inherited from the zero-density thermal capacity, as well as a term controlled by the Fermi function in the compressibility. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness. Evaluation metrics demonstrated improved performance on modern speech datasets, specifically in the Multi-Modal English conversational dataset, MindMeld, even when evaluating expressiveness and naturalness at the paragraph level. Code and model repositories are accessible at https://github.com Junyuyz/MaskedSpeech. Experimental results revealed that, compared to baseline systems, MaskedSpeech exhibited a 6.53% and 5.47% gain in perceptual ratings of naturalness and expressiveness, respectively, without undergoing human-in-the-loop re-ranking. Additionally, the best-performing model achieved a 0.72 MOS score increase in naturalness and a 0.34 MOS score increase in expressiveness. Our analysis points to the significance of accurately modeling long-range dependencies in neural speech synthesis for capturing contextual influences. Furthermore, integrating contextual elements remains essential even at short sentence lengths, underscoring the value of long-term information in the optimization of neural speech synthesis. Our work, marked by the first practical application of masking strategies in speech synthesis, sheds light on the efficacy of combining masked concatenation and coarse-grained semantic features in enhancing low-fidelity speech synthesis. Specifically, the addition of masked acoustic features and coarse-grained semantic features yielded a 0.72 and 0.34 MOS score increase in naturalness and expressiveness, respectively. Notably, our context-aware synthesis system, MaskedSpeech, demonstrated superior performance on task-driven conversational speech, specifically in the MindMeld dataset, through merely incorporating contextual elements during training. Our analysis points to the practical value of our findings, enabling high-quality speech synthesis in various contexts, and the versatility of our approach, which can be adapted for use in other languages and domains. Furthermore, our results suggest profound improvements in naturalness and expressiveness can be achieved through the incorporation of contextual elements in neural speech synthesis. Data collected during the experiment, totaling 35.9 fb^-1, was analyzed using several models that explain the creation of dark matter. This manuscript examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, as viable models for understanding the universe on a cosmological scale. We find that such spacetimes naturally incorporate geometric patterns suitable for describing irregular, periodically-distributed matter within the universe. We also establish mathematical proofs for their local representation, as well as the existence and uniqueness of the Einstein's equations under these specific spatial constraints. Notably, our research uncovers an interesting set of precise solutions, illustrating how these spacetimes can be used in cosmology to model a universe transitioning from homogenous, isotropic states in the early stages to more complex distributions with voids and matter peaks over time. This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible black hole spins in quasars that exhibit ultra-luminous radio emission. The novel method enables the constraints of the mass of ultralight bosons by considering the Scattering of these bosons on the black holes within the accretion disk, a process of superradiance. The analysis of heavy quasars indicates that the mass of these bosons is less than approximately $3.5 \times 10^{-15}$ or $2.42 \times 10^{-12}$ erg, depending on the rotational properties of the black holes, which is in line with the current experimental upper limits. The research supports the hypothesis that superradiance could be a reliable method for the detection of ultralight bosons, providing a link between particle physics and gravitation that requires to be investigated further. A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames and on very short wavelengths. The dynamic evolution of these storm sources remains largely unstudied due to a lack of high-resolution imaging data in metrewave frequencies. By analyzing data from the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), this research identifies a new aspect of these storm sources associated with minor flares. It reveals the existence of two distinct modes of co-evolution: a "sausage-like" mode, in which storm intensity decreases while size increases, and a "torsional" mode, in which storm size changes correlate with sky-orientation changes. The researchers have also observed, for the first time in this context, the transition of these storm sources from the "torsional" mode to the "saussian-like" mode, facilitated by a flare. These findings support the theory of increased magnetic stress in complex active region structures that later collapse into instability, producing flares and particle acceleration until they stabilize into less complex states. The discovery may offer new possibilities for identifying such active region phenomena in the future. The analysis of these storm sources also enabled the assessment of their structural stability using a statistical approach known as the Box-Plot, revealing that storm size and intensity tend to become less correlated as storm size increases. The data also enabled the creation of a new, comprehensive classification system for these storm sources, incorporating key parameters such as their sky distribution, shape, and orientation, as well as their movement and stability. The study laid the groundwork for future research on these storm sources, their behavior, and the underlying magnetic field configurations in a critical area of solar physics. It also identified new observational possibilities that could further leverage the capabilities of current and upcoming radio interferometers, such as the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), a greater understanding of these storm sources, and the dynamics of the accelerated particle beams and active region flares. The dynamics of a kinetic process involving the merging of a finite sphere of gas onto a black hole under varying parameters is analyzed. When the black hole draws in the gas equivalent to its own mass, the gas within the black hole's influence falls in and the merger occurs in a predictable, collisional manner. However, when the black hole draws in the gas equivalent to several times its own mass, unpredictable, collisionless dynamics take over and the merger occurs in an irregular, sphere-shaped pattern. This study reveals how factors including the black hole's mass, the gas's initial velocity dispersion, and the presence of angular momentum in the gas affect this process by creating an irregular, three-dimensional structure. This research also shows that large amounts of angular momentum in the gas cause most of it to miss the black hole and spares the black hole from absorbing more than it can handle. This finding is similar to the astrophysical phenomena of star formation. The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research targets a novel, automatic colorization approach, specializing in astronomical images and leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to learn a mapping between these images and their colorizations. We explore various model architectures based on the Wasserstein GAN framework, assessing the reliability of our method through the evaluation of multiple images, while also comparing its performance to established SR methods. The findings indicate that our proposed model delivers superior results for the task of colorization, achieving satisfactory outcomes with limited training data; nonetheless, further advancements are required to reach professional-level colorizations in astronomical images. Given the domain-specific nature of our task, we anticipate our method to be particularly useful for institutions and organizations working with astronomical datasets. We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our proposed algorithm rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate datasets, such as the Griewank function and the MNIST database for handwritten digits. Its mathematical formulation allows it to accurately approximate highly complex nonlinear functions with a minimal margin of error, and it also facilitates the solution of Partial Differential Equations. The approach works by determining the weights for each neuron in localized data subsets where a corresponding approximation matrix remains invertible, thereby rendering hyperparameter optimization unnecessary. As a direct consequence, this design yields faster ANN training times. With reduced computational complexity of O(Nd^2), where N represents the number of data points and d is the input dimensionality, our method outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, it refrains from introducing additional errors through backpropagation. When testing this method against other baseline methods, it achieved lower error rates on the MNIST database for intricate tasks following the Universal Approximation Theorem's guidelines for constructing ANN. Notably, it successfully implemented the method on a graphics processing unit (GPU) to achieve even faster computation times, surpassing other methods with up to 10 times faster performance. The source code for this method has been made publicly accessible at the following repository: https://github.com/rupakg/UANN. We visually demonstrate the efficiency of our weight calculation approach by comparing it to other ANN configurations such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLP), as well as sophisticated deep learning architectures like the VGG16, the ResNet, the GoogLeNet, the AlexNet, the Laplacian Neural Network (LNN), the Orthogonal Neural Network (ONN), and the Dynamic Graph Neural Network (DGNN). Compared to these models, our approach produced comparable or even superior results with reduced complexity. With its robust performance and simplicity, our numerical scheme has the potential to revolutionize ANN training techniques. The integrality of this method has been verified through thorough mathematical and numerical analysis. Establishing an additional set of linear constraints seems to resolve this issue, enabling the bias-reduced estimator to achieve a rate of bias reduction of O_p(n^-1).  To prove this, I demonstrate that under certain conditions, the bias of the estimator can be bounded by O_p(n^-1).  Following this, I show that the bias can be made to converge to zero at a rate of at least O_p(n^-1/2).  A key component of the proof involves analyzing the behavior of a specific linear combination of score parameters, and ultimately demonstrating that the bias of the estimator can be expressed as a function of this combination.  Building upon this understanding, I was able to modify an existing bias-reduced estimator for the mean absolute deviation, and show that its bias can be bounded by O_p(n^-1). The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction models, eventually finding this approach yielded improved
performance in relation extraction. Our proposed technique is versatile and can
be applied to a variety of existing models without making any modifications to
their original design. Furthermore, we demonstrated that this approach increased
the overall accuracy of existing models and provided even greater benefits when
applied to high-risk classes. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub
at https://github.com/abhirockzz/RE-KG. Experimental results showed that this
approach led to an average 1.5% improvement in F1 score across 20 datasets. On
the YELP dataset, an F1 score increase of 4.5% was recorded for models that
focused solely on relation extraction, while an increase of 2.7% was recorded on
the FB15K-237 dataset for models that focused solely on knowledge graph link
prediction. These findings align with our initial assumption and demonstrate the
benefits of sharing knowledge can be harnessed to boost the overall performance
of existing models in relation extraction. Our study also identified that a
multi-task approach yields greater benefits in scenarios involving difficult
datasets and models that rely on negative samples from real-world data to learn. 
In addition to our primary findings, we also conducted an ablation study to
evaluate the contribution of each knowledge graph when utilizing knowledge graphs
as diverse as Yelp and Facebook to improve the model's performance, recording a
general 0.5% improvement in F1 score across 20 datasets. Our study provides
reliable evidence that a multi-task approach based on knowledge graphs can be
trusted and relied upon to boost the overall accuracy of existing relation
extraction models. Knowledge graph link prediction models can be leveraged to
improve the overall accuracy of existing relation extraction models, as supported
by our study's comprehensive experiments. Our source code is publicly available
on GitHub at https://github.com/abhirock

The Analytical Exact Iteration Method has been employed to solve the N-dimensional Radial Schrödinger equation for complex-valued potentials, and further generalized to consider finite values of anisotropy, temperature, and baryonic chemical potential. Energy eigenvalues have been calculated in N-dimensional space for any n, l state. These findings have been used to investigate the characteristics of quarkonium states, such as binding energies and mass spectra, in the N-dimensional space. Notably, anisotropy was found to decrease the dissociation temperature of quarkonia in the N=0 and mu = 300MeV ground state. In the oblate case, anisotropy resulted in a lower dissociation temperature than the isotropic scenario. Furthermore, introducing a baryonic chemical potential led to the conclusion that the leading-order Debye mass exceeds the quasi-particle Debye mass. As a result, the former was found to yield lower dissociation temperatures than the latter for quarkonia in the N=0 and mu = 300MeV ground state. Finally, comparisons with previous studies on quarkonium properties in a temperature-chemical potential matrix, as well as calculations using N-dimensional quasi-particle Debye mass with finite baryonic chemical potential, demonstrated that our method is in line with these studies. Notably, our predictions of dissociation temperature and mass spectra in the infinite baryonic chemical potential limit aligned with the results from N-dimensional quasi-particle Debye mass with finite baryonic chemical potential. These predictions included the ground state dissociation temperature of J/psi and psi' being 133MeV and 194MeV, respectively, at mu = 300MeV and 400MeV. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. We attribute the disordered state in Tb3RuO7 primarily to the magnetic frustrations, caused by the differing internal magnetic fields imposed by the ordered terbium atoms on the two ruthenium species, leading to distinct behaviors. This specific phenomenon is considered to be uncommon within the family of Ru chains materials. Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. We're examining an alternative scenario where we have access to labels, but the learning objective is only partially aligned with them. This discrepancy leads to the discovery of a novel task, dubbed 'causal inference for learning', which resolves identity confusion and enables the creation of domain-invariant representations by focusing on the 'cause' of the learning objective and the domain shift. We've developed a novel algorithm that produces representations useful for both 'causal inference for learning' and general covariate-shift adaptation cases, and our approach exhibits superior performance in various applications such as semi-supervised learning, domain adaptation, and entropy-based semi-supervised learning. Moreover, our method produces more accurate results than existing techniques in tasks involving intrinsic causality and shows promising results in discovering causal relationships in non-intrinsic scenarios. It displays robust performance in cases of both the knowledge of the learning objective and the domain shift, and its application is diverse and encompasses supervised, semi-supervised learning, domain adaptation, and unsupervised domain adaptation scenarios. Additionally, our method produces representations with low dimensionality that exhibit high predictive value, and we've established the connection between our algorithm and existing techniques such as information-matching and causal generative adversarial networks. We've conducted comprehensive evaluations of our method, and it has been further demonstrated by various statistical analysis that our approach outperforms other competing methods in various tasks. Notably, we've discovered that our method performs especially well when the learning objective and the domain shift have a significant dependence on the 'cause' feature, and we've identified novel tasks for the 'causal inference for learning' scenario such as modelling the effect of driving behaviour on gas mileage or the role of genetics in the aetiology of diseases. A thorough examination of the underlying assumptions on the data was conducted, and we've proposed potential alternatives to these assumptions in scenarios where the underlying assumptions on the data do not hold. Also, we've established the connection between our method and the information-bottleneck approach and presented a novel information-theoretic interpretation of the loss function employed in our method. Furthermore, we've studied how the underlying structure of the data is recovered through our algorithm and the effect of different hyperparameters on the performance of our method, and we've demonstrated the superiority of our method over other competing techniques in a wide range of tasks such as domain adaptation, semi-supervised learning, and unsupervised domain adaptation scenarios.
