Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level. Additionally, this geometric model facilitates the analysis of distributed deep learning systems and the communication between network layers and nodes. Lastly, we demonstrate how geometric constraints can be utilized for regularization, exemplified by our evaluation of geodesic regularization in residual networks. Overall, this geometric model provides a unified and predictable understanding of deep learning architectures, enabling the interpretation of deep learning models and their algorithms. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ arising from the prime factorization of $d$ in relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Specifically, we investigate the occurrence of generators of such ideals among the lattice minima and explain their impact on the principal factorization type of the cubic field and its associated field extension when applying Voronoi's algorithm. Moreover, we focus on a specific class of cubic fields, namely those with discriminants that are powers of $3$, and demonstrate the feasibility of determining the principal factorization type in these fields by analyzing lattice minima. To support our conclusions, we present detailed computational results based on our theory for a large sample of cubic fields and field extensions. We also make a conjecture regarding the generality of our findings, particularly concerning the relation between lattice minima and generators of ambiguous principal ideals in number fields. To demonstrate the feasibility of our approach, we present a concrete example of how our theory can be utilized to determine the principal factorization type in a specific cubic field and its extension by $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ arising from the field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{48605},\zeta_3)$. To facilitate the computation, we utilize the functionality 'latmin-gen' within the software package MAGMA. A research framework is introduced to uncover and analyze decision-making processes from deep neural network classifiers in jet substructure tagging techniques. To achieve this, the study uses a novel method, incorporating 'augmented' variables, known as XAUG variables, alongside standard input, then applies a layer-by-layer relevance analysis to both types of networks. XAUG variables are merged with intermediate network layers and analysis is propagated backwards to primary inputs. Analysis of XAUG-powered deep neural networks reveals significant insights into their performance and behavior. Results show XAUG can enhance low-rank correlations in small datasets and propagate features through density-based estimators in simulated data. Visualizations and quantitative tools, including new variables, reveal insights into the inner workings of deep neural networks. Interestingly, XAUG analysis of a state-of-the-art jet substructure tagging network demonstrates that final activations are dominated by non-local variables, yet still capture valuable local information. Additionally, XAUG can effectively capture local features in deep neural networks on small datasets and propagate these to further layers. Importantly, the study shows that banding or density-based analysis of activated XAUG variables across events can be an effective, flexible, and user-friendly tool for understanding and potentially improving model performance and behavior. In particular, this technique is shown to reveal correlations and features in degraded radiation fraction data and dense energy clusters in hadronic decays. Further, the study demonstrates that expert XAUG variables can be used to analyze the inner workings of deep neural networks and that this technique is generally applicable to a range of techniques, including QCD-based jet mass and hadronic decays. Overall, the study shows that combining XAUG variables with a backward analysis of relevance in deep neural networks can provide new insights into their inner workings. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Our study, primarily focused on the fermionic Hubbard model, reveals that the new algorithm significantly decreases the computational cost associated with the determinant, thereby enabling us to perform simulations that were previously inaccessible due to the severe sign problem. Moreover, we demonstrate that these simulations yield highly accurate results by validating our findings with the known exact data on the fermionic Hubbard model's phase diagram. Our framework has the potential to be a valuable asset in deep learning-inspired computational quantum many-body physics, enabling the study of a wide range of intricate models suffering from the sign problem. Furthermore, this approach can be adapted to deal with a related problem encountered in bosonic systems, known as the fermion or particle sign problem. Our study also proposes an efficient procedure to generate suitable neural network weights for the transformation, which can be universally applied to a broad class of complex-valued neural networks. Our research thus offers a promising, efficient technique to tackle systems heavily impacted by the sign problem, allowing us to reach hitherto intractable system sizes and accurately obtain the desired statistical estimates. Our method can be a valuable tool in studying quantum many-body systems and it also shows great potential for being applied to a variety of models in diverse fields like condensed matter physics, quantum chemistry and biophysics. Specifically, mass ratios in these systems have been found to follow a distinct pattern, with the mass of the secondary proto-star (M2) increasing in proportion to the mass of the primary proto-star (M1) at lower masses, but failing to do so at higher masses. This notable phenomenon has been addressed by a team of researchers who carried out numerical simulations of binary formation to explore its underlying causes.

They conducted a series of simulations by increasing the total mass of the core to 40, 60, 80, and 100 solar masses, while also considering magnetically weak cores to see how binary formation patterns would change.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, incorporating feature engineering and multiple algorithm testing. Notably, our results indicated that the primary factor differentiating non-propagating rumors from those that spread is the presence of negative information. Furthermore, we found that the most effective features for predicting a rumor's spread include its topic, urban-rural distinction, and online health discourse. Lastly, we applied our findings to design an intelligent system for detecting and inhibiting harmful rumors based on real-time data processing and feature extraction. Our proposed method demonstrated superior accuracy over traditional machine learning methods, specifically 94.12% on a test set comprising news titles and categories. We successfully developed and released an open-source system in collaboration with Tencent Computer Society, ultimately contributing to pandemic control efforts by providing a data-driven approach for rampantly spreading rumors about the COVID-19 pandemic in China. This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used in a fully connected neural network for classification of urban areas, specifically to identify specific types of roofs and construction materials based on a subset of AIRSII dataset. Our findings reveal that all methods yield substantial classification improvements when trained on reduced, discarding dimensions without significant loss, and perform best at compressing dimensions 260-301; however, AE and DAE produce slightly lower accuracies overall due to introducing noise during compression, which can impede feature extraction in this particular dataset. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that hyperspectral pixel classification benefits from dimensionality reduction spectral methods, particularly those centered around 260-301 dimensions. Additionally, our study shows that supervised dimensionality reduction methods (AE, DAE) outperform their unsupervised counterparts (PCA, KPCA, ICA) in this specific urban roof and construction material identification use case. The proposed dataset and codes are publicly accessible for reproduction of our results at https://github.com/SamMarques/Hyperspectralclassification. The AirII dataset can be downloaded from http://www.pgay.purdue/cal/airsII/. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. Our objective is to explore the existence of this trainable sub-network in the realm of natural language models, and we will accomplish this by examining and evaluating the most recent model compression techniques, such as quantization, knowledge distillation, and pruning. We will also examine other areas such as language model pre-training, transformer architectures, and joint compression and optimization techniques that involve learning. Our results show that combining these techniques yields significant reductions in model size without affecting performance and a related code can be found at https://github.com/erogulla/compression-of-natural-language-models. Our findings also suggest that previous approaches have concentrated on the low-level aspects of compression and have overlooked promising higher-level techniques such as pruning and knowledge distillation. We therefore recommend future research to focus on the other approaches that have been less successful so far. Additionally, we observed that previous efforts in compressing models and understanding the structure of NLP systems lack a unified comparative framework, and we therefore propose an evaluation metric to compare different techniques and models. Our evaluation metric and related code can be found at https://github.com/erogulla/evaluation-of-natural-language-models. We used JET to evaluate and compare different compression and learning techniques for NLP and we were able to demonstrate the existence of a near-optimal sparse sub-network in NLP models and we were able to achieve significant reductions in model size without affecting performance. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function choice affects performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. We also demonstrate that combining multiple loss functions using weighting can serve as an effective means of resolving this parameter, facilitating efficient exploration of deep learning models. Our techniques are illustrated by example classifications, supported by comprehensive numerical evidence and open-sourced for public access. Our research suggests that future work should involve systematically evaluating loss functions over time and possibly re-optimize them periodically, similar to adapting learning rates, in addition to examining how data density and class distribution impact our findings and investigating the application of our techniques to models employing vector quantization and hashing methods. Furthermore, we propose several theoretical contributions, including an innovative method for deriving loss functions from probability density functions and a novel classification framework based on clustering-like loss functions. Our study offers theoretical insights and facilitates efficient optimization of loss functions, enhancing the overall stability and accuracy of neural networks. By adopting this approach, we can develop more robust neural networks capable of withstanding attacks and providing stronger security protections in scenarios like malware detection and adversarial training. In contrast to existing research on loss function evaluation, our work focuses on thorough justification and seeks to understand the underlying principles, rather than merely evaluating performance, as we seek to develop more intelligent learning strategies. Through our investigations, we discovered that certain loss functions exhibit consistent and robust performance, whereas others show significant variations depending on data distribution, leading us to propose the notion of loss function stability as an essential criterion. Moreover, we observed that certain loss functions could achieve better performance than others but proved difficult to optimize, whereas others required significant modifications to accommodate binary and multi-class data, highlighting the need for loss function adaptation. Our study also shed light on the relationship between loss functions and model accuracy, as well as the impact of hyperparameters, and we introduced an innovative approach for automatically selecting loss functions and hyperparameters through global optimization. A new approach called GW-EPF is developed to investigate the mechanism of exciton condensation within the framework of GW approximation based on first-principles calculations. This method focuses on the critical behavior of electrons undergoing a phase transition and allows it to condense into a lower-energy state. Applied to the monolayer of TiSe2, the results show that the excitonic effect plays a significant role in the superconductivity of this material and needs to be considered within a finite energy range rather than asymptotically. Furthermore, the observed softening of the phonon mode in TiSe2 is linked to the formation of a bond between electrons and holes, which is caused by electron-phonon interaction rather than an intrinsic mode. Additionally, the GW-EPF method reveals that the charge density wave (CDW) in TiSe2 is primarily driven by electron-phonon interaction but also involves excitonic effects, and the material's SC/CDW coexistence can be understood within the same theoretical framework as a result of competing energy scales. Finally, the observed CDW in TiSe2 is found to persist deep into the superconducting regime, and the GW-EPF method predicts a higher critical temperature for Sperating the SC and CDW phases than what is currently observed. Given its level-of-theory independence, the GW-EPF method can be applied to other materials to investigate exciton condensation and its relationship with other many-body phenomena. Finally, the results of these calculations confirm that TiSe2 is a unique material in which the boundaries between superconductivity, charge density wave, and exciton condensation are blurred. The implementation of the GW-EPF method will be made publicly available through the APF library. This study provides essential insights for understanding the electronic structure and phase behavior in strongly correlated materials. Based on these results, the possibility of exciton condensation in other 1D and 2D superconductors needs to be reevaluated. This research paves the way for future applications of the GW-EPF method in a range of theoretical and experimental contexts. Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Our approach has been successfully tested on multi-class image classification tasks, such as the ImageNet Reduced dataset, and yields improved performance over current state-of-the-art methods. Our method may be adapted for use in reinforcement learning by replacing the discriminator with an action classifier. Our code is publicly available at the repository address. 

Keywords: active learning, transformer, ImageNet, deep learning, computer vision, generative adversarial networks, reinforcement learning.

Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework. Furthermore, this paper examines an extension of the harmony condition, tailored to accommodate both cut rules, yielding an intuitionistic version of this modified harmony condition. Lastly, this paper shows that this intuitionistic modification results in a duality-compatible version of the harmony condition. This theoretical framework's benefits can also benefit other proof-theoretic approaches to analyzing logical concepts, as witnessed by an examination of an alternative formulation of S4 logic's cut-elimination theorem. Ultimately, this paper argues that the harmony condition offers a distinct, evidence-based understanding of cut-elimination. Introduction to the Computational Ludics framework is provided in the appendix. Readers familiar with this framework may skip to Section 2. Additionally, the paper offers an overview of key concepts from both the framework and its extension to second-order logic, as well as an independent proof of cut-elimination for S4. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance. We evaluate the proposed method in complex 2D and 3D state spaces and find that it yields better results, both in terms of efficiency and effectiveness, when compared to existing approaches. Notably, when applied to a 3D navigation task, human labeling time was reduced from 548 hours to just 189 hours while achieving comparable results to a task optimized for human labels. Crucially, we observe that even when using poorly defined region boundaries, our method continues to perform well, indicating its robustness and utility in real-world applications. Overall, our proposal provides a practical solution for balancing human labeling costs and optimal reinforcement learning performance. The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, initially modeling treatment and outcome using machine learning, then adjusting predictions with ATE estimators.  While machine learning techniques have improved the first step, the second step has received less attention despite its equal importance.  A new method, Normalized Augmented IPW (NAIPW), closes this gap by incorporating the first step predictions into the second step via the ATE estimator.  NAIPW enhances the accuracy of treatment and outcome predictions, as well as the robustness of standard errors, without increasing computational complexity.  Through simulations and a case study analyzing college enrollment rates by income, NAIPW demonstrates superior performance over traditional IPW methods.  NAIPW offers a simple, efficient solution to enhancing machine learning-based causal inference.  The package naipw in Python enables users to execute the proposed NAIPW method. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficient sampling is possible using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Finally, parameter values are then extracted through a straightforward transformation. We present results from simulations involving models of both identical and non-identical extreme rainfall in Cumbria, UK. The novel method is found to improve sampling efficiency when comparing parameters from different sites. The findings of this research support the use of the parameterisation method for Bayesian inference on extreme value parameters based on a Poisson process. In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario involving the linear Markov decision process and finding that even with the adversary only modifying the reward in the data set, a certain threshold of optimality gap cannot be avoided. Conversely, in contrast to robust supervised learning, which has seen significant breakthroughs with little dimension-related impact and similar theoretical bounds to the non-robust variant, our worst-case analysis reveals a significant increase in the optimality gap as the number of herbs (dimensions) grows, albeit with the degree of growth dimpling down. Despite this challenge, we introduce specific assumptions about the data set, which allows us to adapt and offer a robust policy through the adoption of the worst-case worst-performing policy determined by the data set. Our theoretical findings show promising results and suggest that making small adjustments in the data set can lead to nearly optimal outcomes, which is something we plan to explore in future research, including developing algorithms based on this approach. Additionally, our methodology, which is novel and unrelated to existing methods, can be adapted into an algorithm that performs well under particular data set assumptions, even when the percentage of compromised data is not known in advance, exhibiting robustness across various percentages of compromised data and exhibiting promise in preliminary simulations. Ultimately, our study opens the door for future research into robust offline RL, which we believe has vast potential. The code for this research is shared publicly. We hope that our research will contribute to a robust offline RL framework that will enable safe and efficient learning in a variety of real-world applications where data may have been compromised. 

Keywords: Adversarial Machine Learning, Reinforcement Learning, Offline RL, Robustness, Decision Theory.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison. We propose utilizing a testing framework that simulates gradual data changes to standardize performance assessment and provide a critical analysis of the limitations of current methods in identifying out-of-distribution examples. In addition, we introduce an improved method for out-of-distribution detection that incorporates data augmentation and prior knowledge of class distributions. This approach achieves superior accuracy on in-distribution data and competitive results for background shift examples, while also providing more plausible predictions for semantic shift data. However, it falls short in handling challenge data, highlighting the difficulties in effectively detecting out-of-distribution examples, particularly for semantic shift, and highlighting the need for future research in this area. Our code and data are publicly available for reproduction of our results. We hope this work will contribute to clearer definitions and a more nuanced understanding of out-of-distribution detection and detection failure to advance the dialogue in the community. From a theoretical perspective, our findings also suggest that certain data discrepancies can arise from disparate probability distributions of labels, even in the absence of actual label data, which has implications for deep learning and data analysis. In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two given functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M$ and $M$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to pairs of $n$-dimensional vectors, $g \otimes_f h$ is calculated as the sum of the products of the function values of $g$ and $h$ for each possible pair. This framework encompasses multiple other well-known convolutional problems. A naive approach for computing $f$-Convolution would involve exhaustive enumeration, however this can be improved upon. We propose an alternative algorithm utilizing Fourier transform-like techniques for an efficient computation, when certain conditions are met. Specifically, if the domain $D$ can be expressed as a union of discrete additive sets $A_i$, and if the function $f$ complies with certain requirements, then a new algorithm can be obtained with a time complexity of $M^{O(n+1)}$. This is in line with many known special case results. We further demonstrate the applicability of this new algorithm in computing three specific convolutions, known as the $n$-fold homomorphic convolution, the $n$-fold semidirect product convolution and the $n$-fold lexicographic convolution, for which specific time complexities were previously established. We verify that these results are indeed achievable with our new algorithm. We also present a more general theorem, allowing for the computation of an even larger class of convolutions, known as generalized convolutions. These can be defined by a system of inequalities, as long as certain conditions are met. We establish a time complexity of $M^{n+1} \cdot \log^2 M$ for such a computation. This new class encompasses the $f$-Convolution we initially considered, as well as further examples. We further examine a related problem, involving the search for vectors satisfying a given set of conditions, which can be expressed through the use of convolutions, as well as other algebraic structures. With a distance of tens of astronomical units from its host star, GJ 229B exists near the boundary between the planetary and stellar domains, offering an opportunity for its atmospheric analysis to shed light on formation mechanisms. By utilizing a novel approach involving a high-resolution model of spectral interdependence, we were able to investigate the influence of clouds on the dwarf's observed emission and discovered a perfect agreement between theoretical and observational data without the necessity of atmospheric features alteration or photoerosion to explain the anomalous properties of GJ 229B's spectral energy distribution. With a reliable solar irradiance spectrum, we were able to investigate the role of chemical species and clouds in shaping the dwarf's atmospheric features and spectrally active emission, revealing a good agreement between our model and observational data, particularly in regions sensitive to atmospheric thermal structures and chemical compositions. To describe the anomalous properties of GJ 229B's spectral energy distribution, we proposed a model involving dust opacities, which were found to adequately explain the observed emission at wavelengths over 3.7 $\mu$m without the necessity of atmospheric features alteration or photoerosion. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In particular, our study combined three-dimensional models with two-dimensional plumes to evaluate the transmission risk between two people, incorporating factors like respiration, speaking, and coughing. Additionally, our research involved modeling the movement of a person through a bus to examine the impact of surrounding airflow on the spread of pathogens. Our results revealed how pathogens spread within a bus are influenced by turbulence and circulation patterns caused by passenger movement, contradicting a previously distributed and widely-used "well-mixed model". The latter model failed to consider the effects of turbulence and passenger motion on airborne pathogen circulation, leading to inaccurate predictions of transmission risk. Consequently, we used our research to create a graph showing how varying the bus occupancy and turbulence levels affect infection probability, thereby providing a useful outcome. Ultimately, our study's findings highlight the limitations of relying on the 'well-mixed model' for predicting disease transmission on urban buses and encourage the development of more realistic and varied models of airborne pathogen circulation to inform public health policies. Such an approach could enable more precise assessment and guidance for specific environments, like urban buses, by factoring in unique factors that influence airborne virus transport and transmission risk. Moreover, we suggest that similar models can be applied at larger scales, like offices and other enclosed spaces, to inform infection risk assessment and mitigation strategies. In that sense, our research could contribute to the ongoing discussion of reopening economies during the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly by considering the potential impact of increased mobility and circulation of airborne pathogens on disease transmission dynamics. Lastly, our study also highlights the practical usefulness of numerical models in understanding and predicting infection risk, thereby making them a valuable resource for public health officials and policymakers. In that sense, we propose that numerical models like the ones we used in our research could serve as a useful tool for informing infection risk assessment and guiding disease transmission mitigation strategies. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work proposes a formal model for double-sided auctions that adheres to standard ISL0 specifications, allowing for both price-based and log-linear representations. To test the accuracy of this model, we create and test non-verifiable and verifiable price-based and log-linear auction models using the ISARMarkov tool. Our findings demonstrate that small errors in price-based models can lead to significant price discrepancies and supply/demand mismatch issues, but the log-linear model remains accurate even with modified parameter values. Furthermore, we observe that a 1% error in bid/ask pricing can result in 30-40% incorrect unit prices and the verifiable log-linear model offers better price stability compared to the verifiable price-based model. Finally, we note that the double-sided auction verification process demands substantial logarithmic stability, which may not be achievable with certain parameter values on widely used operational market systems and highlight potential remedies. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of double-sided auction verification and the characterization of stable log-linear systems. Moreover, they shed light on the implications of small error magnitudes in economic contexts and the potential price fluctuations due to such errors. In addition, they underscore the importance of verifiable models in price-based matching systems to prevent severe price instability issues. Lastly, they point out the need for further research on the theoretical log-linear stability of double-sided auctions to support formal verification of such systems. To facilitate this inquiry, we publicly release the verification results and provide interactive vignettes that allow users to explore the effects of modifying parameter values in double-sided auctions. These resources can be accessed at https://formalbreakeven.com/publications/Double-Sided-Auctions.html. Alternatively, the ISML double-sided auction model can also be accessed at https://formalbreakeven.com/isdml2/dda.isml. The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large data sets, yet the effectiveness of this method diminishes in cases where strong nonlinearity affects its accuracy. Conversely, sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics is able to model complete system models successfully, yet it is limited by its inability to separate pure displacement signals from other movements. We aim to overcome these individual drawbacks by integrating the strengths of both techniques and developing a new method, the Linear and Nonlinear Disambiguation Optimization (LANDO), which trains a kernel to differentiate between linear and nonlinear components of system dynamics. By doing so, LANDO refines the dynamic mode decomposition technique and provides a more accurate understanding of system behavior. Our work includes applications to different systems of various dimensions to verify its effectiveness. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Furthermore, we explored fractional upward embeddings and established two new positive parameterized results. We proved that detecting upward plane embeddings is fixed-parameter with respect to module-number or feedback vertex set, but showed that the module composition parameter is XP at best. Finally, we investigated the parameterized complexity of detecting upward tree-decompositions and planar embeddings with certain angle constraints. Our study significantly expands the applicable domains of previously known upward embedding detection algorithms, particularly improving their time complexities. Using parameterization, we have also successfully approached an earlier NP completion claim and confirmed that detecting upward embeddings is indeed NP complete, resolving an open problem since 2003. Our work uses the concept of parameterized substrategap to ensure adequate node arrangements in the SPQR layout method. We propose this concept for future practical use as an indicator of algorithmic tractability in graph embedding problems. Our findings are corroborated by extensive computational testing, which shows that parameterization can sometimes yield practical solutions even for large graphs. On the other hand, parameterization can also aid in ruling out certain algorithmic approaches by identifying potentially sprawling solution spaces. Our study presents a new perspective on graph embedding problems, suggesting that parameterization can offer design insights and new techniques to explore graph embedding challenges. To illustrate this, we present an alternative algorithm for constructing upward simple paths in graphs, which is only feasible due to the parameterization of the underlying graph structure. Our work is a testament to the versatility of parameterized computation, demonstrating that even discrete parameters can facilitate computation. We hypothesize that this discrete parameter may lead to more practical algorithms if we lock it at a fixed value, and propose this idea for future investigation. Moreover, we conjecture that this discrete parameter is equivalent to graph treewidth and propose this conjecture for future verification. Furthermore, we present an open problem for the parameterized complexity of detecting upward simple cycles in graphs. Our study is a collection of novel algorithmic findings and new concepts, and we hope that this work will contribute to the advancement of parameterized algorithmic research in graph embedding

Image-based goal navigation is a fundamental problem in computer vision. Previous methods use goal-related images as memory cues to guide navigation. However, they fail to utilize previously collected data. Despite being readily available, these memories often lack significance and would require an infeasible search for retrieval. This paper introduces MemoNav, a model that tackles information overload by employing a novel method to selectively gather meaningful memories, demonstrating improved navigation outcomes when compared to existing techniques. MemoNav leverages a dual network design, where one network assesses the relevance of memories and another prioritizes the collection of important memories. Both networks are trained in an end-to-end fashion. Experimental results demonstrate that MemoNav consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, showcasing superior overall performance with the added benefit of reduced memory retrieval time. Additionally, human evaluations confirm the high informativeness of the memories collected by MemoNav. Our implementation details, including video links and the model's code, are available on our website at https://memonav.github.io/. This model has been successfully tested on environments with 100 and 400 objects, achieving notable gains in navigation performance. Specifically, on the Environment101 benchmark, MemoNav increased the success rate by 5.7% and reduced the navigation time by 34.6%, while on the Environment400 benchmark, it increased the success rate by 11.6% and reduced the navigation time by 18.6%. These advancements were achieved with memorized items, thereby enhancing generalization. MemoNav's design is versatile and can be applied to various computer vision tasks with comparable effectiveness. This research could lead to breakthroughs in vision-and-language navigation, as well as other related areas, by addressing the long-standing challenge of effectively leveraging collected memories to support vision-based navigation. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Ultimately, our research facilitates a deeper, broader understanding of operator growth and entanglement dynamics within Lie-symmetric systems.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. The paper provides information about the breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state by employing a novel experimental technique. The investigation of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state, rather than through the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state, can be performed through an advanced analysis of the energy distribution of the three $\alpha$ particles from the decay. Using beta-delayed charged-particle spectroscopy on $^{12}\mathrm{N}$ via the Texas Active Target Time Projection Chamber, a highly sensitive measurement of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay ratio can be made without interference from overlapping events. The analysis using a Bayesian approach reveals that the direct decay fraction is less than 0.043% at the 95% confidence level. This value is in line with previous studies and the small influence of finite range effects on the decay analysis is observed. Such a high precision measurement of the direct decay fraction strength confirms that the Hoyle state mainly exists as an $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ system consisting of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital. The statistical weight of the structure representing three non-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is greater than 99.8%, indicating that this system can be accurately described by the conventional non-orthogonal cluster model. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially for the capacity, by offering Direct Sales or Wholesale models with standard Quality of Service agreements. This research examines the validity of these models among Commercial and Industrial Content Providers, revealing significant drawbacks. First, the models hinder fair competition among Content Providers, as those paying more for bandwidth cap their competitors' access to quality content. Second, the models force Content Providers to reveal sensitive financial information. Third, the models inadequately compensate ISPs for the capacity they sell, as the costs don't reflect the volume of data transferred. To address these concerns, this paper proposes a model in which ISPs negotiate profit-sharing agreements with Content Providers, determining the amount to pay for quality content deliveries. A corresponding game-theoretic approach allows for finding individual rational outcomes, ensuring the stability of Nash Equilibria. This design enables multiple Content Providers to share costs, prevents price collusion among them, asks only general financial questions, and rewards ISPs for data volume, not initial capacity requests. This model can be implemented using standard profit-sharing methods and is particularly beneficial for large Commercial and Industrial Content Providers. An analysis of actual data for selected companies in three European countries demonstrates that our proposed approach could significantly lower their expenses for quality content deliveries. This design does not assume knowledge of future data transfer volumes; therefore, risks and uncertainties surrounding this design are minimal. An initial simulation in Python confirms that a profit-sharing model offers better outcomes for Content Providers and higher revenues for ISPs compared to the current direct and wholesale models. This research offers theoretical and practical contributions, marking an important step towards a joint, profit-driven architecture for the entire online content ecosystem. Key findings include the following. Firstly, we prove that the local defining ideal associated to a given Hessenberg function within this specific coordinate system can be decomposed into vertices. Lastly, applying our analysis, we derive an explicit splitting of a key region of Flags(ℂ^n), effectively decomposing its local defining ideals across all indecomposable Hessenberg functions. This achievement is coupled with existing work on indecomposable Hessenberg functions to achieve a comprehensive decomposition of the entire Flags(ℂ^n) space. ADHD is a widely prevalent psychiatric condition that has been challenging to diagnose accurately. In contrast to prior studies, which often relied on the entire brain, this study focused on pinpointing the essential regions for utilizing a deep learning model. By using rsfMRI data from the ADHD 200 global competition, the researchers employed leave-one-site-out cross-validation to derive an integrated outcome. Notably, their findings indicated that using merely 15 crucial regions of interest for training yielded a 70% accuracy rate, surpassing the existing benchmark of 68.6% achieved with all regions. Furthermore, the researchers developed and tested novel models, namely Separate Channel CNN RNN with Attention, Separate Channel dilate CNN RNN with Attention, and Separate Channel CNN slicing RNN with Attention, to identify the most effective structure. A fundamental concept called von Neumann entropy is employed in quantum information theory to measure disorder or uncertainty, with applications including characterizing random quantum states and estimating quantum communication complexities. In this research, we introduce two novel, highly efficient algorithms for approximately calculating the von Neumann entropy of a quantum system: the first, a quantum algorithm, achieves an approximate result with a margin of error $\varepsilon$ in $O\left(\frac{\tau^2}\varepsilon^3+\frac{N^2}\varepsilon^2\right)$ quantum computations, while the second, a quantum-learning-with-classical-postprocessing algorithm, reaches an approximate result with a margin of error $\varepsilon$ in $O\left(\frac{\tau^2}\vareassistant\frac{N\log N}{\varepsilon}+\frac{N^2}\varepsilon\right)$ quantum computations, assisted by classical processing. Both of these findings significantly reduce the previous best-known estimates for non-trivial applications, which were influenced by classical computing limitations, now overcoming a long-standing velocity barrier for approximating von Neumann entropy, especially when $N>>\tau$. Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed by recent studies using machine learning techniques to forecast diagnoses based on CTNs. We have discovered through data analysis that using CTNs for diagnostic coding is not feasible due to several issues. This study presents an innovative solution to utilize CTNs for coding purposes by integrating them with electronic health records (EHRs), particularly medical records that include coded data. We develop a new semi-self-supervised approach, consisting of two phases - generating and selecting - to identify relevant CTNs that contain sufficient coding information to aid the coding process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through successful forecasting of ICD-10 codes from CTNs using a robust model, achieving a high convergence rate of 0.994 and scoring 0.764 in terms of mean absolute error. Furthermore, we show that our proposed method can enhance coding accuracy by 10% when compared to using CTNs alone without any prior medical records. This study offers two valuable contributions: first, it highlights the limitations of using CTNs for diagnostic coding, providing insight for future research; second, it presents an innovative and efficient method to integrate CTNs and EHRs for accurate forecasting of diagnostic codes. Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup due to a lower asymptotic complexity of $O(N^{3/2}K^{1/2}\log{P})$ with $N$, $K$, and $P$ representing the number of data points, clusters, and data dimensions, respectively. Furthermore, the algorithm achieves a notable reduction in variational circuit complexity, allowing for an up to $5.9\times$ faster execution time on a noisy device compared to a deterministic algorithm. Using highly precise numerical devices in our experiments, we've studied the behavior of variational solutions and observed that our method exhibits well-defined and healthy solutions similar to their deterministic counterparts, even in scenarios where the optimal solution may not be unique and clusters overlap. Additionally, we've verified the effectiveness of our clustering method with highly accurate results in distinguishing quantum states of up to three qubits, opening the door for quantum machine learning applications. Our work presents a novel approach to addressing multiple challenges in quantum computing, including coherence loss, limited gate fidelity, and limited observation precision, using a combination of low-frequency measurements and data compression techniques. The techniques developed here can be easily adapted to various quantum information processing tasks, such as measuring the entanglement of multi-qubit states and characterizing quantum processes. We've successfully tested these techniques on a superconducting qubit processor with up to seven qubits, leveraging the inherent data compression properties of our quantum clustering method to significantly reduce the required circuit complexity. Our experiments have consistently aligned with numerical simulations, demonstrating the effectiveness of our techniques and providing valuable insights into the behavior of variational solutions. We've further verified the applicability of our techniques in various quantum computing scenarios, including distinguishing quantum states of up to three qubits and characterizing quantum processes. The techniques presented here have the potential to address fundamental limitations of current algorithms, facilitate data-driven state preparation, and offer valuable insights into the nature of quantum states. The novel approaches developed here can be adapted to tackle complex problems in diverse fields, such as chemistry, materials science, and physics

Our analysis encompasses all prime-field microlensing planets from the 2018 dataset provided by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder, revealing 24 total discoveries or recoveries - ten previously unpublished planets with definitive or probable planetary nature: KMT-2018-BLG-2004-Squint, OGLE-2018-BLG-1126, and seventeen more characterized by their planetary nature based on various criteria. Together with three previously published prime-field planets, a detailed sample of twenty-one prime-field planets is presented. Using the method of De and Bennett [2022], the distribution of planet masses in the sample is analyzed, showing it complies with the mass distribution model established by Rice et al. [2022] for their sample of secondary- and prime-field planets. A comparison between our mass distribution analysis results and that obtained by De and Bennett [2022] using their model but a different dataset shows consistent findings. Our analysis further verifies that prime-field planets tend to have smaller planet-to-star mass ratios than those found in secondary planets. Building upon this finding, our study also explores various methods to identify planetary candidates that can be classified as having a small planet-to-star mass ratio in real-time anomaly data. Lastly, our research recovered the planet of planet 2018-BLG-1126, confirming its small mass ratio and verifying that its true parent star is a white dwarf, thus characterizing its planetary nature in the process. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Our method offers superior performance over the current state of the art in various 3D rendering-based inverse problems such as scene understanding, appearance and rigidity recovery, and geometric shape recovery, as evidenced by our results and code releases. Additionally, our method has been successfully applied to recover texture and rigid pose in real-world vehicles. The obtained results are also compared to the outcome of a simplified phase model where the oscillations' amplitudes are eliminated under an adiabatic process. The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree construction time. Demonstrating statistical equivalence on a temporary basis reveals that combining these methods accelerates spanning tree generation without altering their uniform distribution properties. We've developed a dual approach, the ABW algorithm, allowing for distinct exploration stages - first examining the current and previous tree structures, and second generating a new set of edges - to achieve a faster sampling speed. The ABW algorithm has been implemented in an open-source environment for validation purposes. Testing reveals that the ABW variant with the largest examination stage range produces the fastest sampling speeds, and while it doesn't reach the efficiency of the state-of-the-art best-first search method for small tree-size scenarios, it outperforms all other considered algorithms in terms of computation time for larger tree sizes. Lastly, we have successfully used the ABW algorithm to solve a previously proposed challenging problem and provided an alternate solution. The study's results indicate that merging the probing stages of Aldous-Broder and Wilson's algorithms generates uniform spanning trees at a faster rate, and this finding has practical value in applying random spanning trees to tackle complex problems. However, adding variable refractive index significantly changes how we assess stability in the dark solitons. Notably, only isolated (weakly trapped) solitons are stable, while solitons in finite-energy systems with embedded radiation modes lose energy and eventually collapse. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement during the modular coil design process, leveraging planar control coils and integrability objectives to improve quasisymmetry and nested flux surface volume. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by optimizing a coil set inspired by NCSX design, which not only achieves a range of rotational transform targets but also surpasses the NCSX design in nested flux surface volume. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future.

By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, driven in part by the proliferation of systems supporting content creation, sharing, and management. Among these systems are tag-based platforms that enable users to collaborate in annotating shared items such as images and URLs, leading to user-generated metadata pools and collaborative behavior. To unlock this potential, a comprehensive understanding of current systems is required, which involves characterizing them based on usage patterns, the underlying social processes they facilitate, and the resulting benefits. This study addresses this gap by systematically evaluating and comparing 29 social tagging systems across multiple dimensions, using established metrics for reuse, temporal analysis, interest overlap metrics, and collaborative patterns. Our extensive review leads to several significant findings, highlighting key differences and similarities, outlining best practices, and revealing areas for improvement as well as new research directions for the social media and collaboration research communities. Notably, while reuse dominates most systems, they exhibit unique patterns of user involvement, varying levels of interest sharing, and distinct patterns of user collaboration that can inform the design of future applications. Interestingly, systems with similar purposes and designs exhibit differing levels of usage and collaborative behavior, suggesting the necessity of tailoring systems to their specific user groups. Furthermore, user engagement in these systems tends to be stable over time, with interactions becoming more complex and collaborative over time, which could be attributed to various factors. Our study also uncovers correlations between usage metrics, reveals the effectiveness of user-generated metadata, and identifies areas for future collaboration and interaction within these systems. Ultimately, this work presents a comprehensive picture of current systems, offering actionable advice and guidance for designers and researchers seeking to develop novel applications and theories in collaboration and social media. Additionally, our study provides a basis for comparing future systems and enables empirical analysis of the theoretical underpinnings of social tagging systems, which could lead to a deeper understanding of the underlying social processes involved. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address the need for standardized evaluation procedures in lifelong reinforcement learning, we introduce a comprehensive framework called L2Explorer, built around a powerful AI model that can learn and adapt to a diverse range of tasks within a rich, video game-style environment. This framework enables the study of key aspects of lifelong reinforcement learning, including transfer learning, curriculum learning, and multi-task learning. By utilizing advanced observation capabilities and controlling multiple robotic characters, we simulate a scenario in which an AI must navigate and interact with a three-dimensional world while performing a variety of tasks, similar to searching for hidden objectives. Our evaluation framework incorporates a robust testing procedure that evaluates the ability of models to adapt to new tasks, generalize across multiple settings, and learn autonomously from experience, among other key assessment metrics. Furthermore, we have developed a benchmark environment called OpenL2E, comprising a set of core challenges and supplementary extensions with modified gameplay and simulation parameters that mimic real-world conditions, including the introduction of new elements, altered dynamics, and disappearing objectives. Our research employs a multi-faceted approach to evaluate the efficacy of different lifelong reinforcement learning methods within this benchmark environment, and the resulting findings provide a thorough understanding of the performance of various techniques. The source code for L2Explorer, including the framework and benchmark environment, is now freely available under an permissive license, and we invite the research community to build upon this technology and contribute to the advancement of lifelong reinforcement learning. In the future, we plan to expand the range of tasks within OpenL2E to cover even more realistic scenarios, and we envision a future in which AI models can effectively learn and adapt to complex and dynamic problems in real-world domains. The development of standardized evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments will play a crucial role in driving this advancement, and we believe that L2Explorer and OpenL2E can serve as valuable tools in achieving this goal. Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be installed at Keck 1 in 2023. This instrument will be a combination of four near-infrared devices, utilizing the Keck Advanced Laser Time-Average Telescope (KALTIM) technique to enhance its sensitivity and coverage. Liger's Data Reduction System (DRS) is currently in development, and this paper will detail the planned software architecture and interactions within the instrument framework. Additionally, we will discuss key components of the Liger DRS, such as data extraction and correction, spatial motion correction, and image reconstruction. We will also present a preliminary calculation of the expected performance and efficiency of the Liger DRS. This work is part of a collaboration between the California Institute of Technology and the Keck Observatory, supported by the Keck Observatory Long Range Tenth Plan and an iSPF award from the Keck Observatory.

Due to anisotropic splitting in the cavity, ground state degeneracy is lifted, yielding fine structure modes along the trap's axis and orthogonal to it. This study's primary objective is to provide evidence and disproofs for the deterministic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang type equations including non-local gradient elements. The specific focus lies within a particular class of nonlocal problems formulated on a compact manifold without a boundary. The formulation is based on an equation which combines a sum of two Laplacians with a nonlinear coefficient and an additive term resulting from the product of another coefficient and the mean curvature. The considered variables and their derivatives up to the second order are part of the combined entity. The considered class of nonlinear problems incorporates a wide range of equations, such as the modified KPZ equation, the fast diffusion flow with a nonlinear diffusion component and the gradient dynamics of van der Waals interaction. The considered problems can be reduced to one spatial dimension for analysis purposes. The primary tool employed in the analysis is the approach of a priori estimates where the focus is on the determinacy and the dependence on initial data within the selected class of solutions. The selected class of solutions is part of Bocconi's Sobolev space and its subspace. The key finding is the proof that solutions belonging to a particular subspace of Bocchi's Sobolev space are determined solely by the properties of the initial data. The  COVID-19 pandemic, triggered by SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. As a result, the world is relying heavily on public health precautions such as social distancing measures to curb the virus spread and maintain the healthcare system functionality. With the isolation of communities, access to reliable information has become restricted. Consequently, the health minister in South Africa updates the public every day on COVID-19 infections, including affected individuals' demographic and travel details. Meanwhile, the National Institute for Communicable Diseases provides daily updates on testing numbers, case counts, and fatality rates via infographics but often fails to release patients' ages or other critical transmission details. Recognizing the need to effectively share this information, the University of Pretoria's Data Science for Social Impact research team developed an open-access data platform comprising a data warehouse and an online dashboard, enabling transparent and efficient data sharing. This endeavour revealed challenges pertaining to data availability, credibility, and governance in public health crises within South African context. This research aims to address these concerns by presenting the successful implementation of a public-facing data platform as a model solution. Additionally, the study offers invaluable insights for other academic and research institutions seeking to replicate this initiative, as well as guidance for policy makers looking to leverage available data effectively to address the COVID-19 outbreak. This research is a collaborative effort involving the University of Pretoria's Data Science for Social Impact, the University of the Western Cape's Forensic Data Analytics and the National Institute for Communicable Diseases. This research is a rapid intervention, acknowledged by the National Research Foundation as an approved and funded project (number: R5I-5-2020). This research will continue to evolve as long as the COVID-19 pandemic persists, providing daily updates through the publicly accessible data platform at <https://covid19.up.ac.za/> and the publicly available data sets at <https://up-dsfi.github.io/Covid-SA-Open-Data/> and can also be accessed via the University of Pretoria's Data Science for Social Impact. This research is a public effort to address the data-driven concerns and share information efficiently, as well as a model solution for data governance and sharing in public health emergencies. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. Such instances are referred to as near-arithmetical. Additionally, it's observed that subsets meeting this criterion, of size k, and contained in the integers, I, exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions even if we allow a k/4 fraction of elements in A to be freely chosen. It's noted that this behavior is akin to that of a k/2 k/2 k/2 1/4 pseudocompact space, which is topologically distinct from a compact space. The proof involves reinterpreting the criterion as one describing near-arithmetical structure in the above-mentioned space when it's endowed with a specific \sigma-compact generating set. It's observed that local arithmetical structure within subsets of size k, and contained in I, can manifest as a global \sigma-compact structure in I when endowed with a specific generating set, which is compact, and results from combining all possible first k terms of arithmetic progressions that are contained in I. It's noted that this \sigma-compact structure can exhibit pseudocompact behavior, even if it's topologically distinct from a compact structure, which arises from combining all possible first k terms of arithmetic progressions that are contained in I. The proof also involves a novel application/interpretation of a result by Bergelson, Hindman, and Aluísio Burroni. In medical contexts, diverse information often arises from various sources, which when combined enables healthcare professionals to form more precise opinions. For retinal analysis in particular, recent advancements have led to increased use of multiple imaging methods: standard two-dimensional fundus photographs and more detailed three-dimensional imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography. Our study employed three distinct multimodal data fusion strategies centered on deep learning to tackle challenges in retinal analysis: early combination, intermediate fusion, and hierarchical integration. Noting that early and intermediate fusion approaches typically fail to exploit information shared by different data sources to their full extent, our hierarchical method focuses on fusing characteristics from various dimensions within a network, while also uncovering connections between disparate datasets. We implemented these strategies on classification tasks involving glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy using a mix of public and proprietary OCT-based datasets, which demonstrated that our hierarchical method performed optimally and laid the groundwork for improved diagnostic procedures. Considering the case where $\Omega$ is a 2 or 3-dimensional ball, and the functions $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ only vary depending on the radial distance $r$, we find a sequence of transmission eigenfunctions that tend towards zero as the radius increases. This property states that the weighted $L^2$ norm of $v$ or $u$ remains small near the problem's boundary. This is equivalent to saying that the weighted $L^2$ norm of $\mathbf{n}^2 \frac{\partial u}{\partial \mathbf{n}}$ or $\sigma \frac{\partial v}{\partial \mathbf{n}}$ remains small near the problem's boundary. To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and facilitate its practical use, discovering new intent categories from user inputs is essential but remains understudied. Current methods are often inefficient, inaccurate, and require extensive labeling. We address two key research questions for this challenge: first, how to enhance the representation of utterances for intent discovery; second, how to effectively identify intent categories from user inputs with limited supervision. We propose a novel end-to-end framework called Pre-trained Contrastive Intent Discovery (PCID) to tackle these questions. PCID leverages a pre-trained language model to improve utterance representation, employs a self-supervised contrastive loss function to reduce noise, and combines multi-grained information for more accurate intent discovery. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of PCID over existing methods on standard benchmarks and showcase its ability to handle complex real-world scenarios effectively. The code and trained models can be accessed via a shared repository. PCID has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency and effectiveness of intent discovery. For example, our model achieves a high accuracy of 0.9165 an adaptive number of iterations on the Schema.org dataset with only 10 minutes of training time. Additionally, our method exhibits notable success in reducing false positives to less than 5% on the Yelp Classification dataset. These findings validate the research questions that enhanced utterance representation and contrastive learning are crucial for high-performance intent discovery. The significance of our work lies in its potential to streamline the intent discovery process, enabling a rapid and efficient adoption of our model in practical scenarios. Moreover, we show that our method can successfully identify novel intents not listed in the training data, including new Amazon Review dataset categories identified through our model. These novel intents were later verified as valid and useful by domain experts. Our work and associated code/Models can be found at https://github.com/jtimo/jtimo.github.io. A detailed analysis is provided on the coupled system of these variables in terms of 3D consistency, Lax pair, bilinear form and continuum limits. The analysis reveals that the variable S1,0 itself adheres to a 9-point lattice equation and upon continuum limiting, it is related to the Lax pair's eigenfunction of the Korteweg-de Vries equation. Interestingly, the S0,0 variable is connected to a 7-point lattice equation in the discrete context, whereas its continuum limit corresponds to a constant. An underlying idea behind these findings is that higher-order lattice equations tend to have increased support points in the discrete case, whereas they become constant in the continuum limit. This concept may hold potential for future research applications. Lastly, special parameter conditions leading to 1D and 2D lattice equation formulations for S0,0 and S1,0 are identified, along with their corresponding Lax pairs.
