We've conducted a thorough analysis of the source of these errors and found that the underlying cause lies in the self-correlation within proposal boxes. To overcome this challenge, we've developed a novel proposal representation technique utilizing spatial attention to emphasize relevant region features. By doing so, we've significantly reduced the false positive rate, with code available on GitHub and experiments conducted with the Minipatch dataset, showing notable improvements over existing methods. Our proposed technique has the added benefit of increasing TP-R, enhancing model efficiency by reducing proposal numbers, and facilitating stronger baselines. We've demonstrated superior performance with our proposed method in the Minipatch dataset evaluations. Additionally, we've strategically designed a new dataset, called the Synthetic False Positive Minipatch Dataset (SFPMD), to further simulate and address the false positive issue, serving as a resource for the research community. We've observed considerable reductions in false positives on the SFPMD using our proposed method. We plan to make this dataset publicly available to aid in advancing the research in VRD. Our approach is flexible and can be adaptable to other computer vision tasks with similar box-level data. A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It's demonstrated that the QCC is directly linked to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) by a factor dependent on weak measurement strength. However, this measure only captures a portion of a quantum system's quantum nature in contrast to the TQD. Furthermore, our results reveal that remaining quantum features can be extracted not only via further von Neumann measurements but also through a series of infinitesimally weak measurements. We exemplify these outcomes using a Bell-diagonal state. Additionally, our findings highlight the significance of non-trivial empty circles in quantum interaction diagrams, which were previously overlooked in analysis. We hypothesize that these structures may play a crucial role in understanding the inherent quantum characteristics of a system in a way that's difficult to grasp through existing measures. To support our theory, we also introduce a new approach to studying quantum entanglement, which we illustrate using Bell-diagonal states. This novel approach, referred to as quantum connection cost (QLC), allows us to delve into the underlying connections underlying quantum systems and their inherent quantum properties. A crucial advantage of this measure is its capacity to distinguish between quantum systems of differing connectivities, a property we illustrate using an example. We conclude by noting that both QCC and QLC offer fresh insights into the quantum nature of a system and its relationships and can be applied to various practical scenarios involving quantum communication where understanding and quantifying quantum correlation is crucial. Moreover, these measures may contribute to the development of more precise quantum teleportation techniques. In contrast, our proposals differ significantly from existing theories as we've introduced distinct methodologies and perspectives on quantum interaction and connection costs. We anticipate that these novel ideas will stimulate further discussion and research in the field. We've also provided a detailed, step-by-step derivation of QCC and QD expressions in Appendix A, alongside additional technical support in Appendices B, C, and D. Moreover, the associated code used for numerical computations is available at a public GitHub repository, as mentioned in Appendix D. We've followed the standard guidelines for numerical calculations as outlined in the journal's authors' guide and provided all relevant numerical data and context in the main text and appendices. Additionally, the associated code can be utilized for replicating the results by running the included scripts. We've ensured the transparency of our approach by making the underlying code publicly accessible. We've used publicly available software and tools

We propose a new graph neural network called dynamic graph message passing network that efficiently models long-range relationships by adaptively selecting relevant nodes in the graph. This is particularly important in computer vision applications where prioritizing structural information over redundant information is essential. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders, demonstrating a strong correlation with the number of LUTs required. Our enhanced model accommodates intermediate precision truncations, enabling selective data loss and thus, data recovery. We prove that optimal MCM models are solvable in polynomial time when certain conditions are met. However, most cases fall under the NP-complete category. Our experimental results show significant improvements over previous methods, especially for large data sizes and when intermediate precision is limited. These findings validate the proposed hardware cost model's effectiveness and the importance of considering the data range when seeking optimal MCM solutions. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub. \\

The intersection of quantum computing and deep neural networks has recently given rise to a growing research field, known as quantum deep learning. Despite previously being separate entities, advancements have revealed that quantum circuits share parallels with artificial neural networks, paving the way for widespread adoption. This paper delves into the foundational aspects and core principles of quantum deep learning, highlighting key breakthroughs along the way. It also explores the challenges inherent in quantum deep learning research from multiple viewpoints, followed by a discussion of prospective future directions and practical applications. Additionally, the appendix provides a detailed benchmarking analysis of widely used quantum deep learning libraries. This comprehensive review is intended to serve as an entry point, enhancing understanding of quantum deep learning for academia and industry professionals. Experimental evidence and practical examples are presented to illustrate the differences and similarities between classical and quantum models, with an emphasis on fully connected quantum neural networks. Furthermore, the manuscript illustrates the practical implementation of quantum deep learning models using cutting-edge quantum circuits, leveraging examples in Google Tensorflow and PyTorch quantum. Finally, the limitations and potential hurdles in quantum deep learning research are examined, followed by an analysis of promising areas of exploration. High-definition hyperspectral images possess the capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments. We explore the application of hyperspectral images in detail-level semantic segmentation through an inherent objectivity boost resulting from their enhanced object differentiation. A bi-focal fusion strategy utilizing hyperspectral image cues in conjunction with conventional RGB images leads to improved performance. Specifically, an extended hyperspectral encoder integrated with an RGB feature enhancer and a bi-focal decoder with simultaneous RGB and hyperspectral decoders enhances the semantic segmentation quality on the Cityscapes dataset. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques on the Cityscapes 34-category benchmark while showcasing comparable performance on the 19-category dataset. Notably, our approach excels even when training only on the dataset's partial annotations. We also introduce a novel evaluation metric and demonstrate the essential role of hyperspectral images in this novel framework. Through qualitative analysis, we observe that the proposed method on partially labeled data reaches a comparable level of performance to that of fully labeled datasets but with increased object differentiation. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/SagivLuz/HyPeS.iers.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. This unique case adds to our understanding of a complex and dynamic process that may influence how stars like our sun cool and evolve. It also highlights the significance of zonal flows in shaping this evolution, particularly through tidal inertial waves that may be stimulated by a nearby companion, and how these flows compare to those caused by a star or planet that has been engulfed by the star. Finally, these flows do not appear to be caused by the star's conventional magnetic activity, and have not yet detected any signs of a star-star or star-planet interaction, although further observation is needed to confirm or rule out these possibilities. In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new set of fundamental principles for the RAM model and deriving a significant outcome from these principles. Specifically, we demonstrate that if a RAM with bit size n can perform basic arithmetic operations like multiplication and division in constant time with a limited number of additions, then so can a RAM with a linear number of processors, performing these operations in constant time with a fixed number of additions. Unfortunately, this proof relies heavily on the P $\neq$ NP hypothesis, as conventional techniques for showing the impossibility of certain operations would not apply to this specific scenario. Additionally, we note that even though certain previously IMPOSSIBLE operations are now possible under specific conditions, they remain impossible in all other situations. These findings lead us to propose a new problem regarding a specific type of RAM with unique properties. This research contributes to algorithmic literature by providing a revised foundation for the RAM model and opens up new avenues for future research in algorithmic literature. The primary techniques employed in this research involve limiting processor capabilities and examining the consequences of sharing workloads among processors to establish the impossibility of certain operations. This research presents a novel method for generating LCD codes using group rings and a standard transformation that maps group ring components to a subring of $n \times n$ matrices, resulting in LCD codes that are also group codes due to being ideals in a group ring. Under specific conditions for the group ring element $v$, the proposed construction yields reversible LCD codes, which includes the case when $v$ is invariant within the group. Furthermore, necessary and sufficient conditions are established for LCD code existence in the context of group rings. Additionally, a previously unaddressed aspect of group rings regarding LCD codes is the existence of non-existent codes, which can be determined by examining the determinant of the $n \times n$ matrix. Lastly, several examples of group LCD and reversible LCD codes are presented along with their respective parameters. This study finds that the group ring construction offers more flexibility in generating LCD codes compared to previous methods. Moreover, the example of a reversible LCD code with premium parameters, specifically a rate $0.875$ binary reversible LCD code of length $256$, has not been previously reported in existing literature. This research is a continuation of previous studies on LCD codes and group rings and provides fresh insights into the field. We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero homology classes in the graph complex, providing novel perspectives on the cohomology structure and forging links between graph theory, motivic Galois groups and quantum field theory. Specifically, our integrals enable the computation of homotopy groups of the general linear group and its relation to graph connectivity. Ultimately, our study marks a significant breakthrough in understanding graph cohomology through period integrals of invariant differential forms. This research provides fresh insights into the deep graph theory implications of our findings. Notably, our work offers a new interpretation of graph homology and cohomology and establishes a novel connection between graph theory and algebraic topology, extending beyond previous findings. Additionally, our integrals indicate a profound relationship between graph theory and the motivic fundamental group of the space of metric graphs, a key concept in algebraic geometry and the study of which offers numerous unsolved challenges. Our integrals also suggest the existence of an interesting map from the graph complex to the singular chain group of the general linear group, paving the way for further research in the area. Furthermore, our project develops novel and innovative techniques to express invariant differential forms as rational integrals over the graph moduli space, a key achievement facilitated by our previous study on the algebraic Torelli map and its associated map to the graph moduli space. We conclude our research by highlighting the diverse applications and implications of our findings, coupled with the numerous unexplored challenges and open problems in the field that our work has uncovered. We specifically note the pressing problem of computing period integrals through a direct method, an inquiry that stems from our study and holds significant significance in the field of algebraic geometry and graph theory. We further point out the unresolved issue of establishing whether all graph homology classes can be expressed as period integrals, an area of study in which our work provides crucial insights and has yet to be fully elucidated. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  Notably, our findings are consistent with the category-orthogonal feature theory, suggesting that auxiliary variables are essential for processing categories with shared visual features, like vehicles and furniture.  This research provides the first evidence of category-orthogonal features being transmitted between recurrent neural networks iterations.  Overall, our results illustrate how recurrence in recurrent neural networks can enhance object categorization by sharing auxiliary variables across iterations.  This research provides evidence supporting the role of recurrence in object categorization and highlights the importance of transmitting auxiliary variables across iterations to achieve superior performance.  This study is the first to demonstrate transmission of category-orthogonal features across recurrent neural networks iterations and sheds light on the processes underlying this transmission.  Future work can build upon these findings to investigate how these features affect other tasks and conditions and examine the specific role of different feature types in object categorization.  Additionally, developing new architectures that efficiently transmit auxiliary variables could yield improved practical outcomes.  Lastly, these results may lead to new strategies for designing object categorization systems, such as combining feedforward and recurrent models, and could have practical implications for developing self-driving cars that can navigate cluttered environments. Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for one-dimensional systems with a single synthetic dimension, along with $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry and spin-parity symmetry. We also investigated the properties of an extended Hatano-Nelson chain, which demonstrates substantial correlation effects; interactions abolish the skin effect that exists in the non-interacting system. The findings of this study underscore the instability of the skin effect against correlations, which is consistent with the reduced point-gap topology in one spatial dimension. The discoveries presented here provide novel insights into the topological characteristics of correlated systems, thereby initiating new areas of research within the field of non-Hermitian topological physics. Our analysis also sheds light on the reduced point-gap topology in one spatial dimension, which serves as a significant representative system for studying correlations in non-Hermitian topological systems. The underlying mathematical framework of this reduction can be generalized to multiple synthetic dimensions and is likely applicable to various systems beyond one-dimensional systems. The findings of this study are further substantiated through numerical simulations of a two-site lattice, which showcases the decreased point-gap topology resulting from correlations. The reduction of point-gap topology in one-dimensional systems with correlations indicates that correlations cause a degradation in the topological classification, which may lead to novel phenomena and new routes to realize topological non-Hermitian systems through interactions. We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in more resilient controllers. In addition, we discover that using the optimal Pre-Conditioned Recurrent Kriging approximation of the dynamics function, rather than the standard Gaussian Process model, significantly boosts performance. Our findings are substantiated through practical experiments in robotic balance and walking tasks. This research presents a breakthrough in developing robust controllers using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which up to now has focused on optimality rather than robustness. This study offers a new perspective on Robust Reinforcement Learning that combines constraint-based methods with traditional approach. Most importantly, this research delivers a practical test of Pre-Conditioned Recurrent Kriging, a highly efficient method of scaling up Gaussian Process models to large datasets. The resulting tools have successfully solved the balance problem for the humanoid robot Jaco and have also been adapted for walking on a 7-DoF robot called LWR. Our research has also sparked new areas of inquiry such as adapting the constraining method to work with multiple types of uncertainty and exploring the connections between entropy and regulatory control. We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive Scott model is achievable. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, unlike other approaches to dealing with partiality. Furthermore, we formalize a proof that any PCF program over a base type can be transformed into an equivalent Scott model denotation, utilizing a predicate that identifies total or terminable programs. While some properties of the Scott model denotations necessarily necessitate inference, we find that nearly all key properties including surjectivity can be formally proven without such inference. Finally, we provide an additional theorem that establishes a bijective relationship between the denotations of equivalent PCF programs, which requires a particular understanding of equality in univalent type theory as initially described by Coq-equipped with type univalence and later by Isabelle/Matrix and by Lean. This proof highlights an important insight into the nature of PCF and its denotations as traditionally understood within set theory, and serves as a positive example of the versatility of univalent type theory in formalization. Moreover, this proof underscores that many key results can be formally proven without necessitating any assumptions not inherent to the base theory. We use the proof assistant Isabelle/Matrix and Lean to formalise the above results. We particularly note that lean offers a practical and efficient toolset to work with, and provides support for a Scott model and lifting monad through the, for example, basic lifting framework and Scott model frameworks respectively, which have however been adapted and extended to suit the constructive framework of univalent type theory. We draw particularly note on the useful and efficient toolset that lean provides in this particular area. We conclude with a observation that predictively and constructively dealing with partiality as provided by the lifting monad and employed in this formalisation and many other areas offers great versatility to formalisation tools and can provide a viable and practical tool to use. We employ a predicative and constructive approach to deal with partiality, which provides a versatile method to deal with it as demonstrated by many areas such as modelling dependent type into univalent type theory

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without excessive computation time. Additionally, the developed framework is versatile and can be applied to various mobile robot configurations with unique shapes. The associated video can be found here: https://youtu.be/jGK27zOzAcY. The developed code is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/AE-Lab-CMU/MRA_CBF. More information can be found on our project website: https://mra-learn.com. Expansion of this work to real-world systems is currently in progress. Key Findings: The proposed QBC approach exhibits better performance in tracking while avoiding obstacles, particularly when factor-ing in the robot's spatial structure, resulting in an average time complexity of O(k^3)*log(k). Comparison with other methods reveals its efficiency and scalability, with notable improvements in computation time for both simple and complex models. The development of a quick and efficient algorithm enables real-time application on real-world systems, with human-in-the-loop testing and results expected in the near future. Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to directly calculate the nondegenerate locus. The method employs Gröbner showbases and signature vectors to determine the nondegenerate locus without relying on saturation ideals or equidimensional decompositions. The method also generalizes to multivariate polynomial systems with an arbitrary number of equations. The nondegenerate locus has been obtained for iconic algebraic varieties, such as ellipses, parallelograms, circles, cardioids, astroids, lemniscates, spirals, rational normal curves, and Nash manifold. The method further allows for symbolic computation of projective equidimensional decomposition and projective nondegenerate locus. The proposed algorithm has been independently verified and validated using interactive proof systems to enhance reliability. The method has been implemented as a part of the Gröbner basis software package, Mathematica, with documented documentation and example cases showcasing its applications. The study further estimates that the computational efficiency of the algorithm could be 15 times faster than existing methods for moderately complex cases. The theoretical complexity of the algorithm is analyzed in terms of bit size, with a specific expression that reflects this, and is shown to be directly proportional to the number of monomials in the polynomial system. The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the tetrahedron graph under our novel framework. The codegree squared sum, or co2(G), is introduced to measure codegree magnitude in a 3-uniform hypergraph, with exco2(n,H) representing the maximal codegree squared sum among n-vertex H-free hypergraphs. Utilizing flag algebra computations, we determine the codegree squared extremal numbers for K4^3 and K5^3 and demonstrate associated stability properties, revealing the structural resemblance of extremal K4^3-free hypergraphs to the conjectured extremal hypergraphs of Turan's tetrahedron problem. Additionally, we identify key general characteristics of exco2(n,H), such as the existence of a refined asymptotic approximation and the existence of extremal hypergraphs possessing high symmetry. The codegree squared extremal numbers now stand as prominent candidates for capturing the underlying structure of extremal hypergraphs. Furthermore, our findings provide significant insight into the classification of extremal hypergraphs across a broad range of hypergraphs. The novel framework of codegree magnitude measurement also encompasses measurement of higher magnitude codegree, such as the codegree cube or codegree fourth moment, allowing for the investigation of even more intricate properties of extremal hypergraphs through the analysis of their moment vectors. Thus, our work opens up new avenues for exploring the underlying structure of extremal hypergraphs, as well as the potential connections to complementary problems in extremal combinatorics. The codegree magnitude framework may also be applied to the examination of extremal values in diverse objects, such as point configurations and algebraic varieties. Consequently, the proposed framework may contribute a fresh perspective to the study of extremal values in a broad range of mathematical objects. The novel concepts and corresponding extremal finite tools developed in this research may also find applications in the analysis of infinite objects, such as measure spaces and continuous structures, as demonstrated by an accompanying example in distribution theory. The extremal finite tools and corresponding concepts could also be utilized in novel fields, such as infinite extremal theory and quantum mechanics. Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus generating considerable interest among scientists in the fields of astrophysics, physics, and particle astrophysics. We thoroughly analyze the distinct characteristics of gamma-ray pulsar halos, with a focus on their distinct features, and review theoretical models aimed at understanding the underlying physics and to predict observable properties using simple formulas. Lastly, we highlight potential research opportunities and necessary advancements for further study in the areas of pulsar halo identification, gamma-ray pulsar halo measurement, and theoretical development. With significant prospects for future breakthroughs, particularly in the study of cosmic-ray propagation and particle production, and with the impending arrival of the Cherenkov Telescope Array, this field is poised for substantial growth. Pulsar halos may also act as indicators for undiscovered pulsars, with a potential increase in their detection rate expected in the coming years. We anticipate an exciting and productive future research endeavor in the field of gamma-ray pulsar halos. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel based mask editing for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results with limited training data.
Our evaluation of multiple Convolutional Neural Network architectures confirms their effectiveness for weather classification, and our code is publicly accessible for others to build upon our research. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving an accuracy of 93.6%, and validating the utility of data augmentation for small-scale datasets. Moreover, our evaluation reveals the pre-trained ResNet-18 model can accurately classify weather conditions with an accuracy of 92.9%, and integrating sensor data with image classification can reach an accuracy of 94.9%. Additionally, our evaluation of vehicle-mounted camera data confirms the potential of our approach for real-world weather prediction, with an accuracy of 85.4%. Furthermore, our proposed method demonstrates improved robustness to perturbations over existing models, and our approach to weather classification is comparable to that of top-rated classification models. Soft grippers are increasingly popular in robotics due to their versatility and flexibility, despite limited use in industry thus far. A key hurdle has been employing model-based control strategies, given the difficulty in developing and maintaining accurate models. This research proposes an innovative solution where a reduced-order model is created and updated in real-time using an iterative process that doesn't require explicit model parameters. Using the Koopman operator theory, the approach relies on measuring the output and using data-driven methods to detect deviations. This model can then be utilized for the development of models and controllers. To demonstrate its efficacy, experiments were conducted on a soft gripper using digital twin technology to demonstrate precise control capabilities. The results show successful reproduction of multiple grasping strategies using this novel approach. Furthermore, online detection of anomalies and changes in system dynamics is also possible, enabling the model to adjust and improve its representation of system behavior. This capability is particularly useful in systems with varying dynamics. A comparison with traditional machine learning methods is also presented, demonstrating the superiority of this approach in terms of computational efficiency and predictive performance. This research aims to facilitate the practical application of model-based control techniques in soft robotics. A significant advancement towards this goal is making model updates and system control both conceptually and computationally connected. The proposed method is a crucial step in realizing this goal. Moreover, the research provides a useful contribution by democratizing the use of advanced mathematical theories in robotics. Specifically, the model's focus on system behavior and its detection of anomalies can enable novel representations and interpretations of soft robot dynamics. This research also enables the exploration of new challenges in control theory that incorporate learning and adaptive updates. For example, developing optimal control strategies that work in the presence of unknown system parameters and limited knowledge of system outputs. These theoretical advancements are closely tied to the characteristics of soft robotic systems, which present practical obstacles to developing effective models and controllers. To overcome these limitations, the proposed method employs data-driven learning and adaptive updates to the model. As a result, the developed controller and model are highly adaptable and responsive to changes in system behavior. Future work using this approach will focus on extending its applicability to multi-fingered soft grippers and verifying its efficacy in a variety of grasping tasks and applications. Extension to the use of multiple sensors is also being considered to broaden the framework's capabilities. One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given model, which can be achieved through an iterative process called gradient descent (GD) until the cost function reaches its minimum point. Nonetheless, the GD method may not always reach the minimum point due to its simplistic nature. In contrast, natural gradient descent (NGD), an adaptation of GD with a metric tensor, ensures a downward trajectory toward the minimum point. Nonetheless, the metric tensor is notoriously difficult to calculate in practice. This paper presents a novel method to circumvent this challenge by defining a universal metric tensor from the Fisher information matrix and demonstrates its application on four different machine learning models: linear regression, logistic regression, feedforward neural networks, and restricted Boltzmann machines with a positive matrix derivative. The proposed method successfully lowers the cost function at a faster rate than GD and outperforms other optimization methods such as ADAM and RMSProp in the given examples. Moreover, the proposed method exhibits a level of regularization that prevents overfitting and enables the use of larger step sizes, which can also be interpreted as a form of eligibility trace in the context of reinforcement learning. In summary, the proposed method serves as a reliable alternative to NGD for many machine learning models. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Building on this foundation, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding an unprecedented 89.3% concordance in predictive accuracy using a dataset from 422 non-small cell lung cancer patients. Moreover, this model facilitates the discovery of critical underlying patterns, thereby enabling researchers to gain a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between different data modalities and their collective value in informing survival time predictions. Upon evaluation using 50 holdout cases, this model exhibited an impressive 0.744 McAuley for predictive accuracy evaluation. Crucially, this study is the first to analyze the impact of multimodality, revealing a substantial 26.3% improvement in predictive accuracy when integrating visual medical scans with text-based clinical information. Additionally, cross-validation experiments revealed a consistent 88% concordance in predictive accuracy across 422 patients, thereby validating the efficacy of this model in survival time prediction. Furthermore, this study was successfully replicated using data from multiple different cancer types, demonstrating the broad applicability of this model and approach. With its exceptional performance and broad applicability, this research presents a groundbreaking solution for survival time prediction, which could significantly contribute to clinical decision-making and patient care. The code for this model is available in public repositories for reproducibility purposes.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies. We also introduce a set of standardized benchmarks for natural language state representation learning tasks. These benchmarks encompass a diverse range of scenarios, including the use of extensive datasets, multiple agents and modalities (such as images and speech), and a varying number of available actions. We hope that by establishing these benchmarks, we can foster a more cohesive body of research, facilitate comparative analysis across different approaches, and promote the development of natural language state representation methods that are both versatile and efficient. We experiment with several benchmarks, revealing a significant gap between the performance of modern natural language models and the optimal performance achievable through adversarial training. This gap is more pronounced in tasks involving multiple modalities. We also investigate the use of natural language models in various reinforcement learning techniques, such as policy-based methods and value function estimators, and find that they achieve greater success when employed in tasks involving a single modality. Nonetheless, a significant disparity remains between the performance of these models and that achieved adversarial training. Finally, we demonstrate that using an adversarial state representation and multiple episodes can enable natural language models to address representation learning problems. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained in a zero-shot manner. When access to the original data isn't possible, a pseudo-soft label assignment method based on network decision boundaries is proposed and tested. Experiments on multiple networks and datasets demonstrate that decision-based black-box knowledge distillation can achieve comparable results to distillation methods with access to the original data and parameters. Additionally, this method outperforms other black-box knowledge distillation methods in various scenarios. The code and additional information can be found at https://github.com/zwang1999/ZeroShotDBB. Our method has been tested on CVPR 2022 and this report describes the results in detail. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a novel Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. This Co-Imitation Learning approach takes advantage of peer agents' performance experiences without requiring expert input. We break down the problem into two components: first, peer agents' performance experiences are converted into valuable expertise through the analysis of their policies, and second, the extracted expertise is utilized for the learning agent's benefit. Our proposed method is a two-stage process that involves peer agents' behavior analysis through Model-Based Approach and the application of this analysis to support the learning agent through Model-Free Approach. We evaluate the Co-Imitation Learning framework in diverse reinforcement learning environments and find that it offers a substantial improvement in performance compared to existing methods. Moreover, our framework exhibits a versatile range of applications, including third-party tool utilization and peer-agent assistance. We highlight the benefits of our Co-Imitation Learning framework and identify areas for its further development and incorporation into future research. Our code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/farzad700/CoImitationLearning. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate the axion parameters, including the axion decay constant, to the neutrino parameters within this DM system. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms such as the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. In addition, it also includes sterile-neutrino creation via both the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms as well as a more recently proposed model involving CPT symmetry. The model is found to fit within observed dark matter abundance, and thus determines an upper limit for the axion scale within the model ranging from approximately $10^{11}$ to $10^{13}$ GeV, and similarly it also sets an upper limit for the neutrino scales within the model ranging from approximately $10^{10}$ to $10^{12}$ GeV. The model, however, fails to explain the recent observations from MINOS and MINOS+ regarding $\ell_\nu$ appearance, and thus requires reduction in sterile-neutrino masses or their interactions with the W boson to fit within these observational limits. The model, however, remains consistent with constraints imposed by XENON1T, and significantly we find that the model offers scope for future experimental verification within a number of areas including neutrinoless double beta decay, long baseline neutrino experiments such as CLCN, and ultra-dark matter sensitive projects such as LUXe and XENONnT. Lastly, we also found that the model remains consistent against a broad range of astrophysical and cosmological observations. The model, however, requires future gravitational wave detections from the LIGO and VIRGO collaborations to confirm certain predictions within this model. The model presents numerous ground-based experimental opportunities to verify the model, and significantly we found that the model presents both exciting and challenging prospects for future experimental investigation

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm capable of approximating the output probabilities of $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuits $U$ within a specified inverse polynomial error margin, using a time complexity of $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)2^{\alpha m}$. Furthermore, the investigation yields refined bounds on the stabilizer rank of symmetric product states $|\psi\rangle^{\otimes m}$, ultimately leading to the creation of a strong simulation algorithm for circuits comprising Clifford gates and multiple instances of a fixed Z-rotator, operating at a time complexity of $\text{poly}(n,m) 2^{m/2}$. An additional suggestion is presented for potentially enhancing the upper bounds through the design of specific linear codes. This research may facilitate the development of more efficient classical algorithms for approximating quantum circuit output probabilities. Related resources, including the mathematical proof and a related arXiv post, can be found at the link below. https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04102 and https://tinyurl.com/2020arx602.04102. This research was made possible through funding by IARPA, IES, and NSF. L.B.'s research was further supported by funding from Dowling, Sockel and the University of Oregon. Additional support came from Samsung and MIT-IBM Watson. The authors would like to express their gratitude to Gleason and Mezzadri for sharing their work and code on the CMU arXiv preprint. This research is related to a joint project with Brusco, Granade and Klivans involving quantum circuit output estimation. Specifically, it addresses a question posed by Mezzadri. We have also received inquiries from Fehmi Sarib about the connection between the traffic light problem and the stabilizer rank of $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$.

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than necessary to cause SRAM access failures, then applies the SHA-256 hash function to convert these faults into random data. We validate the practicality of TuRaN through SPICE simulations and evaluate its reliability through real-world experiments conducted on two distinct test chips. Furthermore, we demonstrate the high quality of the random numbers produced by tuRaN using the NIST standard randomness tests and note that the generated random numbers pass all the tests with exceptionally high pass rates of 99.97%, 99.98%, and 99.99% for samples of sizes 10k, 1M, and 10M, respectively. In comparison to existing SRAM-based TRNGs, tuRaN surpasses them in terms of throughput, outperforms them in terms of energy efficiency, and rivals them in terms of area efficiency. We envision tuRaN as a high-quality, efficient, and versatile SRAM-based TRNG that can efficiently support a wide range of applications in cryptography and other fields. We also intend to make the tuRaN source code and simulation tools freely available to the research community so that various implementations of tuRaN can be replicated and verified. Additionally, we aim to facilitate the design and fabrication of tuRaN on FPGAs and ASICs through the open-source hardware initiative. The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, which can be characterized by loop topological features and connections. To address concerns regarding numerical stability in loop-tree duality-based calculations, we examine case studies involving numerical evaluations of planar and non-planar two-loop triangles under varying kinematic conditions. Our analysis reveals that triangle coefficients, which describe the behavior of certain propagators, play a crucial role in ensuring numerical stability in loop-tree duality-based calculations. Furthermore, we investigate the causal representation of one-loop Feynman integrands in various scenarios, including rational and non-rational cases, and demonstrate its compatibility with the concept of coverings. The causal representation provides a unified framework for representing Feynman integrands, offering new insights and perspectives on both loop-level and tree-level quantities. Although our discussion primarily focuses on scalar Feynman integrands, we also touch upon the extension of causal representation to compute off-shell two-point functions. The approach of causal representation and its numerical evaluation offer promising prospects for numerical phase-space integration projects like SCIOUS. It has the potential to contribute to the goals of reducing dependence on Monte Carlo integration and implementing amplitudes in terms of trees, as outlined in the SCIOUS report. In particular, our work aligns with the recommendations to numerically compute essential building blocks, like master topologies and tree-level amplitudes, and to understand the behavior of singular structures in Feynman integrands. The numerical evaluation of multi-loop Feynman integrands has far-reaching applications, such as informing the development of next-generation particle physics detectors, particularly in searching for dark matter at the LHC, and studying rare decays. The causal representation approach has the potential to significantly impact these efforts by providing a numerical evaluation method that is consistent with unitarity. To further demonstrate our findings and facilitate replication, we provide public implementations of the numerical code and detailed analysis, which can also be used for computing multi-loop Feynman integrands in various scenarios. The causal representation offers a general framework for numerical evaluation, and we anticipate that our work will be useful in future studies, particularly in evaluating rare processes and extending the reach of particle detector capabilities. In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity. Our findings are supported by experiments exploring the influence of initialization methods on graph convolutional neural networks. Our research establishes that popular training techniques can efficiently control geometric complexity, and, therefore, model complexity, especially in high-dimensional data sets, and particularly for deep learning models. Our practical study also identifies specific circumstances under the Geometric Complexity Theory that favor the success of certain training methods. Our proposed framework and findings are freely accessible online at geometriccomplexity.com. Our code is publicly available at github.com/gc-tutorial/gc-tutorial. Our dataset can be downloaded at github.com/gc-tutorial/dataset and imported into Tensorflow at tf-geometric-complexity. Additionally, we have developed a Tensorflow hub module that imports pre-trained models and demonstrates their complexity control, tf-geometric-complexity. Our research highlights that simple model architectures, encouraged by geometric complexity, can lead to superior performance in graph classification tasks, and showcases novel geometric complexity-based features that achieve state-of-the-art results in several benchmark data sets, and surpass existing complexity-based feature methods. Our research breaks down the Geometric Complexity Theory into an interactive website that guides users through the various concepts and techniques, from initialization methods to feature learning, and demonstrates their effectiveness using real-world examples and experiments. Our research demonstrates that geometric complexity is a reliable indicator for model complexity and, therefore, generalizability. Our study is multi-faceted, and addresses various questions, such as what geometric complexity is, how it is measured, and why it is an effective model selector. A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice. With this methodology, the Wilson coefficients can be directly extracted with a precision of $2\%$ or better for several parameters, such as $C_9$ and $C_{10}$, following the analysis of the full LHCb dataset. This method will significantly benefit from the upcoming CMS activation at HL-LHC, where the precision could reach $1\%$ or better for multiple parameters. Furthermore, this approach remains feasible even in scenarios where Wilson coefficients are only constrained by one observable, such as $R_K$, resulting in the direct determination of $C_9/F_1^s$ with a precision of $10\%$ or better. Using this approach, the sensitivity of $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays can be completely characterized by a single variable, $q^2$-integrated differential distribution, called the $q^2$-weighted decay rate. This method does not rely on specific Wilson coefficient interpretations but rather directly determines its representation through the coefficient of this weighted decay rate. Therefore, this novel method offers a more efficient and sensitive approach for the direct extraction of Wilson coefficients based on $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays. Its feasibility and performance will be studied using the LHCb's full Run 1 and 2 dataset. This analysis confirms the improved sensitivity and precision that can be achieved, particularly with future data. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite recent breakthroughs in using pre-trained language models, the accuracy of automated scoring still falls short of human levels, especially for more complex writing samples.  One strategy to enhance performance is data enhancement through the application of transfer learning techniques, particularly useful for smaller sized datasets.  This research investigates various data augmentation methods in conjunction with pre-trained transformer models to improve automated scoring accuracy.  Multiple approaches to augmenting a dataset are examined, focusing on text manipulation and the incorporation of external knowledge.  Our findings indicate that BERT-based models yield the best results, achieving an average correlation above 0.90 when pre-trained and fine-tuned on the most effective augmentation methods.  Among the augmentation methods, adding redundant information through repeat and concat transformations or incorporating external knowledge through word embeddings demonstrates the greatest potential to enhance state-of-the-art performance.  Our top performing model, using a BERT-based classifier with repeat and concat transformations and external knowledge embeddings, achieves a correlation of 0.934 for our target evaluation metric.  This model not only surpasses the current state-of-the-art but also showcases the applicability of transformer models to complex educational tasks. A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions such as the size of differences in socioeconomical standings and the weight given to the benefits the opportunities provide to future generations. The theory developed from this model is then used to examine how changes in policies affecting higher education access were implemented in Chile in 2011. The findings from a joint analysis of administrative data and surveys of students and their families support the predicted outcomes of this policy change. The analysis also reveals that the most disadvantaged students did not take advantage of the new enrollment rules because they lacked knowledge about the changes, faced barriers in seeking information, and had reduced chances of rising to better socioeconomical standings regardless of their qualifications. The study indicates that, for the most disadvantaged students to benefit from opportunities like higher education, it's essential to address the underlying issues limiting their social mobility. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context. Consequently, the conclusion that bosons possess integer spin and fermions possess half-integer spin follows naturally. Our reasoning avoids the complexities of relativistic wave equations and spin-orbit interactions, yielding an understanding of wavefunction permutation properties as an intrinsic consequence of quantum mechanics based on the principles of parity, angular momentum, and wavefuntion normalization. Furthermore, this approach reveals a built-in method for determining particle exchange statistics based on the properties of wavefunctions, which in turn demonstrates how fermion and boson behavior emerges from the quantization of systems. Ultimately, this formalism highlights that relativistic spin is a derived concept rather than an inherent characteristic of particles, as suggested by the Klein-Gordon and Dirac equations. To verify the soundness of this parity-based formulation, we examined the wavefunctions of numerous non-relativistic atomic states, which show that the proposed formulation accurately predicts the exchange statistics of these states. Lastly, we employed a similar approach to investigate relativistic bound wavefunctions, as demonstrated for the hydrogen atom using both the Klein-Gordon and Dirac equations. Notably, the results show that the wavefunctions of relativistic hydrogen display the same permutation properties as their non-relativistic counterparts, which underscores the key insights of this formulation and sheds light on the relationship between wavefuntion properties and particle exchange statistics. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to address a new problem can negatively affect performance on earlier tasks handled by other teams. To address this issue, the authors developed a groundbreaking 'continual learning' method and successfully implemented it in solid mechanics for the first time. They utilized recurrent neural networks to predict the behavior of materials undergoing plasticity. Notably, the developed method increased the overall accuracy of predictions without decreasing performance on previous tasks, demonstrating an innovative approach to cooperative data-driven modeling. This breakthrough could enable collaborative teams to work together more effectively, combining their expertise to create highly accurate predictive models. The proposed method could also be applied in other areas, such as multiscale modeling, where different teams often focus on distinct length scales, and it's likely to have broad applications in deep learning for physical fields. Additionally, the study's findings provide new insights into how brains handle'staircase' learning challenges, where tasks build upon each other in a sequential order. While such learning mechanisms can facilitate cooperation, it also presents difficulties for overcoming 'developmental bottlenecks.' The authors demonstrated that cooperation, fueled by the shared desire to understand the fundamental laws governing the world, can help overcome these limitations, but more research is needed to address the 'bootstrapping' problems that arise from these challenges. The developed method was successfully tested on a range of materials science problems, including the prediction of material failure and stress-strain patterns in metals. The study's code is now openly accessible, allowing for further collaboration and innovation. The authors' research serves as a model for future collaborative efforts, highlighting the potential of deep learning and continual learning to understand complex physical systems and improve our understanding of the world around us. The study's findings also raise important questions about the nature of learning and how we can overcome inherent 'bottlenecks' in our knowledge, and it's predicted that these investigations will have far-reaching implications for many fields, including education and the development of artificial intelligence. The study's leaders are now working on a new project involving the cooperation of expert teams in various fields, and they're committed to advancing our understanding of physical systems through the continuous application of new deep learning methods. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. We also demonstrate that degree-degree correlations can be harnessed to achieve superior error-rate performance for a given code density and design density. Moreover, our research shows that degree-degree correlations can be leveraged to create LDPC codes exhibiting greater error-correction capacity than conventional ones, with no increase in code density or design density. We have made these findings publicly available through the establishment of a degree-degree correlated LDPC ensemble generator tool. Furthermore, our work has identified areas for future research, including the development of novel degree-degree correlated LDPC ensemble generator algorithms and the exploration of various degree-degree correlation functions. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are demonstrated through numerical examples. Additionally, we provide evidence that safely generating large safety areas comes at a significant computational cost expense. This information could be useful in choosing between MPSF and SL-MPSF designs. Finally, we explore extending the safety filter design to more complex systems affected by uncertain conditions. The safety filter design presents a novel approach to safely generating control inputs that are effective and feasible for high-dimensional systems and systems under uncertain conditions, which is a novel contribution. The proposed design has promising applications in areas such as autonomous driving and aerospace operations. The associated materials, including code and data, are available online at the given URL. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in an estimated 73.4% leakage of the secret key. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states. Consequently, our research offers a potential solution to the pressing issue of quantum hacking and could lead to the development of more robust QKD systems utilizing strong phase noise. Our analysis compares the performance of vacuum+weak decoy state QKD systems with various sources of randomness in the source phase. Ultimately, our results indicate that utilizing a quantum conductor as a random source may compromise the security of QKD systems, whereas a quantum oscillator appears to provide more security assurances for more robust quantum key distribution systems. Our study has significant implications for the design and implementation of more resilient QKD systems. Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of kiloparsec-scale, kiloparsec cold clouds under conditions typically seen in galaxy clusters. Our results indicate that filamentary segments of these clouds quickly cool and separate from the surrounding hot intracluster medium before ultimately fragmenting and creating numerous smaller clumps. These fragments act as nuclei, fostering further condensation through processes including Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, thereby nearly doubling the cold gas within a 75 million-year period. Cloud expansion appears to be determined by factors such as density and localized heat-producing mechanisms that either cause the clouds to shrink and crumble or to grow through shattering. Magnetic fields are found to have a moderating effect on the cloud's growth while its topology plays a role in the evolution of both the cold and warm components. Conversely, anisotropic thermal conduction may cause the clouds to grow faster, thereby resulting in increased amounts of warm phase, contradicting previous assumptions. Ultimately, densely packed structures on the order of 500 pc or larger play an important role in long-term, cooling-related galaxy cluster evolution. Additionally, magnetic fields may significantly impact the process of shock formation within these formations. Our study indicates that the intricate, sinuous appearance of nebulae observed in galaxy clusters is not just a product of in situ cooling but rather a testament to the long-term, destructive and creative impact of these structures on the surrounding ICM. Furthermore, our results suggest that the phase space of galaxy cluster cooling is influenced by factors other than simply mass and radius. Our data is consistent with the hypothesis that the phase space of galaxy clusters could serve as a template for understanding the behavior of nebulae in groups of galaxies. Ultimately, our study indicates that the formation of central nebulae in galaxy clusters is best understood through a delicate balance of factors including cooling, magnetic fields and thermal conduction. However, the long-term, destructive and creative impact of cold clouds on the surrounding ICM remains an important and unresolved problem in galaxy cluster physics. Moreover, our results imply that galaxy clusters may actually have more cold gas than is currently detectable through UV and H-alpha observations, particularly if the surrounding ICM has high levels of metal contamination. Finally, our study indicates that a high level of magnetic field anisotropy may significantly impact galaxy cluster evolution

By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication systems, and enabling flexible data transfer policies. Simulation results based on real-world data demonstrate significant energy savings and data processing efficiency improvements. Specifically, we achieved a 8.65% improvement in processing efficiency and a 7.38% improvement in energy efficiency. Additionally, we present a mathematical proof of the efficiency of our data transfer strategy, showing that average waiting times are minimized when network parameters are set according to a specific ratio. This theoretical finding provides a valuable framework for designers and engineers building future MN systems. Simulation code is publicly available on GitHub for verification and replication of our results. Moreover, we will investigate the impact of attacks on edge computing systems and develop methods to detect and mitigate the effects of attacks, ultimately presenting a comprehensive framework for designers and engineers building future MN systems. The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, an unfeasible task under current testing conditions. To overcome this challenge, we're exploring a novel approach that utilizes extremely basic acoustic units, akin to phonemes, but defined by limited, distinctive audio samples rather than written rules. To mitigate the need for a vast speech corpus, we're leveraging transcriptions based on these units instead of standard phonemes. Although this method necessitates a large set of acoustic units, each with distinct and learned meanings, we're utilizing a large, annotated speech database of wild child-directed speech for unit discovery. Preliminary experiments in English reveal promising results, especially in terms of the synthesized speech's naturalness, although the system still struggles with defining the boundaries of individual units, a task complicated by the inherent ambiguity of speech sounds. To tackle this issue, we're developing a new metric that assesses unit segmentation rather than just its individual units. The proposed approach shows potential for addressing the difficult challenges of boundary prediction and the excessive generativity of acoustic unit-based models, an area of research potentially applicable to natural language generation. To validate the effectiveness of our transcription method, we're comparing it to a system that combines transcript approximations through both human and machine analysis. Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot.
