We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-shot resource conversion in various resource theories, effectively rendering more restrictive protocols unnecessary.
By employing this metric, we were able to refine the performance limits of one-shot and multi-copy probabilistic resource distillation protocols.
Concurrently, we introduced a comprehensive technique for calculating achievable probabilities in resource transformations through a series of convex optimisation problems.
This approach enabled us to precisely assess the trade-offs between probabilities and errors in the distillation of maximally resource-rich states.
Furthermore, we successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our methods in the analysis of quantum entanglement distillation. Our methods are versatile and can be applied to study a broad range of quantum resource theories. This research was carried out in collaboration with Dr. T. Kuwahara from the University of Gdansk, Poland. Our findings significantly contribute to our understanding of the manipulation of quantum states, significantly tightening the constraints on probabilistic convertibility. This research could have a significant impact on the development of future quantum technologies by shedding new light on the underlying physical processes involved. Additionally, our work may stimulate the development of new optimization techniques applicable to diverse fields beyond quantum information. Through our research, we have shown that novel insights can be gained by approaching the study of quantum operations through the lens of convex optimization. Furthermore, our study reinforces the importance of fundamental bounds in the analysis of quantum operations, particularly in the context of resource theory. This research could also lead to the identification of new practical applications of quantum information processing techniques. We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, our research estimates the percentage of produced particles originating from the quark-gluon plasma, with results spanning from 35% for the most peripheral collisions to 90% for the most central collisions. Ultimately, we suggest that a significant portion of the particles produced in low-energy collisions may hold crucial insights into the properties and behavior of the quark-gluon plasma at very low temperature. These observations could be further investigated within the context of the PHENIX experiment. With future data collections from the RHIC, our research predicts that even lighter collisions may yield substantial gains in understanding the quark-gluon plasma at very low temperatures. Specifically, we estimate that collisions with nucleon-nucleon centrality of $I_c \approx 4\%$ may harbor essential information related to the quark-gluon plasma at temperatures around $T \sim 30$ MeV. This research is expected to be pivotal in elucidating the transition between the quark-gluon plasma and the hadronic phase at very low temperatures. Furthermore, we apply our research to study the properties of the quark-gluon plasma at very low temperatures and extremely high baryon density, where estimates suggest up to $10^5$ quarks and anti-quarks would be produced as a result of the initial energy state. These outcomes could be further verified within the context of the HIC-MAX IV experiment. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we develop a general framework for robustifying models against all types of transformation attacks. Additionally, we introduce adaptation-specific smoothing methods for all categories of transformations. Our approach provides adjustable security trade-offs by regulating the level of smoothing for a given model through a controlled smoothening parameter. Experimental results demonstrate that TPC successfully protects a variety of neural network-based point cloud models in simulated attacks, especially stretch-based attacks, without substantially compromising their accuracy. TPC's discrete nature also enables us to achieve this protection with very little compromise of performance. Furthermore, we show through our experiments that models trained with Adversarial Training outperform other methods in enhancing robustness but come at a higher cost to performance. We also propose a method for automatically detecting suspicious requests for models, which could have been manipulated through subtle alterations. Our technique is an innovative adaptation of the TrAC approach used in image-based attacks and relies on an objective function that identifies the smallest transformation needed to alter a model's shape. Our study reveals that this objective function is effective in identifying artificially altered vehicle models while also demonstrating that they can be distinguished from genuine ones. To provide additional security, we also propose an algorithm for automatically detecting and fixing potential flaws in 3D models. Our approach relies on an accurate and efficient method for identifying and resolving discrepancies between model meshes. Specifically, we use a simple framework that relies on a unique identifier for each mesh vertex to locate discrepancies and repair them. We show through our experiments that our mesh checking and fixing approach is more efficient than other methods used in other types of transformation attacks. Our study also reveals that our piecewise approximation of 3D models, which relies on simplifying and transforming (e.g., shrinking) existing point clouds, offers more efficient performance with comparable results. Additionally, we show that our piecewise method can repair damaged or corrupted 3D models by locating and correcting discrepancies within the model. Our study also provides additional support for a recent finding that a significant proportion of widely used vehicle models have potential security flaws due to subtle alterations

In evaluation experiments for sound event detection and classification, a standardized sound clip is usually played to inform participants about the target sound. However, the actual sound produced by this clip can vary significantly depending on the device and location in which it is played, which might affect the outcome of the experiment. Our study specifically examined these variations in relation to a sound clip of a door opening. We investigated the changes in sound configuration and the perceived characteristics of the clip among which participants were asked to identify the door sound through their ears. Additionally, a group of participants was also visually present during the experiment. Our results indicate that the unknown factors influencing sound production can impact certain sound characteristics but also suggest that visual participation can alleviate these variations to some extent. Nevertheless, participants who heard the door sound through their ears had increased difficulty identifying it correctly due to these unpredictable changes in sound production. Our findings imply that the reliability of existing evaluation studies that relied on a single sound sample to represent a given sound class may be compromised. Our research further highlights the importance of utilizing multiple sound examples within such studies to guarantee accurate classification of sound events. These outcomes are significant for researchers working on sound classification and detection techniques as well as for the development of more practical applications that rely on a single sound example. A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and the presence of double Hf5 borides' characteristics, which show exceptional superconductivity at low temperatures. In an investigation using a density functional, showing that hydrogen atoms introduce electron-phonon coupling essential for superconductivity to occur, and that high energy phonons near the Fermi level are present in this system, indicating a considerable likelihood for superconductivity to exist. However, a subsequent calculation, using a more advanced screened density functional, reveals that the electron-phonon coupling strength is significantly reduced, and that the superconducting scenario becomes highly unlikely due to the weak interaction between electrons and phonons. As a result, an estimate for the upper limit of the superconducting critical temperature in this system is around 0.5 K. Finally, an analysis of the impact of hydrostatic pressure on the electron-phonon coupling and critical temperature reveals a pronounced decrease in both properties under increased pressure. Conversely, an examination of the impact of hydrostatic pressure on a related hydrogen boride compound shows a modest increase in critical temperature under similar conditions. Overall, our findings indicate that the superconductivity in this system is significantly underwhelming when compared to other materials with similar properties. Rather, this compound is expected to exhibit very weak superconductivity or no superconductivity at all. As a result, further research using experimental techniques to determine the material's properties is highly recommended to confirm our theoretical estimates. Additionally, our study using a screened density functional highlights the significance of accurately modeling and simulating electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions to correctly predict a system's superconducting properties. The code and data used in this research have been publicly posted, and the relevant materials can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/ylzhen/hb3_SCC. In particular, our study used the OpenKIM API with the code name "ijump/bondbreak", and the KIM model "phbonn2", which both play essential roles in reproducing our results. Furthermore, our study also used the VASP software package to determine the material's properties, and the PBEsolx generalized gradient approximation to model and simulate the interactions within and between electrons and phonons. Finally, our study also used the TRIM tool to determine the material's phonon spectrum, and the SPC/HF potential to model and simulate the interactions between atoms

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using a heuristic approach. Given a matrix of polynomials and a vector of error terms, we seek a degree-d polynomial that minimizes error. However, because of a lower bound on error magnitude, an optimal solution may not exist. In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises at a few hundred MeV for momentum and chiral chemical potential. Importantly, this radiatively corrected contribution is consistent in magnitude for ρ0 and ω mesons. A local parity breaking medium with a chiral chemical potential of approximately 150 MeV is considered quark matter-like. In this quark matter-like state, the transverse dispersion relations of ρ0 and ω mesons converge, indicating a unified mass of approximately 240 MeV, which is in line with current experimental knowledge. This model's predictions for these mesons may be tested experimentally using the ALICE and STAR collaborations' data, particularly the vector meson coherent production measurements. The implications of the results on the mass spectrum of a medium with local parity breaking and chiral imbalance are significant, as they indicate the possibility of a common mass for different mesons in this medium, which is in contrast to their masses in the vacuum as predicted by the Gell-Mann-Levy model. Lastly, this model also predicts an in-medium mass for the K meson as a function of chiral chemical potential and momentum. When compared to lattice QCD data for this meson, under the same conditions, notable discrepancies are observed in terms of momentum dependence but not mass spectrum, which suggests that radiative corrections play a crucial role in the spectrum of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance. However, these corrections appear to be less significant for heavier mesons in such mediums, which is in line with the results of other models. Eventually, this research may contribute to a deeper understanding of the properties of matter in extreme conditions, such as quark matter, which may be formed in the center of neutron stars. The study also sheds light on the behavior of light vector mesons in the atmosphere of compact stars and may have implications for future experiments involving the ALICE and STAR collaborations. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can approach zero, but remains greater than zero. This protocol relies on local communication among network nodes, requires polynomial-time computation, and accurately estimates the network size with an error margin of O(n^(-c)) - where c > 0. Unlike existing research, our approach doesn't require any pre-existing structure or central control, and it's the first algorithm of its kind to achieve this level of accuracy. Furthermore, we studied the minimum communication needed for this task and found that two rounds suffice - with limited malice present, we were able to devise an algorithm that requires just one round. Our results are validated through rigorous analysis and comprehensive simulations. At last, we explore the fundamental limits of this problem, specifically how many malicious nodes can be tolerated while still allowing an algorithm to function reliably. Our analysis suggests a sharp boundary exists - where the number of malicious nodes can't exceed O(n^(1-delta)) - and this study and estimation could influence future research in this area. This work presents significant advancements in robust network size estimation, bringing us closer to fully distributed and efficient algorithm development for critical network parameters, such as diameter and average distance. In particular, we showed that averaging local estimates leads to accurate results, and this approach to efficient algorithms may seem surprising at first. This research focuses on underlying problems, shedding light on the feasibility and limitations of robust network size estimation and providing fundamental insights for future research. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and black hole initial data with scalar field and gravitational wave sources. Our results show that this method achieves rapid convergence in diverse cases. Furthermore, we found that recovering distorted, intense wave signals from initially chaotic or disordered states is feasible, underscoring the potential of this approach to illuminate the behavior of field configurations in intricate spacetimes. Our strategy's success in a broad range of scenarios positions it as a practical and versatile tool for studying the interactions of signals and matter fields in general relativity. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, a technique which includes the effects of telescope optics. We've compared and assessed five different models, leveraging time-variable data to distinguish between their variations. Our on-site verification suggests that while some models are reasonably accurate, others are inferior and need improvement. We've developed a verification tool that can efficiently compare various models by minimizing their differences and identifying any discrepancies. This tool is adaptable for comparing different models across distinct observing conditions and can even be applied reverse-engineeringly to refine atmospheric models using our on-site data. We've obtained refined values for key parameters such as the dispersion's power-law index and the spectral gap. These results set a foundation for future on-site verifications to be performed quickly and efficiently, potentially leading to improved atmospheric models that can in turn enhance our understanding of the atmosphere and the stars we observe. They also raise important implications for future telescopes like the Extremely Large Telescope. Our data and verification tool are available online for everyone to access. Moreover, our method is versatile and can be used to assess the accuracy of other modeling techniques not just in astronomy but in various fields that rely on modeling and simulation. They can also be applied to other fields such as atmospheric modeling and meteorology by adapting our technique and comparison method to suit their specific needs and observations. A similar technique could potentially be used to verify and improve models of the atmosphere through the analysis of the atmosphere's own measurements. This could lead to improved weather forecasting and a better understanding of the atmosphere. A similar approach to the verification of astronomical models could be applied to other fields by leveraging time-variable data to distinguish between different models and their variations. A comprehensive comparison of different models across distinct observing conditions could be carried out to identify and prioritize any discrepancies and their implications. This could lead to improved accuracy and a deeper understanding of the atmosphere through the analysis of the atmosphere's own measurements. A comprehensive dataset of atmospheric measurements could be used to improve atmospheric models and advance our understanding of the atmosphere. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement limits detection below quantum noise, due to itself emitting quantum noise that can be measured. Since multiple pathways of this quantum noise overlap in time, simply increasing the observation time or collecting data from more locations can greatly improve the detection chances. In fact, the ability to simultaneously measure various phases of this noise over extended time periods, through either higher-order interferometry or multiple interferometry with controlled phases, offers significantly improved sensitivity. Furthermore, the capability of unambiguously identifying the particular bosonic dark matter signal not only through its desired peak but also through its characteristic pattern of interwoven phases, greatly enhances the ability to accurately measure its associated mass. In particular, the ability to detect phases of quantum noise that occur hours or even days apart, through the use of long optical fibers or spacecraft, holds the potential to significantly improve the measurement precision of ultra-light dark matter masses, potentially to the level of a few orders of magnitude. In fact, the idea of utilizing high-order interferometry or simultaneous measurements across controlled phases to boost sensitivity has already been successfully demonstrated in experiments involving ultracold Bose fields and is now being adapted for ultra-light dark matter detection. Importantly, the associated measurement limitations can provide valuable insights into the theoretical properties of the underlying dark matter wave function, particularly its decay properties, potentially up to energies far exceeding 1 GeV. In effect, the ability to detect long-time quantum interference has effectively converted a previously restrictive detection limitation into a valuable theoretical constraint, thereby enhancing our understanding of dark matter while simultaneously refining our knowledge of ultra-light bosonic matter properties. Lastly, the detection of this wave-like field near its Compton frequency not only provides strong evidence for the bosonic nature of dark matter but also opens up new avenues for investigating a broad range of wave-like phenomena, extending far beyond the realm of dark matter research. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing stabilisation techniques to maintain stability. These schemes are validated and their performance compared in a series of numerical experiments involving both specially designed and standard rotating shallow-water models. These tests reveal that the concurrently solved approach is more robust and less prone to instability issues compared to the projection-based method, especially when solving complex rotating system simulations involving significant strain and rotation. Consequently, the concurrently solved strategy is recommended for use in transporting vector-valued fields in rotating system simulations, particularly those involving geostrophic balance. It's worth noting that the projected method still holds value due to its smoother solutions and lack of artefacts, even if it's not as stable, especially in the limit of high numerical strains. Ultimately, the choice of method should be dictated by the specific problem at hand, considering factors like the level of strain and the desired level of accuracy. Future work can build upon these results by further assessing the performance of these schemes in more diverse numerical examples and potentially extending their use to three-dimensional environments. Additionally, they could be coupled with other numerical methods to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the transported field's behavior. It's also suggested that the projected method could be further developed to utilize the transported field's normal and tangent components to provide an even more accurate representation of its behavior. This potential modification could lead to even more precise results, particularly when dealing with curved and complex geometries. Furthermore, the possibility of utilizing different finite elements, like the Brezzi-Dipendra-Hitrik elements, is another area of potential improvement. These elements could provide more stable and accurate results, even at lower spatial resolution, to effectively model vector-valued fields in rotating system simulations. This potential implementation could lead to even more robust and accurate numerical models of rotating systems, particularly when coupled with the concurrently solved approach. In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as continuous, continuous-staged Runge-Kutta methods, which have now been generalized into Continuous Highorder Runge-Kutta methods (CHORK). Despite not being restricted to Hamiltonian systems, CHORK methods maintain many of the properties that made HBVMs successful, such as preserving quadratic integrals and providing sharp error estimates. This work presents an order reduction result for CHORK methods formulated specifically for second-order ODEs, and demonstrates their potential through various numerical experiments. Furthermore, the paper concludes by outlining open directions for research and future exploration. These directions may hold the key to developing even more accurate methods in the future. As an interesting note, the underlying theory presented in this paper can also be applied to provide a unified explanation for the creation and analysis of different methods such as Nystrom, Nystrom type and RKN methods. These methods have been widely employed and analyzed over the past twenty years for solving second order Hamiltonian differential equations. By extending the concept of integrating factors, this paper also provides a new framework for developing and studying methods that are specifically designed for Hamiltonian systems, a technique which could hold great value in the future for researching energy preserving and continuous methods. It is also interesting to note that despite the numerous advantages that CHORK methods offer, they can only provide second order accurate solutions, which is a inherent property due to the use of monomial coefficients in the construction of these methods. Therefore, it becomes necessary to develop high order methods that can provide more accurate solutions while preserving important dynamical properties, which is an area that this paper seeks to investigate further. These new research directions could lead to the development of new methods that could well become the standard for future research in the area of Hamiltonian boundary value methods. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. Initially, it demonstrates that the ubiquitous inclination of plots technique, which involves plotting data in an non-physical coordinate system, greatly facilitates the extraction of physics principles from data. Notably, this approach renders many physical laws almost self-evident. Secondly, it illustrates that compensation for systematic measurement errors necessitates the inclusion of additional parameters. Notably, this study reveals that noise models previously proposed in the literature are insufficient to account for the discrepancies encountered. Thirdly, it differentiates between two distinct forms of model assessment metrics, namely, discrepancy assessment and performance assessment. Finally, it underscores the significance of discrete numerical differences in physics, which is often overlooked in data-driven and machine learning approaches. In conclusion, this work emphasizes that discrete numerical differences in physics should not be neglected, and the physics community's skepticism towards purely data-driven approaches is understandable. However, it is argued that these discrete numerical differences present an opportunity for growth in physical knowledge, and not solely a source of uncertainty and bias. Ultimately, the integration of physical uncertainty and bias into machine learning algorithms is essential for the successful application of AI in physics. Moreover, the dual role of discrete numerical differences in verifying physical assumptions and as a source of learning bias remains unexplored and warrants further investigation. This study concludes by highlighting several areas for future research and development. We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by conducting simulations using the Finite Element Method. A design optimized for a 1D nanobeam cavity yielded a notable source efficiency of 97.7 percent and an impressive Purcell factor of 38.6 for an isotropic dipole, primarily due to a combination of high index contrast between GaAs and SiO$_2$ materials and an effective cavity design that facilitated interference and minimized losses. However, we also identified mode mismatch as a limitation of our platform and devised an optimization technique to achieve high efficiency in single-photon sources. This method incorporates a taper section to smoothly bridge the mode mismatch between the cavity and the nanobeam, ultimately enhancing the Purcell factor and source efficiency. Furthermore, we observed the resilience of our design in the face of real-world fabrication imperfections affecting hole variation and waveguide loss. Our optimized design provides a foundation for developing high-efficiency single-photon sources integrated into integrated photonics circuits for quantum communication applications. Moreover, the techniques employed here can be adapted to enhance single-photon sources integrated into other photonic structures. With a focus on integrated photonics for quantum technology, we studied the performance of an integrated single-photon source coupled to a photonic structure and used numerical simulations to optimize its efficiency and Purcell factor. Our optimized design achieved nearly unity efficiency and a substantial Purcell factor of 38.6 for an isotropic dipole, primarily due to high index contrast and waveguide effects. Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison across multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity in a straightforward context reveals that multi-objective optimization may not consistently generate significant diversity. By contrast, multimodal optimization tends to yield solutions with superior fitness levels. Furthermore, integrating an autoencoder allows for the automated discovery of phenotypic features, which, in conjunction with quality diversity, facilitates the creation of a more extensive and diverse solution set. Ultimately, we offer strategic guidance on the appropriate applications of these optimization techniques.

The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as noted in our previous study. The central space is found by considering spaces with their dimensions reduced, like cities on a map, and showing that their sizes converge in a way that depends only on the cloud they belong to. The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy. This evidence suggests a two-pronged effect: jet modification and energy depopulation, with the medium exhibiting enhanced interactions with jets. These results are the first to demonstrate jet modification and energy depopulation simultaneously in heavy ion collisions. They are consistent with theoretical models integrating jet modification and energy depopulation and offer insight into medium interactions with high-speed jet constituents and energy within the medium. This research remains a high priority for the PHENIX experiment, which will continue to collect data for two more years to address these remaining questions. Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. We've successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of this new approach through experiments using a 980-nm laser, a 3D transparent artificial tissue phantom, and a 3D photoacoustic imaging setup. Notably, we've successfully formed multiple complex structures simultaneously within the scanning volume, and the results show a significant 5.3 times improvement in image resolution over a conventional GA method. The image clarity was also enhanced by a factor of 3.3 as indicated by the WMA-GA's ability to maintain 90% similarity in subsequent iterations. The use of an iterative, real-time, continuous wave (CW) SLM system enabled rapid and high-precision control of wavefront manipulation, and the integration of our proposed fitness function and a mutation-based optimization technique facilitated rapid structure formation and optimization. This breakthrough technology has potential to form intricate structures and focus light within or through disordered mediums at an unprecedented speed and precision. The effect of tissue phase aberration on our findings and the feasibility of extending this technology to the 2 micron range for biomedical applications are also discussed. Meta-analyses that include multiple trials with paired data underpin numerous applications in medicine and social sciences.  In recent years, researchers have become increasingly aware of the importance of accounting for correlation in individual trial data in meta-analyses.  Several cluster-robus t estimators have been proposed over the years, primarily for univariate meta-regression analyses, but only a few have been formally tested, with many more remaining theoretical.  This study assesses the existing cluster-robus t estimators for bivariate meta-regression analyses and introduces new estimators through an asymptotic framework.  By applying this approach, researchers can now easily derive new estimators for both within-study and between-study variance components.  We also provide a method for assessing the influence of individual studies.  The proposed methods are validated through simulations and demonstrated in a well-known dataset from epilepsy research.  All necessary code is accessible on GitHub. This study extends the existing methods for bivariate meta-regression analysis by providing a more straightforward method for estimating the covariance between means and new estimators for both within-study and between-study variance components.  We validate the proposed methods through simulations and demonstrate their utility in a real-world dataset from epilepsy research. The proposed methods are now available on GitHub.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our method offers significant computational savings without compromising accuracy, however further optimizations are needed to make large-scale simulations feasible. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. We compare the efficiency and accuracy of HDTM against existing methods, revealing its significant advantages in terms of simplicity, scalability, and coherence. In particular, HDTM produces hierarchies up to 5 times larger in size and nearly 10 times deeper in depth compared to traditional models, while reducing computation time by nearly 10 times through efficient Gaussian-Mixture model clustering and distributed processing. We demonstrate two practical applications for HDTM, showcasing its potential to improve information retrieval with customized search filters and multi-level categorization systems. In the future, we intend to expand HDTM to incorporate ranked information hierarchies and explore its potential in topics evolution analysis. In addition, we plan to integrate HDTM based information retrieval systems into real-world applications like search engines and knowledge management platforms. In particular, we can use HDTM to improve the knowledge base search component in knowledge management systems, enabling more accurate queries based on hierarchical categories. Similarly, we can use HDTM to improve the search experience for users of services like Google Knowledge Graph. In general, HDTM can be employed in any scenario where deep and wide categorical structures are involved. We envision future research to further validate our approach, extend its applicability, and introduce HDTM based information retrieval systems to major industry leaders and organizations. We provide our implementation details, including cluster seeds and model parameters, so that others can replicate our results and build upon our work in the following repository: https://github.com/ShahidN/UDDT. In the future, we plan to open-source our model and distributed processing code, making HDTM freely available for academic and industry use. We believe this will enable a broader collaboration and contribution, ultimately driving the advancement in information retrieval and retrieval-facilitated information navigation across the research community. Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving a total of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair. The findings show that suppression of both prompt and non-prompt mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, at an extent comparable to that found in previous 2.76 TeV collisions. The study also found that suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons does not vary by rapidity but decreases slightly at high transverse momentum levels above 25 GeV/$c$ when compared to lower momentum levels. The study found little change in the J/$\psi$ yield structure in the rapidity and transverse momentum distributions in lead-lead collisions, suggesting a uniform effect of the hot and dense medium on the collision. The nuclear modification factors were found to be greater for $\psi$(2S) mesons than J/$\psi$ mesons, representing a gap of about 10% in transverse momentum and about 5% in rapidity, indicating that the $\psi$(2S) meson is more susceptible to the effects of the hot and dense medium in lead-lead collisions. We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings. 
Next, following in the footsteps of Hyland et al. and Abramsky et al., we construct a topological category from the metric spaces, enable subobjects to be represented as continuous logic predicates, and establish a connection between this category's structure and continuous logic. 
In particular, we show that the composition of relations corresponds to the composition of subobjects, relation implications correspond to the preorder of subobjects, and relation summations correspond to the topology-generated finite join of subobjects. 
Furthermore, we demonstrate an analogy between the hyperdoctrine framework and categorical logic framework for continuous logic that both Hyland et al. and we have developed. 
Ultimately, we show that the framework simplifies certain proofs related to the framework's compactness theorem, basing these proofs on the properties of complete metric spaces. 
In conclusion, the proposed structure serves as a rigorous foundation for continuous logic, enabling a combination of the frameworks for continuous and continuous logic. 
In particular, we show that the framework for continuous logic can be embedded in the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic through a monotone structure-preserving mapping. 
Furthermore, we show that the framework for continuous logic and continuous logic are equivalent as hyperdoctrine frameworks through a certain type of mapping. 
In particular, this type of mapping, which we call a correspondence, must be invertible and bijective, must preserve composition, and must preserve monotone mappings. 
In addition to these results, we show that the framework for continuous logic and continuous logic are equivalent as hyperdoctrine frameworks through a certain type of mapping. 
In particular, this type of mapping, which we call a correspondence, must be invertible and bijective, must preserve composition, and must preserve monotone mappings. 
In addition to these results, we define an analogue to a topological category for relations and show that it provides a structure for continuous logic that is equivalent to the framework for continuous logic provided by Hyland et al. 
In particular, this category for relations and the framework for continuous logic provided by Hyland et al. are equivalent as hyperdoctrine frameworks through a certain type of mapping.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up. Our method has been
verified through testing the Linux kernel's source code and demonstrating
comparable results to existing methods (up to 2x performance improvement) with a
subsequent increase in system scale. Additionally, we introduce a novel approach
for determining singular values, accelerating the decomposition process. Our
work aims to assist software testers and developers in making informed decisions
regarding which parts of a system require retesting when implementing changes.

These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Finally, the accuracy of the model was validated through the incorporation of patient demographics and medical history, revealing that the technique is resilient to imbalances in the dataset. Our method demonstrates superior performance over conventional methods such as Logistic Regression, Random Forests, and Neural Networks in predicting suicidal ideation. The distinctive response characteristic of a topological insulator manifests as a nonlinear magnetoelectric effect, whose field-theoretical properties and computational models are explored. This contrasts with another phenomenon where a magnetoelectric interaction traps a charge equal to $\pm e/2$ upon exposure to a magnetic monopole, commonly referred to as the Witten effect. The time-reversal symmetry being explicitly violated, as in the case of a Zeeman field influencing the internal system, allows for a magnetoelectric interaction to induce a Witten effect as well as a quantized transverse current in a topological insulator at finite chemical potential. Such properties are found in various topological insulator models such as the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger and Rashba models on a sphere and have been found to possess a stable position on a torus as well, displaying a robust behavior. Furthermore, the found characteristics are found to be valid for both real and imaginary magnetoelectric coupling. Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, when discrepancies arise between expert and agent domains due to varying dynamics, perspectives, or morphologies, imitation tasks become increasingly difficult.  This paper proposes a new framework that establishes correspondences across disparate domains using only unaligned trajectories containing states from the expert domain.  The framework leverages cycle-consistency constraints in both the state space and a domain-agnostic latent space to facilitate this correspondence.  Additionally, it ensures temporal alignment using a normalized position estimator.  Once the correspondence is established, the learned demonstrations can be directly transferred and applied to the target domain, empowering imitation.  The approach is demonstrated to be effective across a diverse range of complex domains.  The proposed method is dubbed Cross-Domain Imitation from Observations, or CDIFO for short.  CDIFO relies on an automatic encoder that extracts domain-independent features, alongside a discriminator that compares the behavior of the expert and the agent.  The agent then competes with the expert's behavior in the target domain.  CDIFO's efficacy is confirmed through experiments on diverse challenging domains such as diverse robot pusher domains, latent motor skill sharing, and navigation in various domain scenarios.  CDIFO is compared against prior art, specifically Behavioral Cloning (BC) and DeepMind Hackathon Approach (DMHA), revealing itself to be the most effective method in most of these domains.  The approach is not perfect, however, as it struggles in domains that involve changes to the goal or the state space.  CDIFO lacks robustness in these goal-changing domains, while also being outperformed by DMHA in state-space changing domains.  CDIFO's source code is freely available for anyone to use. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  Therefore, providing offenders with mental health treatment as part of their sentence appears to be a cost-efficient investment for reducing crime rates both for the individual and society.  Additionally, it may also improve the offender's mental health.  Complementary analyses of an alternative dataset also yield similar outcomes, confirming the reliability of these findings.  Ultimately, making mental health treatment as part of probation the standard practice could lead to considerable social and economic benefits for all parties involved.  The research also highlights potential limitations and difficulties in accessing treatment which could impact its effectiveness, suggesting the importance of addressing these issues in the future.  Furthermore, it also reveals the value of long-term treatment which could decrease crime rates, suggesting the importance of a lifetime of care and support.  The research also highlights potential drawbacks and challenges of which judges should be aware, suggesting the need for individualized assessment and varying the length and type of sentence based on unique Offender circumstances.  The data also reveals the importance of preserving connections between Offender and community, suggesting the importance of a sentence that promotes relationships rather than incarceration.  The research also emphasizes the valuable role probation officers play in reducing crime and improving mental health, highlighting their position and role within the justice system. Specifically, state-of-the-art deep learning architectures were applied to establish unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal verification systems which were compared under optimal and impaired conditions. Moreover, a comparison of fusion methods using simple score aggregation and soft attention techniques was also conducted. Experimental results obtained on the SpeakingFaces dataset showed that the addition of thermal images to auditory and visual data significantly enhanced verification accuracy across all noise levels. Additionally, a novel approach utilizing soft attention for feature fusion was observed to yield superior performance relative to basic score aggregation methods. Note that this dataset features a limited quantity of thermal images; consequently, the obtained improvements are anticipated to be more pronounced with larger, high-resolution thermal image datasets. This research may serve as a benchmark for evaluating person verification systems using thermal images in future studies. Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon the one-sided differential privacy framework by accounting for inter-record dependencies. Furthermore, the paper quantifies total privacy breaches when the adversary possesses record interdependence information, as well as demonstrates the creation of an optimization problem for an efficient trade-off between utility and privacy. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed technique is illustrated through numerical simulations using authentic building management system data. Results show that the proposed mechanism, tailored to handle inter-record dependencies, can yield substantial improvements in utility while mitigating significant privacy losses. Moreover, the findings suggest that inter-record dependencies can increase privacy breaches by as much as 27.35%. These outcomes provide valuable insights to data governors for making informed decisions about the level of protection needed for their data records. Lastly, the proposed mechanism and its accompanying methods can be adapted for applications in any setting that deals with dependent data records. These adaptations can facilitate novel applications in various fields such as engineering, medicine, and computer science that were not mentioned here due to space constraints. Ultimately, the proposed mechanism and its underlying methods can be utilized in numerous data privacy applications that were not discussed here due to space constraints but hold promising potential. These applications include dependently private shortest path search and other data-sensitive applications in geography information systems, for instance. Additional information can be found in the document that accompanies this paper. Key techniques used in this research include the development of a dependence-aware private entropy function, a dependence-aware privacy breach metric, and an innovative utility-gaining mechanism inspired by the trust region method. These techniques were employed within a novel framework known as the Trust Region Differential Privacy (TRDP) framework, which provides a novel approach to private data analysis using trust region optimization. TRDP differs from previous differential privacy frameworks in that it accounts for the dependence among data records and utilizes trust region optimization to provide a precise bound on privacy breaches. Furthermore, the effectiveness of TRDP is illustrated through its application in various data privacy problems, such as private classification and entropy search, using authentic building management system data. These substructures may have connections to the formation of planets themselves.
Our investigation into the AS 209 gas substructures employed thermochemical modeling using RAC2D and precise observations from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales project.
Our observations of C$^{18}$O J=2-1 revealed a distinct trough at 88 au that overlapped with the areas of several millimeter dust continuum emission gaps.
We observed that CO column density could be linked to surface-density fluctuations or chemical alterations, while C$_2$H column density was tied to changes in the C/O ratio rather than surface density changes in gas.
However, our models require the presence of a massive planet (with a mass similar to that of Jupiter) to explain the depth and width of the C$^{18}$O trough at 88 au.
We discovered that the C/O ratio in the AS 209 disk increased in regions affected by the CO gap and that this increase was consistent with the idea that the planet's influence caused gas surface density to drop, resulting in a reduction of oxygen that is then taken up by the forming planet.
Our findings suggest that the planet in the AS 209 system could very well be responsible for the CO gap it exhibits. 
We propose that future observations at higher angular resolutions could directly observe the planet itself.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address these limitations, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we fine-tune VICTOR on a wide range of fashion visuals. We expand upon the Polyvore outfit benchmark, introducing a dataset dubbed Polyvore-MISFITs comprising imperfectly matched outfits, to train and test our proposed model. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our proposed VICTOR outperforms or matches state-of-the-art performance on the Polyvore dataset while achieving an impressive 88% reduction in computational requirements, striking an ideal balance between accuracy and efficiency. We publicly release the VICTOR implementation at https://github.com/stevejpapad/Visual-InCompatibility-Transformer. Moreover, the developed model has been deployed on a live app, making it available for end-users to interact with at https://outfitgrader.com. Additional details on our method, along with a demonstration video, are available at https://stevejpapad.com/victor. (This work was done while the lead author was a research intern at Google Research, Seattle.)

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, and attributes this finding to the broader concept of 'economic irreversibility,' illustrating its analogy to the principles of thermodynamics. A fundamental inequality provides a framework for the implementation of such measures. A novel theoretical approach underlying this methodology contributes to the body of econophysics research. Specifically, our study aligns with the economic concept of sunk costs, where past investments become irrelevant to informed decision-making, and the decision to implement control measures should prioritize future health and economic gains. Prior investments in the wrong sectors, including those that may have exacerbated the pandemic, should not influence the present decision to implement control measures. Similarly, the decision to implement such measures should not depend on past mistakes but rather on the need to protect public health and revitalize the economy in the face of an unprecedented crisis. In line with this view, our findings show that timely moderate measures remain effective even when the decision to implement control measures comes after the pandemic has spread. Furthermore, the algorithm developed in this research allows for the determination of the optimal duration and intensity of control measures necessary to stabilize the economy and control the outbreak. A novel method is introduced for attribute selection in multi-attribute decision-making (MADM), where the weights of attributes are dynamically assigned according to the significance of their impact on public health and economic losses. This methodology is then applied to analyze the effectiveness of different policies during the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States. Experimental validation of our model against real-world data demonstrates its accuracy and demonstrates that our theoretical approach can inform and improve pandemic control decision-making. A broader understanding of 'economic irreversibility' offers a new framework for measuring the effectiveness of countermeasures and could be applied to analyzing the impact of policies governing natural disasters, which share similarities with the principles of thermodynamics. This research contributes to the body of econophysics research and offers a new theoretical approach for understanding the trade-off between public health and economic losses during emergencies. Specifically, our study illustrates how the principles of thermodynamics can be applied to pandemic control and economic analysis, and a novel algorithm based on this theory is used to analyze the effectiveness of policies during the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States. Moreover, our findings highlight the need for informed decision-making that prioritizes public health and economic recovery over past investments and losses. This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Experiments have demonstrated that at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa, the material's anomalous Hall effect is entirely eliminated. The pressure-dependent magnetization study revealed that as pressure increased, Mn$_3$Sn shifted from a conventional antiferromagnetic ground state to a helical state, where a required characteristic for the anomalous Hall effect is absent. X-ray diffraction experiments indicate that this phenomenon is not caused by structural changes within the material. The investigation further reveals that when Mn$_3$Sn enters the helical state, its in-plane magnetization exhibits unique temperature dependencies, corroborating the theoretical predictions of spiral magnetism's impact on the material's anomalous Hall effect. This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary. Our investigation also provides a detailed characterization of the asymptotic behavior of the eigenvalue as $r$ approaches $0$ or becomes very large. These findings hold broader implications for the general $m$-dimensional ball scenario. Our discussion includes an exploration of the geometric and analytical effects of the Steklov boundary condition on the eigenvalue. We rely on a combination of analytical and geometric approaches, particularly singular perturbation theory, to understand the influence of both $r$ and $\beta$ on the eigenvalue. The primary tool employed is the interface to perturbation theory provided by the Klimentovich-Zaslavskii frequency spectrum, a key concept in Hamiltonian dynamics. Our work includes a detailed proof that the large-scale behavior of the Steklov eigenvalue is equivalent to the leading zero of the Steklov eigenfunction's Fourier expansion, a property known as the "zero frequency" phenomenon. We demonstrate the asymptotic freedom of the Robin eigenvalue as the radius of the system's enclosed ball becomes very large. Our analysis reveals new insights into the spectrum of the Steklov and Robin operators, particularly regarding the embedding of their spectra into the spectrum of the identity operator. We show the existence of a critical value of the Robin parameter $\beta_0$ such that the Robin eigenvalue exhibits different behaviors to the left and right of this value. We also include a broader theorem regarding the embedding of the spectrum of the Steklov operator into the spectrum of the identity operator, specifically highlighting the influence of geometric and analytic considerations on the embedding of the spectrum. Our discussion includes a discussion on how the Steklov eigenvalue changes as a perfect square of the linear size of the system's enclosed ball, a property known as the "linear size" phenomenon. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large datasets typical of this domain to a manageable size, and second, a hypergraph learning framework is established to recover the real-world hypergraph structure while accounting for its inherently imperfect projections. Our method is rigorously evaluated on two domain-specific datasets, where its effectiveness is assessed in terms of accuracy, preprocessing efficiency, and the impact of dataset size. Our results indicate that supervised hypergraph reconstruction surpasses baseline graph-based methods in domain-specific knowledge incorporation and generalization across different dataset scales. Notably, a notable improvement is seen in accuracy when the dataset size is increased. With further research, this technique could be applied to other domains as well. It is now made available on GitHub: https://github.com/hjiao32/SURH.

After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities in daily returns among cryptocurrencies and their comparators as far back as 2016. Finally, our investigation involved assessing whether cumulative errors in predicting cryptocurrency prices would fall within the predicted bounds as dictated by the Black-Scholes model when considering stable relationships with comparators' daily returns, thereby not refuting the efficient market hypothesis. A notable discovery was that our study is the first to demonstrate price stability in cryptocurrencies, and our analysis is an essential foundation for further research in this area. Moreover, our research has practical implications that can benefit investors and businesses operating in the field of cryptocurrencies. By integrating analytical methods including field theory, probability and integrability, we resolve the large deviation issue of the KPZ equation at early time periods. Expanding the existing weak noise theory, which reformulates large deviations into a nonlinear hydrodynamics problem, we reveal its complete solvability through a link with the integrability of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Employing the inverse scattering technique and a newly developed Fredholm determinant framework, we arrive at exact solutions that depend on the specific initial conditions of the KPZ equation, allowing for further generalization to other initial conditions. Our breakthrough offers a theoretical model with perfect correlations, providing a complete solution to the weak noise regime for any KPZ initial condition. The findings can also be extended to address issues in certain spin glass models and their underlying mathematical structures. The work may also pave the way for further generalizations in other well-known probability theories such as first-passage-time distributions and Distributions Dependent on Multiple Parameters. The exact large deviation results we obtain could be useful in understanding the entropic properties of the KPZ equation, while its validation against numerical and experimental findings remains a subject of ongoing research. The methods and approaches developed here may have applications in other areas of theoretical physics, such as the TASEP model and their underlying integrable structures. Additionally, we explore the broad implications of our work, connecting the underlying hydrodynamic heights with the underlying helical waves of the Zakharov-Shabat system through the inverse scattering technique. The depth of this connection awaits further understanding and analysis in the fields of integrability, hydrodynamics and probability, particularly in generalizing the weak noise theory to address higher eigenvalues and frequency modes. The key to resolving the nonlinear hydrodynamic problem also holds promise in addressing questions related to disorder, randomness and the underlying probabilistic structures that arise in these systems. In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2-10 nm wavelength, yielding high peak powers of hundreds of megawatts, with a potential for delivering over a thousand pulses per second to enable groundbreaking attosecond science applications. Initial results are presented along with proposals for further improvement, including the use of a undulator taper with a slowly changing period to extend pulse durations to multiple femtoseconds. This could enable the production of pulses within a few hundred extreme ultraviolet frequencies, thirty times longer than current attosecond pulses produced at the same facility. This extension would greatly increase the potential for revolutionary scientific breakthroughs in biology, chemistry, and materials science by enabling the exploration of individual events over longer time spans. Furthermore, this concept can be applied to generate long pulse durations in the water window, enabling novel applications in biological and surface physics. Additionally, this technique holds vast potential for generating high-repetition-rate attosecond pulses in the water window, a capability essential for the development of a fourth-generation light source at the European XFEL. This proposal has been discussed and agreed upon by the FEL community and is currently being implemented at the FLASH facility for initial experimental evaluation. A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points. The applicability of both approximations is similar but not identical, with the physical option being more widely applicable, especially near critical levels, and demonstrating a clear, distinct inner region behavior characterized by quasi-stationary and quasi-steady characteristics regardless of any negative or zero effective vertical diffusion value. Furthermore, this approximation shows promise in the context of deep-water waves, suggesting an exciting research avenue for theoretical modeling and further study in this area. An interesting observation is the presence of two distinct turning points in the model, distinguishing between upper and lower boundaries of velocity perturbance solutions, with solutions exhibiting a "sandwich-like" structure within the interior region of the water column. In contrast, the geometrical approximation yields solutions that vary predictably in response to changes in tuning and detuning parameters but exhibit a more nuanced "heterogeneous' structure within the water column due to the influence of turbulence. An in-depth numerical example, specifically a model based on the Atlantic Ocean's hydrology, reveals how the effective parameters of viscosity and diffusivity interact and modulate baroclinic wave modes, including their amplitude and spatial distribution. In particular, when the effective viscosity and diffusivity parameters are relatively small, these geometrical approximations show a high degree of accuracy in predicting baroclinic wave characteristics compared to more complex, detailed models of the system. However, as the viscosity and diffusivity parameters increase, the accuracy of these geometrical approximations decreases, especially in terms of predicting quasi-stationary and quasi-steady characteristics within the inner region of the water column. An associated proof by contradiction demonstrates that the effective parameters of turbulence must be such that they avoid a situation in which geometrical approximations predict a singular behavior within the water column, leading to potentially important theoretical outcomes in the area of geophysical fluid dynamics. Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and
allowed for the identification of biased districting plans. The associated code can
be found on the repository https://github.com/danielabdelnaseer/Districting-Analysis. We
also provide a report with detailed findings: https://danielabdelnaseer.github.io/Districting-Analysis/. This work was presented at Conference on Artificial General Intelligence, 2021.
