In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources. The energy emitted from the accretion process initially manifests as brief, high-frequency bursts at each close approach, but eventually, the surrounding disc becomes a sustained source of radiation, emitting electromagnetic and gravitational waves in a continuous pattern. We investigated the effects of varying white dwarf mass, radius, and composition (for which we calculated specific bounds), as well as black hole mass, spanning from stellar mass to supermassive sizes. Our analysis indicates a potential correlation between our simulated X-ray source patterns and recently observed aurorae in SS Cyg and other white dwarfs, and we predict Gravitational Waves will be detectable for close black hole-white dwarf binaries with a distance of no further than 0.02 parsecs. Moreover, for our simulated white dwarf model, we discovered that radiation spectra exhibit patterns of harmonic relationships, and our estimation of GW energy emission suggests a significant portion could be observable by LIGO, especially for our lowest frequency range predictions. Our findings provide a foundation for further research into the electromagnetic and gravitational radiation emitted by such binary systems, and we propose that our models could be a first step in understanding the recently discovered X-ray sources and the processes behind them. Additionally, our work indicates that for our simulated white dwarf model, we might be able to see an increase in black hole mass due to matter accumulation, a phenomenon with notable implications for our understanding of mass transfer in such binary systems. To further explore our findings and refine our predictions, we recommend future research using more advanced hydrodynamic models that could offer greater clarity on the processes behind electromagnetic and gravitational radiation emission. Furthermore, we envision future studies incorporating more sophisticated white dwarf models that might yield even more accurate and diverse predictions for radiation patterns and their underlying physical mechanisms. The quantum hydrodynamic model we employed provides a preliminary understanding of radiation emission in such binary systems, and we expect future research to build upon our results, particularly if future observations match our theoretical predictions for radiation patterns. Hebbian theory aims to explain how brain cells modify their responses to stimuli, ultimately leading to the ability to learn. A notable aspect of Hebbian theory is the idea that cells sharing relevant information can strengthen their connection. This concept has inspired the development of various artificial neural networks used for machine learning. However, achieving true biological plausibility in artificial neural networks requires considering the underlying chemical properties of real neurons. In this research, we use a simple, chemically realistic model to demonstrate how a Hebbian learning mechanism can be implemented using a programming language called DNAswell. This model uses a unique DNA encoding method and a digital droplet system for analysis. A simulation showing the learning process with two input stimuli and associated output patterns is also presented. Additionally, the digital droplet system was used to test the learning model in a real-world laboratory setting. Our results confirm that the model can learn and adjust to the given input patterns. Furthermore, this study highlights the practical application of using digital droplets as a laboratory tool for testing DNA-programmed models. We, however, leverage limited, domain-specific labels and incorporate various contextualized neural networks to educate the model, which in turn, improves its performance on data-hungry tasks. Our proposed approach innovates on three fronts: initializing with contextualized embeddings, enhancing with contextualized intermediate representations, and augmenting with contextualized tagging. Experimental results across multiple languages show that this method outperforms conventional self-training and establishes a reliable baseline for data-hungry parsing tasks. Moreover, we improve BERT-dependent parsing models by initializing their embeddings with BERT and enhancing their intermediate representations with ELMo. Notably, this technique achieves the highest possible performance with our limited annotations. A series of analyses using various evaluation metrics demonstrate the success of this method. Though it may seem counterintuitive that more advanced models result in better performance with limited annotations, our results show that this technique can result in significantly better output with fewer annotations than simpler models. Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (polynomial time) complexity, having demonstrated the capability to be contained within PTIME and yet unseparated from it. A prominent challenge lies in resolving the isomorphism problem for unordered Cai-Furer-Immerman graphs, known as the CFI-query, which has remained undefined within CPT despite being classified as a PTIME decision problem. A significant development has been achieved in understanding CPT's expressive power in addressing this issue by formulating a partial characterisation of solvable instances based on symmetric XOR-circuits for these specific graph types: In essence, for the CFI-query to be defined within a given graph class via a CPT-definition, each XOR-circuit component in the gradient approximation (a concept introduced by Creignou and Zarba in 2005) must be recognisable by a symmetric circuit within the considered graph class. This discovery has led to a refinement of the initial CPT-definition by introducing the concept of 'S-cpt': a decision procedure that, unlike standard CPT, allows itself to reference parameters (part of the input data), yet only does so in a non-essential manner (can be adapted to function without them). Consequently, it has been established that S-cpt defines a containment relationship with CPT. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that under specific assumptions (particularly the presence of a particular type of structures known as 'finite clausal propagators' introduced by Zarba in 2005), the CFI-query can be resolved through an adaptive decision procedure that operates within S-cpt and thereby also CPT. Nonetheless, a query remains: Can we resolve the CFI-query within S-cpt (and consequently CPT) without relying on such assumptions? If not, a further assumption would need to be made: Either the CPT approach is inherently incapable of deciding the CFI-query, in which case it would confirm a long-standing conjecture suggesting its containment within PTIME without an equivalent decision problem, or the CFI-query could be shown non-decidable in PTIME, which would address a related open issue in complexity theory. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple from a given set of probabilities as simply 'p'. Our main findings are presented in two theorems. Firstly, the lower bound for p when n is equal to 4 is greater than or equal to 0.81, and this lower bound increases as 'n' approaches infinity. Secondly, the entire range of possible p is contained within the range [0.5, 1) when n is equal to 5, and this range narrows as 'n' approaches infinity, where it approaches 0.75 from above. Our generated data supports our conclusions. We then proposed an alternative framework for measuring 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' probability, and demonstrated that as 'n' approaches infinity, the entire range of possible p converges to 0.75. Our new framework yields more accurate results, particularly for larger 'n', and we can precisely calculate the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that is 'nontransitive'. Our work provides a thorough examination of 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' probability, and we utilize numerical methods to validate our theorems and findings. Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when signals are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have involved the use of deep learning, which has significantly improved signal quality and diagnostic accuracy, far exceeding previous limitations. A novel deep learning approach is being developed using a Tiramisu autoencoder to effectively filter out motion artifact and make ECG signals more interpretable even during high-impact motion. By achieving accurate denoising and IBI estimation, this approach accelerates diagnostic processes and achieves better results. Notably, our technique has successfully estimated IBIs from ECG signals with signal-to-noise ratios of up to -30 decibels and achieved average root mean square error of 13 milliseconds. Moreover, the percentage error of IBI estimates remains under 8%, surpassing existing benchmarks. As such, this technique has great potential for use in devices and applications involving remote health monitoring and wearable devices. Experimental findings confirm that this approach remains robust and reliable across various signal lengths. Furthermore, the effects of device sampling rates and P-Q interval on IBI estimation accuracy are also examined. Our findings suggest that this deep learning model produces the most accurate results compared to traditional methods, including the popular Fourier and wavelet techniques, as well as other deep learning models, including LSTM and ResNet. A comparative study of error rates from these techniques shows a significant advantage of our approach, demonstrating significantly lower error rates and a more suitable distribution of IBI estimates. Although deep learning models like LSTM exhibit good performance, they are hindered by poor data efficiency, rendering them less suitable for use in devices with limited power resources. In contrast, the proposed Tiramisu model achieves excellent trade-off between accuracy and data efficiency, making it the best choice for use in devices with limited power resources. This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations across a range of subjects. The second task, called EyeRescue, centers on accurately tracking and predicting human eye dynamics given a pair of images. Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming in terms of data labeling, development time, and expertise. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modifications, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages and discovered that it surpasses the performance of numerous strong baselines while matching or even exceeding state-of-the-art results obtained through more resource-intensive and complicated methods. Moreover, our framework successfully captures rich, semantically significant representations across languages despite the absence of direct supervision. As a result, it's an accessible and adaptable solution for building neural models in underserved languages and a valuable tool for understanding cross-lingual knowledge transfer. A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing.

We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, and this correspondence serves as the foundation for an in-depth analysis of their invariant measures. Through initial investigation, we confirm the existence of two distinct ergodic measures with maximal entropy for these generalized baker maps, and also reveal the underlying cause for the failure of certain entropy-based approaches. Additionally, our study provides a new mathematical framework for understanding unstable dimension variability, and offers a method for numerically approximating ergodic measures for these generalized baker maps. We further explore how the properties of these ergodic measures change as a critical parameter is adjusted, and in doing so, we gain insight into the dynamic system and its singularities. This work has potential applications in various fields such as communication, linguistics, and linguistically motivated generative music to name a few, and can also contribute to the study of one-dimensional maps with "eyes" as well as multidimensional systems with inherent encoding difficulties. Lastly, our findings also shed light on the underlying mechanism for the phenomenon of approachability observed in certain one-dimensional systems. A detailed numerical investigation into these ergodic measures was conducted using a novel algorithm for approximating ergodic measures that we introduced, and this study has been applied to a range of cases characterized by different parameters. The associated ergodic metric spaces, which are naturally extended from their 2D and 3D analogs, also provide a valuable tool for understanding the dynamic behavior of one-dimensional systems with inherent encoding difficulties. To close this introduction, we note that while the generalized baker map was initially developed as a model for complex systems, our study has uncovered its deep connections with various domains including languages, music, and communication, and this dual nature is likely to influence future research in these fields. Moreover, the techniques and methods developed in this work also have potential applications in these knowledge domains. The associated software and additional information are available at https://github.com/emilien-schwarz/heterochaos-baker-map. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome these challenges, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of incorporating prior knowledge through PDCNN, specifically in modeling frequency-dependent signal components. Additionally, the cascaded network design is found to be superior to stacked dilated convolution networks in generating signal components up to 640 samples ahead. Synthetic and interleave-resampled training data are employed to rectify frequency component alignment issues and improve model performance. Our experiments confirm the superiority of QPNet over WN and demosaicing models in terms of mean absolute error in frequency domain, particularly for frequencies up to 250 Hz. Furthermore, the proposed model exhibits a significant reduction in its parameter count, at approximately one-twentieth the size of WN, while still achieving comparable log likelihood values. Overall, our results demonstrate the potential of QPNet, a lightweight, log-scale periodic component-based WaveNet, to serve as a strong baseline in raw waveform generation, particularly in modeling quasi-periodic signals. Future work will involve expanding the model to enable waveform sampling rates beyond 16 kHz. Given the model's current limitations in generating low-frequency components, future research will also focus on addressing this issue. Another potential area of improvement is the incorporation of non-autoregressive priors using, for example, VAE-based methods to enhance the model's sampling efficiency. We anticipate these advancements enhancing the proposed model even further. Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as numerous different styles are applicable to these operations. Current machine learning-based methods typically disregard this stylistic variability in their pursuit of identifying a unique solution. Conversely, our research aims to harness style-specific information, extracting it from paired images to condense into a two or three-dimensional vector, resulting in a more efficient and understandable framework for style-based image editing. By representing the relationship between global color tones across paired images as a flow conditioned on the input colors, our method proves superior to other low-dimensional encoding techniques, ultimately facilitating the development of an innovative gradient domain-based optimization strategy for inverse color grading. This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmosphere's flow patterns and snowflake trajectories in real time. A state-of-the-art, high-resolution imaging system is utilized to capture snowflakes in motion, mapping the flow patterns and detecting vortex formations above the ground. Concurrently, a high-resolution camera is employed to track individual snowflakes in a smaller sample area within the main field of view, revealing the connection between atmospheric turbulence and snowflake settling patterns. Our research reveals that as snowflakes interact with turbulence at critical velocities, their falling speed is greatly increased, a phenomenon not seen in prior studies. Images captured within the flow patterns show that snowflakes tend to concentrate near the base of vortex formations, moving preferentially downwards. These findings provide significant insights into the processes governing snow deposition patterns, particularly during preferential sweeping events, and could be applied to modeling snowdrifts and ice formation in atmospheric water vapor. Understanding these interactions is essential for comprehending glacier calculus and the development of geophysical models. Additionally, our research highlights the importance of considering turbulence-sedimentation interactions in addition to conventional settling velocities. This knowledge could be applied beyond geological sciences, expanding into technological applications such as coating development and ice formation control. Ongoing research includes analyzing vortex properties and symmetry to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms. This knowledge could further contribute to advancing snow physics research and various related engineering fields. Moreover, our work serves as a foundation for future studies, encouraging researchers to continue exploring atmospheric snow physics and its underlying mechanics. By conducting additional analyses, we aim to elucidate the intrinsic processes governing atmospheric snow deposition. To facilitate this, we have made our processing techniques and code available for other researchers, including raw data, metadata, and analysis scripts, to promote open research practices. This code has been shared on the GIPIX3D platform, a publicly accessible hub for atmospheric snow research, also housing our raw and processed data, as well as detailed research findings and metrics. We intend to expand our atmospheric snow research, extending our findings to various geographical locations, and welcome collaborative efforts from other researchers. This would involve conducting field research in diverse environments, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions, using our fundamental understanding to guide the analysis. By combining our expertise, we aim to further explore the processes governing atmospheric snow deposition and advance snow physics research. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data, such as video feeds, without the need for pre-defined parameters. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that such frameworks can be utilized to facilitate active inference. This study marks the first instance of applying active inference using deep learning techniques to a real-world navigation task involving a robotic system. While still in its initial stages, this work shows that: (a) deep active inference is feasible in practical scenarios; (b) this framework outperforms unguided robotic systems; and (c) this framework exhibits similar performance when compared to a benchmark inspired by biological principles, despite being largely unsupervised and without external guidance. Overall, this project makes significant progress towards translating the principles of active inference into a real-world context, paving the way for a deeper understanding of how animals interact with their surroundings, as well as the development of more effective robotic systems. In experimental facilities specializing in high energy physics, nuclear physics, and cosmology, the acquisition and processing of large-scale, three-dimensional scientific data poses a formidable challenge. The emergence of worldwide distributed computing networks has highlighted the significance of data compression in reducing the data volume transmitted between clusters and servers. This study presents an innovative bicephalous convolutional autoencoder (BCAE) architecture that effectively compresses the three-dimensional sparse data from the TPC detector. The VGG-like structure of the BCAE consists of a encoder with an autoencoder architecture and a decoder with a transposed VGG structure. A parameter adjustment strategy involving an decay rate and a fusion method are employed to refine the BCAE's parameter set. The proposed BCAE offers an optimal balance between compression ratio and reconstruction quality. Notably, this BCAE method outperforms existing methods, including autoencoders with various forms of activation functions, in terms of both compression ratio and total reconstruction error. Furthermore, the BCAE's reliability and generalizability are demonstrated through rigorous statistical analysis on independent test datasets. The efficacy of the BCAE is also shown in a realistic large-scale sparse data scenario resembling detector conditions. This research is expected to benefit a wide range of scientific applications, including those in particle physics and cosmology. Additionally, the findings and methods presented here can be applied to diverse scientific datasets and use cases beyond particle physics and cosmology, as they are equally applicable to other scientific fields. This research could thus enable a wide range of scientific discoveries in domains such as astrophysics and precision medicine. The source code for the proposed BCAE is openly available on GitHub. The dataset used in this research is specifically designed to mimic the characteristics of TPC detector data and is openly accessible via the following link: https://lbnl-tpc-compression.github.io/data/index.html. This dataset can also be downloaded directly from this URL. The BCAE's source code can be found at: https://lbnl-tpc-compression.github.io/bcae/index.html. A simplified model has been created to analyze the correlation between robot motion and actuation, resulting in the development of a new, adaptable robot inspired by the Pacific Lamprey. The new robot, called Trident, successfully demonstrates dynamic vertical climbing at speeds of up to 4.8 cm/s and can also move horizontally at 9 cm/s. Furthermore, its climbing strides can be 14% longer than the Pacific Lamprey's, making this innovative design a promising approach for robots navigating steep surfaces with limited support points. The work presented here represents a key progression toward robots that can easily navigate rough terrain at high speeds. A comparison of the Trident's performance with two alternative designs has shown that even with modifications tailored to improve performance, the results still fell short of the triple-fold improvement in speed that these modifications aimed to achieve. Consequently, further research is needed to bridge the gap between these robots and animals like geckos that can effortlessly climb at much lower speeds. The development of a robot that can move at least as efficiently as a Pacific Lamprey is likely to involve advanced technology such as smart materials with improved adhesion capabilities for more intricate robot designs. This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework. Due to the vast number of possible treatment combinations, a novel strategy is presented to identify a limited number of the most effective combinations. Finally, the flexibility of the framework is demonstrated through its applications to two distinct models. One model considers colon cancer-induced immune response in a therapeutic context, whereas the other assumes an anti-tumor immune response. The colon cancer-induced immune response model incorporates time-dependent probabilistic transition rates, which are shown to have a significant impact on obtaining optimal treatment combinations. Consequently, utilizing this model in a therapeutic context yields superior outcomes in comparison to the anti-tumor model. The introduced framework is herewith named COLCIM. Mathematical analysis of the COLCIM framework's well-posedness, along with theoretical guarantees for obtaining optimal treatment combinations, is provided in the appendix of this paper and can be accessed through the provided reference. The COLCIM framework's software implementation is detailed in the supplementary material provided. Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends heavily on minimizing excessive interference through effective device scheduling. Traditional scheduling methods mainly prioritize maximizing throughput and fairness without considering the age of information (AoI). Delays in updating information can render them obsolete, making AoI crucial for quality assessment. This paper presents a novel D2D link scheduling strategy using AoI as the primary metric. We develop a deep neural network to make scheduling decisions in real-time, as solving the optimal problem faces complexity obstacles. Our approach significantly improves performance in terms of better throughput, fairness, and AoI. Furthermore, it offers more stable and reliable D2D communication systems. Simulations using a matrix representation of urban infrastructure confirm our superior results. Interestingly, when solely considering throughput, our approach still yields enhanced AoI performance, revealing the interdependence of these metrics. Increasing network complexity has minimal impact on computation speed due to our efficient neural network design. Lastly, system capacity can be increased by activating only the D2D links with sufficient signal strength. This rule is incorporated into our neural scheduling system. We compare our solution with existing strategies, demonstrating superior results. Notably, our approach ensures all K-user D2D systems have at least the same signal strength, ensuring comparable performance with existing strategies for smaller networks. Our novel strategy shows promising potential for practical use in wireless D2D systems. We propose these methods for both D2D and traditional wireless communications to ensure consistency. These methods could be used by users and devices for scheduling and routing in a simple and efficient way. From an industry perspective, these methods could be implemented in devices and software for improved performance and quality. We discuss the technical details and provide answers. This study offers a useful approach for practical use. We confirm this through our results and comparisons. In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. We establish a comprehensive single-letter representation of the optimal normalized leakage in this adversarial scenario, along with a stochastic coding method that reaches this optimum. Interestingly, our analysis shows that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates are attainable by certain deterministic coding strategies, where these goals can be concurrently achieved. We expand upon the initial investigation to consider adversaries that submit multiple guesses and can tolerate a degree of sequence error. In this case, we identify tight lower and upper bounds for the more general leakage metric through the application of single-letter analysis. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates can be effectively characterized in this more general adversarial scenario as well. In addition, we prove that both the maximal leakage and compression rates can be expressed as achievable rates solely based on the confusion graph, with these goals also attainable by certain coding strategies, along with a characterization of the optimal leakage for specific cases involving adversaries that submit single guesses and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence. Specifically, we show that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates can be effectively characterized in terms of the relative entropy of the source distribution with respect to a set of equiprobable distributions, along with a characterization of the optimal leakage for specific cases involving adversaries that submit multiple guesses and can tolerate a degree of sequence error. Specifically, we show that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates can be effectively characterized in terms of the conditional entropy of the source with respect to a set of postulated prior knowledge, along with a characterization of the optimal leakage for specific cases involving adversaries that submit single guesses and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence. The proposed technique leads to considerable reductions in circuit access frequency, typically the costliest QAOA component. The q-function has connections to both the instantaneous advantage rate function and the Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we observe that they can be connected to AMESA, especially in the case where the Gibbs measure density is known. Lastly, we note that our continuous-time q-learning framework offers a theoretical understanding of past experiences in reinforcement learning. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a novel key point localization model, vertebrae center activation maps are generated, which are then adjusted along the spine's central axis to produce optimized activation maps that can be aggregated into 1-dimensional activation signals. Building upon this, an anatomically-constrained optimization module is integrated to jointly determine the optimal positions of the vertebrae. The optimization is performed under a flexible constraint that ensures the distance between vertebrae and a rigid constraint that maintains consecutive vertebrae indices. Upon being evaluated using a well-established public dataset consisting of 302 CT images characterized by significant spinal pathologies, the proposed method achieved the highest identification accuracy of 97.6% and surpassed the best comparable approach, which had an identification accuracy of 94.8%, by significantly reducing the relative error. The proposed method is further validated by clinical experts who verified its correctness for all test images. The study concludes that the developed method demonstrates superior accuracy and resilience in the presence of various spine disorders and imaging issues. The researchers further examined the influence of different imaging conditions on vertebrae localization and identification, which led to the development of an adaptive optimization module that enhances the method's robustness. The work contributes positively by shedding light on specific imaging conditions that could impact deep learning-based methods and offering a potentially effective solution. Furthermore, the method is an advanced example of deep spine analysis models, which have generally focused on single specific challenges (e.g., center detection or segmentation) but have not thoroughly investigated the vertebrae localization and identification task. I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical writing, as his mathematical colleagues were too preoccupied with advancing scientific work to bother doing the same. Ultimately, it is suggested that Galileo's scientific legacy was amplified due to his unique ability to connect scientific ideas with broader philosophical themes, rather than despite any shortcomings he might have had. Historians of science should reevaluate the extent to which Galileo's human shortcomings influenced his scientific accomplishments and maintain an accurate picture of how scientific progress often involves the sustained efforts of many individuals over time. Furthermore, it is observed that Galileo's experience offers a relevant lesson for contemporary scientists, who are encouraged to pursue their careers in science, even in fields they may not excel in academically, as demonstrated by Galileo's example. The conversation surrounding science, which occurs when individuals without extensive training in the field can engage with it through everyday experiences and observations, is another vital component of scientific progress that Galileo effectively facilitated and played a crucial role in shaping the scientific revolution. The intersection between science and philosophy, as well as the distinct roles they play in understanding the world, is another important theme that Galileo's story can illustrate and provide insight into. The relationship between these disciplines, as well as how Galileo's unique experiences as a scientist-philosopher can educate contemporary discussions on the topic, is explored in the present work. Lastly, it is noted that Galileo's tale offers an important historical lesson on how to approach and engage with scientific ideas, particularly for those without a strong academic background in mathematics and science, as well as how these ideas can become accessible to a broader audience, as was the case with Galileo's contributions to promoting a more active role for the telescope in scientific inquiry and his efforts to promote experimentation and observation over purely mathematical investigations. The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables more efficient computation. The comparative study involves three scenarios: the MHD-AEPIC model, MHD simulations paired with fixed embedded PIC regions, and full PIC simulations. The examination of reconnection rates, magnetic island spacings, and ion dynamics within these scenarios indicates good agreement among them, thus validating the MHD-AEPIC model as a reliable and computationally economical tool for studying certain aspects of magnetic reconnection. Additionally, this model appears to produce distinct outcomes compared to MHD models that neglect magnetic field fluctuations, especially regarding the spatial distribution of currents and heat signatures. These results suggest that magnetic field fluctuations play a crucial role in determining these physical properties. Furthermore, the MHD-AEPIC model is shown to produce comparable results to full PIC simulations in terms of reconnection rates and magnetic island spacings, thus highlighting its potential applications in studying various reconnection phenomena in diverse astrophysical and space plasma settings. These applications may involve identifying key factors influencing reconnection rates and understanding how they compare to kinetic models. Additionally, the study delves into the inherent characteristics of the model, particularly the continuous adaptation of the PIC region in response to changing plasma conditions, and demonstrates that these adaptations result in the accurate reproduction of distinctive heat signatures associated with magnetic reconnection. In conclusion, this comprehensive research not only contributes to our understanding of magnetic reconnection but also generates new knowledge about the technical aspects of utilizing the MHD-AEPIC model, thus paving the way for utilizing this efficient and adaptable tool to investigate various intricate plasma phenomena. These may include utilizing it to investigate reconnection in quasi-parallel magnetic configurations rather than head-on reconnection. Additionally, the study suggests that employing the MHD-AEPIC model could lead to novel breakthroughs in understanding reconnection processes in Astrophysics and space plasmas. These efforts may involve utilizing it to investigate reconnection in reconnection layers, as well as one- and two-dimensional reconnection scenarios that better reflect natural plasma environments. These research endeavors could help clarify how reconnection processes evolve under different plasma conditions and thereby advance our understanding of reconnection cascade, reconnection rates, and plasma turbulence.
